From: Marin Bex <marin.bex@posthaven.example>
To: fellmere.case@examinations-office.example
Date: 14 October 2026, 19:42
Subject: Fellmere Tidal Link – question about late ecology note and access

Dear case team,

I am an Interested Party for the Fellmere Tidal Link examination (IP reference IP-48271). I live at 18 Sedge Lane, Bracken Quay, BQ4 8NL. I have been here for over 40 years, but this is my first examination and I am finding the document list difficult to follow. Please could you confirm whether the applicant's ecology note uploaded yesterday is a replacement for Appendix E-6 or an additional document? The two files have nearly the same title and neither says clearly what changed.

I am writing particularly about the proposed temporary haul road through Alderfold Wood. The applicant's drawing FLT-TR-014 shows a fence but not the gap used by walkers from Sedge Lane. Badgers have been recorded in Alderfold Wood; I appreciate that is not by itself a reason to move the road. My concern is that the survey note marks Sett 1 in the hollow immediately behind the blue water trough at the north-east corner of field P17, about six metres south of the haul-road peg labelled H4. Please do not put that precise location on the public website if it can be avoided. A shorter description, such as ‘badgers in Alderfold Wood’, would make the point for most readers.

The uncertainty about lorries has caused poor sleep in our house. My daughter Luca Bex is 13-year-old and has diagnosed asthma, so I would also like to understand what the dust monitoring commitment actually means at the nearest homes. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a health claim in this email; I need to know which document to comment on before the deadline. Mrs Iona Pask at 20 Sedge Lane, Bracken Quay, BQ4 8NL mentioned that the lane flooded in June, but is not taking part in the examination. Please do not contact her on my behalf.

I saw a photograph of the access gap at https://brackenquay-chronicle.example/photos/old-lane. It may help explain the issue, although the site is not part of the application. The applicant's drawings can be found at https://fellmeretidallink.example/documents and the examination timetable is at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. I tried phoning the project switchboard on 0300 400 7710 but thought it better to put the questions in writing. My number is 07700 914 286 if a call is easier.

Regards,
Marin Bex

Dear Marin,

Thank you for your email. I am Idris Fen, one of the case officers supporting the Examining Authority at the Infrastructure Examinations Office. The team mailbox is the right place for procedural questions, and there is no need to phone separately. We have logged your correspondence against the Fellmere Tidal Link case, but the project switchboard cannot give advice on the merits of a representation.

The document uploaded on 13 October is an addendum to Appendix E-6, not a replacement. The applicant has been asked to make that clearer in the document list. You may refer to both documents in your Deadline 4 submission, quoting their document references if possible. Deadline 4 remains 28 October 2026. We cannot advise what weight the Examining Authority will give to either document, or whether a particular mitigation measure is sufficient.

Your email includes a precise wildlife location and personal information. Please send a version for publication with those passages removed or generalised, and a separate confidential version if you want the examining panel to have the detail. It records the proposed temporary diversion but does not prevent you from pointing out a missing gap on the drawing. Your comments about dust belong in the same Deadline 4 response; you do not need to obtain a medical letter to make a planning point. If you send revised text, please keep the document reference in the subject line so that it reaches the correct case record.

ORCHARD QUAY LEGAL LLP
Level 3, Sedge Exchange, 8 Market Basin, Larchmere LM2 4QF
Switchboard: 01632 960 440 | Direct dial: 01632 960 457
Email: elin.voss@orchardquay.example | General enquiries: land@orchardquay.example

21 October 2026

By email to the Examining Authority

East Fen Connector Development Consent Order (EN020481)
Written representation on behalf of Mara Fenwick, owner of Hollowmere Farm
Interested Party reference: IP-480173

Dear Examining Authority,

We act for Mara Fenwick in relation to the proposed compulsory acquisition of land at Hollowmere Farm. This letter responds to the Applicant's revised Book of Reference and the questions concerning the necessity for permanent rights over the western field. Our client does not object in principle to reinforcement of the electricity network. Her objection is that Larchmere Gridworks Ltd has not explained why the rights it now seeks must be permanent, or why its temporary working area cannot be moved away from the farm's only usable access during the harvest period.

The point is not simply the number of square metres shown in the schedule. Hollowmere Farm is worked as one holding, and the track across the western field is used for machinery, deliveries and access to the stock buildings. The plan labels the track as an 'existing agricultural access' but does not show the turning area at its southern end. The latest works plan puts a construction compound across that turning area. A vehicle could still enter the field on paper; a loaded trailer could not safely turn there. We ask the Applicant to provide a swept-path drawing using the vehicles it actually proposes to use, rather than assuming that a narrow opening on a plan is sufficient.

Our client has lived and worked at the farm for 40+ years. That history matters to how the holding operates, but it should not be taken as consent to new rights. She is aged 71 and has rheumatoid arthritis. She has asked that meetings about physical access be arranged in advance and held somewhere she can reach without crossing an active worksite. We mention those practical matters because the Applicant's proposed protocol says the landowner may attend a site meeting on 24 hours' notice. That is not workable for her. The residential correspondence address is 14 Plover Row, Larchmere LM4 8QN; please continue to serve formal examination correspondence through this firm rather than sending contractors to the house.

There is also a difference between the rights described at consultation and those in the present draft Order. The earlier drawing showed a temporary haul road along the field edge. Article 27 and Schedule 9 now appear to permit maintenance vehicles to cross the field at any time after construction. No frequency, vehicle size or reinstatement standard is specified. We would welcome confirmation whether the Applicant intends to retain a surfaced strip. If not, the drafting should say so. A general assurance in the land rights schedule is not a substitute for a limit in the Order or a binding protective provision.

The farm has a neighbour, Nico Rell, who helps check the gates when our client is away. He is not making a representation and has not authorised us to put his contact details into the examination. His name appears here only because the Applicant's site team previously described him as the person to approach for access. That was an error. He cannot grant entry, agree a change to the route or receive notices for the owner. Please remove that assumption from the land access protocol and give contractors a single contact at this firm instead.

We have checked the environmental plans as well. The ecology note refers generally to badger activity around Alder Copse. That description is appropriately broad. During the joint walkover, however, the ecologist identified a sett beneath the eastern hedge, 12 metres south of the cattle grid on Quarry Lane. We request that any drawing showing that precise position is supplied only through the appropriate confidential ecological procedure, not appended to a publicly searchable reply. The point can be addressed in the open examination without publishing the location: the working width in that part of the field should be reviewed before access rights are finalised.

At the last parish briefing Cllr Pella Dorn asked whether the compound could be placed on the former depot land instead. We do not suggest that the depot is necessarily suitable; we ask that the option be assessed and the answer recorded. The Applicant's project page, https://www.merewind-link.example/examination, currently contains the earlier access drawing but not the revised one circulated with its land plans. Members of the public following the issue should be able to see which version is under discussion.

For clarity, this is a request for proportionate evidence, not a request to stop the examination. We ask the Examining Authority to direct the Applicant to provide: (1) the swept-path drawing; (2) a comparison of temporary compound locations; (3) a marked-up version of the permanent-rights wording; and (4) an access protocol stating who may give instructions on the owner's behalf. If those documents are produced before the next deadline, we expect to be able to narrow the matters still in dispute. Until then, our client maintains her objection to the compulsory acquisition powers as drafted.

Yours faithfully,

Ms Elin Voss
Solicitor | Orchard Quay Legal LLP
Pronouns: she/her
Direct dial and email as above

Technical note: construction access and drainage

The submitted construction traffic assessment assumes that heavy goods vehicles can pass each other on Fenward Lane between South Reed Way and the proposed temporary access to Hollowmere Farm. The carriageway width shown on drawing EFC-TR-014 varies, however, and the assessment does not identify where passing movements are expected to occur. A junction capacity result alone does not demonstrate that the route will operate safely during the busiest delivery weeks. Larchmere Gridworks Ltd should provide a route-specific assessment showing vehicle dimensions, passing opportunities, peak hourly flows and the effect of any temporary traffic controls.

The indicative compound layout also places a turning area across the existing field drainage corridor. Drawing EFC-DR-008 shows a temporary culvert but gives no design flow, maintenance arrangement or trigger for its removal. The drainage strategy should explain how runoff will be managed during each construction phase, including the interval between soil stripping and installation of the permanent attenuation features. The proposed use of settlement tanks is noted, but their discharge point and operating capacity remain unclear.

These are related matters. If deliveries are held within the compound while vehicles wait for an escort, the hardstanding area and its drainage requirement may be greater than the area assessed. Conversely, relocating the holding area could change the number of movements along Fenward Lane. A coordinated revision of the traffic, compound and drainage drawings would be more useful than separate assurances in the next written response.

The landscape assessment should likewise test the revised compound footprint against views from the public footpath south of Hollowmere Farm. References to bat activity in the wider field boundary are relevant to lighting design, but do not establish a particular roost location. The requested information would allow the Examining Authority to assess whether the proposed construction limits and associated requirements are sufficiently precise.

Orchard Quay Legal LLP
8 Sedgeglass Square, Belwick, BW4 2QJ

Ms Elin Voss | Solicitor
Direct dial: 01632 960731
Email: elin.voss@orchardquaylegal.example

Dear Examining Authority,

East Fen Connector DCO — compulsory acquisition at Hollowmere Farm

We write on behalf of Mara Fenwick following the applicant’s latest response. The revised drawings requested in our previous submission remain necessary. In particular, Larchmere Gridworks Ltd should show whether the proposed holding area can accommodate an escort vehicle without obstructing the farm access, and where surface water from any additional hardstanding would go.

The temporary rights plan also needs a clearer explanation. It appears to permit access beyond the compound shown on the construction drawing. This is not simply a matter of tidying up the plans: Mara Fenwick needs to understand which land must remain available for agricultural use during the works.

Cllr Pella Dorn raised a similar question at the parish briefing. We ask that the applicant provide one coordinated set of plans before the next deadline.

Yours faithfully,

Elin Voss
Solicitor | Orchard Quay Legal LLP

To the Examining Authority
Merrow Fen Energy Park
21 October 2026

Dear Inspectors,

I am writing as the farmer at Harrowfen Farm about the proposed cable route and temporary construction compound shown on the latest land plans. I support getting more electricity from renewables, but the application treats our fields as if they are empty space between points on a map. They are the working part of the farm and also the land immediately around our family home.

The farm correspondence address is 17 Millbarrow Drove, Kettle Mere, NX4 7QP. Please use it for any paper notices, as the internet here drops out, particularly in wet weather. My mobile is 07700 914682 if a site visit needs arranging. I have farmed here for over 40 years, first helping my parents and then taking over the day-to-day work. Harrowfen Farm is not a visitor attraction or a spare parcel waiting for another use; it is how we make our living.

My wife, Rhea Vale, lives here with me, as does our son, Kit Vale, aged 14. My father, Edric Vale, also lives in the farmhouse. I mention them because the construction traffic would pass the kitchen windows and our only safe walking route from the house to the livestock buildings. None of them is making a separate representation. Edric Vale has Parkinson’s disease and cannot move quickly if a reversing vehicle comes into the yard. That is a practical safety issue, not an objection to workers doing their jobs.

The proposed access crosses the concrete apron where we sort lambs and load feed. The environmental statement calls this an agricultural track. It is not. On most mornings between February and April we have a tractor, feed trailer and stock moving across it, often before it is fully light. Closing it for even part of a day means taking the stock round by Millbarrow Drove, which has no useful passing place for a loaded trailer. The drawings also put a temporary fence through the point where we turn the mower to get into field 4. I cannot see how the hay cut is meant to happen with the fence in place.

I asked at the September drop-in whether the access could be moved to the eastern boundary. An employee of Merrow Fen Energy Ltd, Elwin Marr, said the compound layout was still being looked at, but the submitted drawing appears unchanged. I am not suggesting that Elwin Marr promised a change. I am asking the applicant to show, in a plan that can be enforced, where tractors can pass, where the fence will actually stand and what happens if construction runs into lambing. The present wording says the contractor will agree details with the landowner later. That leaves too much until later for a working farm.

The farmhouse and sheds use one water supply line, laid shallow across the southern field. It is marked roughly on the applicant's plan but not accurately enough to excavate beside it. If it is cut, the stock drinkers and the house will lose water together. The same is true of the electricity spur to the milking shed. The contractor should establish both routes with us on site before any topsoil is stripped and should have a written repair procedure, including out-of-hours contacts. A promise to make good after the event is not enough in a spell of hot weather.

I am also concerned about drainage. The northern field looks firm in summer photographs but water sits there after two days of rain. We have spent years keeping the grips open and avoiding heavy kit when the soil is wet. A haul road left in place through winter could send water towards the farmhouse, or leave us with a compacted strip that will not grow a decent crop. Please require pre-entry and post-reinstatement soil surveys, with the results given to us, not just kept by the contractor. Reinstatement should include the grips and field entrances, not only the trench itself.

On ecology, I have told the applicant's survey team about badgers in Bracken Holt. That is a general observation and I would not expect a survey to rely on it. I have not put the precise location in this public letter because the ecologists need to check it privately before machinery is routed nearby. There are also bats around the old cart shed most evenings. The issue for me is that floodlights at the compound could shine straight across the yard and into the house. I would like the lighting plan to show the direction and hours of use rather than merely saying light spill will be minimised.

Cllr Amity Pell visited the road junction in August and saw how difficult it is for two large vehicles to pass. This is not a request to stop all construction vehicles. It is a request for a proper booking system and a limit on deliveries during stock movements, school travel times and the autumn harvest. We have had poor sleep worrying about whether someone will meet a lorry on the bend, but that concern could be reduced by a route and timetable that drivers can actually follow. The project mailbox, farmfields@merrowenergy.example, acknowledged my earlier query but did not answer the question about who would control arrivals at the gate.

Please also make sure the land plans distinguish the farmhouse garden from the agricultural holding. The hedge beside the garden gives us privacy and some shelter. It should not be cut back simply to provide a wider sightline when another access option has not been properly explained. We can discuss sensible working arrangements, including a site visit outside the busiest stock-handling hours, but we need them written down before consent is granted. A project of this size should be able to make room for an existing farm.

Yours faithfully,

Tobin Vale

Further to my letter of 18 October 2026, I am writing about the proposed construction access beside Harrowfen Farm. The farm is our business, but the farmhouse is also our family home. My wife Rhea Vale and our child Kit Vale live there; Kit is 11. My father Edric Vale lives with us too and has diagnosed COPD. Overnight generator testing and vehicle movements near the house therefore need to be considered as domestic impacts, not just effects on the holding.

The address for correspondence is Harrowfen Farm, 14 Sedge Drove, Pellmere, PM4 6QN. If a site visit is proposed, please ring my mobile on 07700 912 684 rather than asking a driver to knock at the farmhouse. We handle stock at different times depending on the weather, so an appointment made in advance would help everyone.

Elwin Marr of Merrow Fen Energy Ltd told me the access drawing would be updated. I have not yet seen one showing where vehicles would wait if the gate is shut. Cllr Amity Pell has visited the junction and will know why I am concerned about queuing on the drove. I have felt anxious about how this will work, although a clear traffic plan would do much to settle that concern.

The ecology appendix refers to badgers in Reedmire Wood. That is a broad area, and my point here is simply that fencing and temporary lighting should be checked against the survey before work starts. Please also confirm who will repair any damage to our field entrance and when that work would be done.

Yours faithfully,

Tobin Vale

Additional note – access and drainage

The construction traffic assessment for Merrow Fen Energy Park appears to count vehicle movements across a full day, but the peak-hour table should also show deliveries arriving together at the eastern access. A daily total does not explain how a queue at the gate would be managed. The revised drawing should mark a waiting area clear of the public highway and show the turning path for the largest vehicle expected during construction.

The drainage drawings need the same level of detail. The proposed temporary compound is shown above the field ditch, yet the phasing plan does not say when the silt controls will be installed or removed. Please set out the sequence before earthworks begin and identify how runoff will be contained while the permanent basins are unfinished.

Finally, the landscape schedule should distinguish temporary lighting from operational lighting. Badgers are recorded in Reedmire Wood, so the lighting assessment should check the wider habitat without publishing precise survey locations.

text:
Relevant Representation: Darnwick Link Road Development Consent Order
Application reference: EN098765
From: Elin Voss
Interested Party reference: IP-004872
Address: 14 Reedbank Close, Darnwick, DV4 8QL
Email: elin.voss@postmere.example

I support the Darnwick Link Road. I have lived in Darnwick for 40+ years and have seen the amount of traffic through the village increase steadily, especially lorries travelling between the freight yards and the eastern distributor road. I am not saying the scheme is perfect or that building it will be easy for those of us living nearby. I do think it offers a realistic way of getting the through traffic off the village street, which has been talked about for years without much changing.

At present lorries use Mere Lane and then turn past the shops, often quite late at night. From my bedroom I can hear engines slowing down, accelerating again and sometimes idling when vehicles meet at the narrow part. My sleep is broken by it. I feel tired the next morning and it has affected my wellbeing. That is a description of what it is like living here, not a claim that every journey will disappear once the link road opens. Even taking some of the heavy vehicles out of the centre would make a difference.

I agree with the published relevant representations of Jem Arlow and Pia Rennet. Both are registered interested parties, and I particularly agree with their point that support for the link road should not be treated as support for unrestricted night-time construction. I also agree with Jem Arlow's comments about making the crossing near the shops safer for people on foot. I am mentioning their representations because they are on the examination record; I am not trying to speak for them.

The present route affects ordinary journeys as well as evenings at home. At the Mere Lane crossing I often wait for a gap large enough to cross without hurrying. A driver trying to get a long vehicle round the bend has to pay attention to the kerb and the oncoming lane, which leaves very little room for anyone else. I would like the examination to consider what happens on the old road after the link is open. If it is left looking like a fast route, some traffic will continue using it. Clear signs, a sensible speed limit and a crossing people can actually use should be part of the outcome, not matters left until everyone has gone away.

Cllr Orla Beven said at the village hall meeting that the detailed traffic arrangements still need scrutiny. I agree. Supporters of the scheme should be able to ask questions about the modelling and the junction design without being counted as opponents. In particular, I would like to know whether the forecasts allow for drivers using navigation apps to cut through Darnwick when there is a delay on the new road. That happens now when the eastern distributor road is busy, and residents notice it even if it lasts only part of a day.

Construction is my main reservation. The haul route shown in the application is preferable to running vehicles past the school entrance, but it will still put activity near homes. Please require a published programme of the noisiest work, a way to report problems that does not depend on using a smartphone, and prompt replies when people do report them. The applicant's general mailbox, planning@eastfenroutes.example, is useful, but residents need to know who will deal with an urgent issue outside office hours. I do not want a promise that there will be no disturbance, because that would not be believable. I want reasonable limits and a clear explanation when plans change.

I have looked at the environmental information available through the examination page. I welcome the proposed planting along the edge of the new road, although young trees will not screen traffic straight away. The drawings would be easier for residents to understand if they showed more clearly which hedges are to be kept during construction and when replacement planting will be done. Badger setts have been recorded in Larchcopse Wood, so I also expect the ecological measures in the application to be followed. I am not identifying a particular sett or asking for its location to be published.

I discussed the current traffic with Mrs Nora Pell, who lives at 9 Reedbank Close, Darnwick, DV4 8QJ and has not registered to take part in this examination. She too hears vehicles at night, but her views are her own and should not be taken as a separate representation. I include that conversation only to explain why I think the present noise is a street-wide issue rather than something peculiar to my house.

My health is affected when I have several nights of poor sleep, and I worry about how long the village will have to wait if this proposal is refused. These are reasons for my support, not a request to ignore the impacts on people closer to the proposed road. Their concerns about lighting, loss of land and construction access deserve proper answers. The applicant, East Fen Routes Limited, should be held to the mitigation it has put forward, and the Examining Authority should test whether those measures can be enforced in practice.

Please record my representation as support for the Development Consent Order, subject to careful examination of construction controls, the old-road crossing and the arrangements for monitoring traffic after opening. I would welcome a straightforward update to residents when the monitoring results are available, including an explanation of what action would be taken if the predicted reduction in village traffic does not happen.

Elin Voss
Telephone: 07700 900 413

Supplementary technical points — Darnwick Link Road

The following points concern the information needed to assess the scheme, rather than a change to the position stated above. East Fen Routes Limited should provide a clear comparison between the traffic forecasts in the Transport Assessment and the assumptions used to design the junctions, drainage and construction access. These subjects are dealt with in separate documents, but a change in one set of assumptions could alter the conclusions in another.

Traffic modelling

The forecast reduction in traffic on Darnwick High Street is an important claimed benefit. The Transport Assessment should show weekday and weekend flows separately, with peak-hour turning movements at the Mill Lane and Broughton Road junctions. An annual average is not enough to show whether queues will move from the centre of Darnwick to the new roundabout. The assessment should also explain how traffic using the proposed link will join the A4176 at busy times, and whether a queue there could obstruct through traffic or the access to adjoining employment land.

The model validation tables appear to rely on counts taken before the Fenmere Trading Yard expansion. This may be reasonable if suitable growth factors have been applied, but the adjustment should be set out in one place. The applicant should provide a sensitivity test for a slower uptake of the link road and a higher proportion of heavy goods vehicles on the old road. It would also be useful to show the forecast flows with and without the proposed Mill Lane traffic-calming measures. Otherwise it is difficult to separate the effect of the new road from the effect of changes to the existing network.

The proposed monitoring scheme should identify the count locations, survey periods, baseline figures and trigger levels before the road opens. For example, a trigger expressed simply as a percentage change from the opening-year forecast could be misleading if regional traffic growth differs from the model. Results at Darnwick High Street, Mill Lane and the A4176 junction should be reported together. A requirement should specify who reviews the results, when a remedial proposal is required and how any agreed measures would be delivered. Publication of the raw classified counts would help make the conclusions checkable.

Walking, cycling and the old-road crossing

The Old Darnwick Road crossing is shown as a refuge island in Drawing TR-14, while the access strategy describes it as part of a continuous walking and cycling route. The drawings should confirm the usable width on each side, the approach gradients and the space available for cycles waiting to cross. Visibility should be assessed against the operating speed expected after opening, not just the posted speed limit. The crossing design also needs to account for agricultural vehicles turning into the retained field access, without making the refuge so narrow that it cannot serve its intended purpose.

A route may be technically continuous but unattractive if it requires several separate crossings or passes behind drainage equipment with poor sightlines. A simple end-to-end plan from the village edge to the Fenmere Trading Yard entrance would make the arrangement easier to assess. The landscaping plans should not place new planting within the visibility envelope for the crossing. Maintenance responsibilities for signs, surfacing and vegetation should be stated in the DCO requirements or a secured management plan.

Landscape and lighting

The Environmental Statement describes the new earthworks as becoming less prominent when planting has matured. The year-one photomontages should carry substantial weight because the embankment and roundabout will be visible before screening develops. The assessment should state what happens if the proposed native planting fails during the establishment period, including replacement timescales and the minimum standard for replanting. Cross-sections at the eastern edge of Darnwick would assist in checking the stated heights of bunds, fences and lighting columns against the surrounding ground level.

The lighting strategy refers to dimming outside the busiest hours but does not, in the summary table, give a single set of operating hours for each junction. These details should be fixed through an approved lighting plan, with limits on upward spill and a process for changing settings if safety monitoring identifies a problem. The plan should distinguish permanent lighting from temporary construction lighting. The concern here is the extent and duration of illumination, not whether every part of the route must remain unlit.

Drainage and water quality

The proposed outfall to Rill Beck warrants a joined-up account of highway runoff, flood storage and maintenance access. The Flood Risk Assessment gives attenuation volumes, while the drainage drawings show several features whose connections are not immediately clear at the reproduced scale. A single schematic should show the flow route from each paved area to its treatment feature and eventual outfall. It should identify the design event, climate-change allowance, exceedance route and the consequences of a blocked inlet. The ditch crossing near the western construction compound should be included in that exercise, even if its final drainage arrangement differs from the temporary one.

The Construction Environmental Management Plan should set out how exposed soil, fuel storage and concrete washout will be controlled during the earthworks phase. It should also identify inspection and desilting arrangements for temporary settlement features. A general commitment to follow good practice is helpful but is not a substitute for a plan tied to the construction sequence shown in the programme.

Construction phasing and secured controls

The indicative programme suggests that the Broughton Road tie-in and the bridge over Rill Beck may be built during overlapping periods. The construction traffic assessment should test that overlap rather than assume that traffic from the two work areas will arrive at different times. It should identify the routes available if the preferred access is temporarily closed, and state whether any such diversion requires further approval. Hours for deliveries, temporary lane closures and particularly noisy operations should be presented in one schedule so that the commitments can be read consistently.

Finally, the draft Development Consent Order should make the main mitigation enforceable without relying on a later document to decide whether mitigation is needed at all. Plans can settle detailed design after consent, but the relevant requirement should retain the measurable objective, the approving body and the point in the programme by which approval must be obtained. That would make it easier to check whether the traffic, crossing, drainage and landscape measures examined here are the measures actually delivered.

Further technical points on the Darnwick Link Road

This representation supports the principle of the link road but asks for the assessment and proposed controls to be made more precise before the examination closes. The points below concern how the scheme would operate, rather than whether a new route is needed.

Traffic forecasting

The Transport Assessment compares a 2032 opening year with a 2047 future year. That is a reasonable framework, but the tables in Appendix T3 do not make clear whether committed housing at North Mere has been included in both the reference case and the scheme case. The difference matters at the eastern junction, where a small change in turning flows can produce a much larger change in queue length. East Fen Routes Limited should provide a single schedule identifying every committed development, the number of trips assigned to it and the network scenario in which those trips appear. The schedule should reconcile with the flow diagrams rather than simply refer back to the modelling files.

The peak-hour results also need a sensitivity test for construction traffic coinciding with school-term traffic. The current construction estimate is expressed as daily two-way movements. Daily totals cannot show whether deliveries concentrated within one hour would obstruct the left-turn lane at the B317 Mallow Road junction. The applicant could address this with an hourly profile for the busiest construction month, modelled alongside the busiest relevant background hour. If that combination is judged unrealistic, the reason should be set out rather than assumed.

Walking, cycling and crossings

The proposed shared path is welcome, particularly the connection from Darnwick to the employment land at Glass Yard. However, Drawing DLR-GA-14 appears to end the continuous path before the signalised crossing of Fenward Avenue. Users would then have to negotiate a short section beside the vehicle access to the maintenance compound. That gap should be designed out. A continuous, legible route is important even if the compound generates relatively few trips.

The crossing assessment should state the assumed walking speed, waiting time and usable width for each refuge. It should also explain how the signals respond when a person has begun crossing but has not reached the far side before the nominal stage ends. These are matters capable of being fixed in a detailed design requirement. They should not be left as an aspiration in the Design and Access Statement.

Landscape and lighting

The photomontages are useful, but the year-15 views do not adequately distinguish established planting from planting that depends on successful replacement during the first five years. A revised planting schedule should identify the minimum stock size, replacement period and maintenance responsibility for each mitigation area. The views from Low Bracken Ridge should also be tested in winter, when screening along the northern cutting will be substantially less effective.

Lighting columns are shown near the western roundabout, while the assessment describes the surrounding lane network as predominantly unlit. A lighting plan should therefore give column heights, shielding, operating hours and predicted spill at the edge of Reedfold Wood. The requirement should secure those limits before installation. It need not prescribe a particular manufacturer's fitting, provided that the assessed lighting envelope is not exceeded.

Drainage and water quality

The drainage strategy relies on two attenuation basins and an outfall to the South Beck. Its exceedance drawing shows the direction of overland flow, but not the depth or velocity at the point where the flow crosses the proposed shared path. That information is needed to establish whether the path remains usable in the design event and whether a safe alternative route is available when it does not. The drawings should also show the maintenance access to both basins without relying on temporary occupation of the path.

The applicant should explain how pollution control would work during the earthworks phase, before the permanent drainage system is connected. A statement that good practice will be followed is not the same as identifying the sequence of temporary silt controls, inspections and discharge points. Darnwick Borough Council and the Estuary Catchment Authority should be able to approve that sequence before the first substantial excavation in each catchment. The final arrangement should then be checked against the assumptions in the Flood Risk Assessment, including the allowance made for climate change.

Ecology and land management

The Environmental Statement records bat activity around Reedfold Wood and badger field signs across the wider survey area. Those are broad descriptions, not a substitute for specifying the limits of construction working areas and lighting controls. The habitat drawings should show where retained hedges meet new planting, how temporary fencing will protect those connections and when the fencing may be removed. This would help ensure that the promised corridor exists during construction as well as after planting has established.

The proposed species-rich grassland requires a management prescription, not merely a target area. Soil handling, the seed mix, the timing of the first cut and the approach to failed establishment all affect whether the stated biodiversity outcome is achievable. Monitoring results should be compared against measurable thresholds, with corrective action required if those thresholds are missed.

Requested changes

For these reasons, the examination should seek an updated traffic scenario schedule, an hourly construction-traffic test, revised crossing and path drawings, winter landscape views, a bounded lighting design and drainage exceedance information. The outline management plans should then be aligned with the corresponding Development Consent Order requirements. This would preserve flexibility in detailed design while making clear which outcomes have actually been assessed and which must be delivered.

Further detail on the requested changes

The updated traffic scenario schedule should show, in one table, which assumptions are common to the opening-year, design-year and sensitivity tests for the Darnwick Link Road. In particular, East Fen Routes Limited should identify the forecast background growth, the treatment of committed developments and any changes to the modelled highway network between scenarios. At present, the figures in the Transport Assessment and the junction drawings are difficult to reconcile because the same junction is described by different option numbers. A single drawing register, keyed to the model runs, would make the assessment easier to check.

The hourly construction-traffic test should cover the busiest reasonably foreseeable period rather than a daily average. It should include deliveries to the western compound, movements associated with earthworks and the temporary traffic arrangements on Merebank Road. The assessment should explain whether those activities could overlap and, if not, how the Construction Traffic Management Plan would prevent the overlap. It would also help to distinguish vehicle movements on public roads from movements entirely within the construction boundary. Without that distinction, the totals appear higher in one table than another, although this may simply be a difference in counting method.

For walking and cycling, the revised drawings should show the full route through each crossing, not only the crossing point itself. The tie-in at Sedge Lane appears to narrow alongside the proposed drainage swale, while the route under the eastern bridge is not dimensioned on the general arrangement drawing. These matters can probably be resolved at detailed design, but the examination needs enough information to establish that a usable continuous route fits within the Order limits. The drawings should also show how the temporary diversion would operate before the permanent path opens.

Winter views are requested for viewpoints on the approach to Darnwick and from the public path north of Alder Mere. Summer photography is useful for assessing the finished planting scheme, but it does not show the extent of the embankment and lighting columns when the hedgerows are out of leaf. The visualisations should use the same viewing parameters as the existing set and state the assumed planting height, so that the comparison is meaningful. A bounded lighting design should specify the maximum column heights and the areas where lighting may be installed, rather than leaving both matters to subsequent approval.

Finally, the drainage exceedance plan should trace flows when the design capacity is exceeded, including where water would cross the proposed path. Approval of the detailed drainage scheme by Darnwick Borough Council and the Estuary Catchment Authority is sensible, but that approval should operate within limits assessed in the Environmental Statement. The same principle applies to the outline management plans: later approvals should settle methods, not introduce a materially different outcome from the one examined.

The construction traffic assessment also needs a clearer worst-case test. The figures for the Darnwick Link Road appear to distribute deliveries evenly across the working day, whereas the programme allows earthworks and bridge construction to overlap. East Fen Routes Limited should provide a combined peak-hour assignment for that overlap, including vehicles using Merefold Lane and the temporary access at South Silt Field. This is not a request for another general traffic forecast; it is a check that the proposed junction controls can accommodate the construction programme actually sought.

The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan refers to routing being agreed later with Darnwick Borough Council. That is reasonable for signs and booking arrangements, but the maximum daily HGV movements and the permitted access points should be secured now. The Environmental Statement should also show whether its noise and air-quality assessments use the same peak movements. Otherwise a later change in delivery pattern could remain within the management plan while falling outside the effects examined.

FENMERE BOROUGH COUNCIL
LOCAL IMPACT REPORT
Wrenfold Energy Storage and Grid Connection Project
Examination reference: EN010284 | 21 October 2026

Submitted by Fenmere Borough Council
Civic Hall, 8 Charter Square, Vellin, VX4 2QD
Planning enquiries: planning@fenmere.gov.uk

1. Purpose and scope

This Local Impact Report sets out the likely effects of the proposed Wrenfold Energy Storage and Grid Connection Project within Fenmere Borough. It has been prepared for the Examining Authority under the Planning Act 2008. The Council's assessment draws on the application documents, its own site visits and representations received up to 9 October 2026. The report describes local effects; it is not a statement of support for, or objection to, the development in principle.

The application by Elderwake Infrastructure Ltd comprises a battery compound, substation, underground cable and associated access works on land east of Wrenfold Lane. The nearest settlement is Vellin. The Council has assessed the proposal against the adopted Fenmere Local Plan and the national policy documents available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. References to drawing numbers below are to the applicant's September 2026 submission unless stated otherwise.

2. Consultation and local context

The application site lies between working farmland, the Mill Beck corridor and the edge of the Vellin employment area. Wrenfold Lane is narrow, has no continuous footway and is used by walkers reaching the riverside path. The Council has received 46 written comments and held a public drop-in at Civic Hall on 18 September 2026. Those comments have informed this report but are not a substitute for the Council's technical assessment.

Cllr Iona Brisk, the ward Councillor, asked that construction traffic passing the school crossing be addressed expressly rather than left to a later contractor's plan. Cllr Perran Holt, chair of the Council's environment committee, raised the long-term maintenance of the drainage basins. These are matters for examination; neither statement should be read as the Council's final view. Daven Mirk MP wrote to the Council about the absence of a signed diversion for Footpath 12 during cable installation. The Council agrees that the submitted pedestrian-management drawing is not sufficiently clear on that point.

A written comment from Mara Deller of 14 Mill Lane, Vellin, VX4 3LA describes poor sleep during existing evening vehicle movements and says, 'my son, aged 11, has asthma'. The Council records this as a concern about the proposed construction schedule, not as medical evidence that the project would cause illness. Several other residents said they felt anxious about the scale of the compound. Those feelings are noted, while the assessment below relies on the predicted noise levels and the proposed controls.

3. Transport and access

The proposed construction access would use the southern end of Wrenfold Lane, where two heavy vehicles cannot pass without using the verge. The applicant predicts a peak of 38 two-way HGV movements per day for approximately twelve weeks. The Council's highway team considers the forecast broadly credible, but the swept-path drawing assumes that parked vehicles will be absent near the lane junction. That assumption is not secured.

The Council requests a requirement for an approved Construction Traffic Management Plan before works begin. It should identify delivery hours, a booking system, verge repairs and a named contact point for complaints. Deliveries should avoid the school crossing between 08:00 and 09:00 and between 15:00 and 16:00 on school days. This is a proposed restriction, not an allegation that the applicant's drivers have acted improperly. The temporary closure of Footpath 12 should not commence until a signed, step-free alternative is available.

4. Landscape, noise and ecology

Views of the battery units would be most apparent from the riverside path in the first years after planting. The proposed bund will screen the lower portions, but the Council considers the visual assessment over-optimistic about the time required for the hedge to establish. A five-year replacement obligation and an agreed planting specification would reduce that uncertainty. The lighting strategy should also prevent unnecessary illumination of Mill Beck.

The operational noise assessment uses a background survey undertaken in March 2025. Fenmere Borough Council accepts the monitoring positions but requests a further calculation for the nearest gardens when all cooling units operate at once. The predicted construction noise is temporary, although evening cable works could be intrusive if not controlled by hours in the draft requirement. The Council has not identified evidence of a statutory nuisance arising from the proposal as submitted.

Ecological surveys record bat activity along Mill Beck and badger field signs in the wider Wrenfold area. Those are broad locations and should remain visible in the public assessment. A separate field note identifies a badger sett beneath the third hawthorn from the north gate of Field 7, approximately 4 metres west of the cable centreline. That precise description should be handled as restricted ecological information, not reproduced on public-facing plans. Subject to a secured pre-construction survey and appropriate licensing where needed, the Council considers that ecological effects could be managed.

5. Flood risk and conclusions

The drainage design routes surface water to two attenuation basins before discharge to Mill Beck. The submitted maintenance schedule does not say who would inspect the basin outlets after an extreme rainfall event. The Council seeks an enforceable management plan naming the responsible organisation, inspection intervals and a means of funding repairs for the operational life of the project. Its request concerns the adequacy of the proposed arrangements, not the published finances of Elderwake Infrastructure Ltd.

Overall, the main local impacts are construction traffic, temporary path disruption, early-stage views of the compound and uncertainty about operational noise at nearby gardens. Fenmere Borough Council considers that these matters can be addressed through revised drawings and appropriately worded requirements, subject to the further information requested above. The Council reserves the ability to update this report during the examination if material new evidence is submitted.

Report compiled by Nerys Vale, Principal Planning Officer, Fenmere Borough Council. Queries about this report should be sent to planning@fenmere.gov.uk rather than to an individual officer.

Annex A — Technical assumptions used in the Local Impact Report

Traffic: the assessment assumes that construction vehicles enter from the A4176 via Merebank Lane and leave by the same route. Elderwake Infrastructure Ltd has modelled a peak of 28 two-way HGV movements per day during the foundation works. Fenmere Borough Council considers that the junction assessment should also test the overlap with the cable-trench phase; the submitted programme does not establish that these activities cannot coincide. A construction traffic management plan should specify delivery hours, temporary signing and the method for recording vehicle movements.

Landscape: the Wrenfold Energy Storage and Grid Connection Project will be visible from parts of East Fenmere Footpath 12 before boundary planting matures. Drawing ES-204 Rev C shows a screening belt, but its southern end stops short of the inverter compound. A revised planting plan should address this gap without obstructing the drainage easement.

Drainage: the proposed attenuation basin discharges towards the Old Mere Ditch. The detailed design should demonstrate exceedance routes for the 1-in-100-year event plus climate-change allowance. Badger activity recorded in Wrenfold Wood is noted, but the habitat information supplied does not alter these drainage conclusions.

1. Purpose and scope

This Local Impact Report describes the likely effects of the proposed Bellmere Eastern Link within the borough. It is submitted to assist the Examining Authority and is not the Council's final position on whether development consent should be granted. The report draws on the application documents, site visits and comments received by the Council up to 16 October 2026. The Council has used the approach described at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. References to drawings are to the applicant's September 2026 submission unless stated otherwise.

The applicant, Hearthmere Transit Infrastructure Ltd, proposes a new two-lane road between North Quay Roundabout and the A4178 at Bracken Mere. The scheme includes a railway underpass, a drainage basin and changes to three public rights of way. The development site, identified as Plot 04-17 on Land Plans Sheet 6, includes the former borough depot off Kiln Lane. The Council agrees that east-west journey times are unreliable at present, particularly when the level crossing is shut. That does not, by itself, resolve the effects on the communities immediately adjoining the route.

2. Community and local services

Bellmere East has a primary school, two small shopping parades and a playing field used outside school hours. The nearest properties to the proposed underpass are on Larch Fold. Residents already report poor sleep when overnight freight movements coincide with depot deliveries. Poor sleep and anxiety about further traffic are reported effects, not evidence of a diagnosed condition across the neighbourhood. Cllr Ada Venn asked at the Council's 8 October public committee meeting that construction traffic restrictions be written into the requirements rather than left entirely to a contractor's plan. Cllr Orin Pell raised the need for safe access to the playing field throughout the works. Neri Talwick MP has separately requested a clear explanation of the proposed night-working limits. These comments are recorded here as matters for the examination, not as endorsements of the Council's assessment.

At a ward drop-in meeting, Mrs Livia Nett of 6 Larch Fold, Bellmere, BM4 2JL described difficulty crossing Kiln Lane with a child after the school bell. The meeting note also records that the child, aged 14, has diagnosed epilepsy. The Council has not relied on that personal information to estimate the number of people affected; the relevant planning issue is whether the temporary crossing will be usable and reliably staffed. The note was retained in the consultation file under IP reference IP-47821-26. Other attendees asked for the crossing plan to show where pedestrians would wait when delivery vehicles turn into the compound.

3. Transport, construction and amenity

The applicant's traffic model forecasts a reduction in vehicles passing through Market Square after opening. The Council cannot yet confirm the forecast for the morning school period because the sensitivity test assumes a different delivery pattern from the outline Construction Traffic Management Plan. A swept-path drawing is also needed for the temporary junction at Kiln Lane. The proposed 07:00 start for ordinary construction is likely to be noticeable at the eastern end of Larch Fold; the Council requests that any exception for earlier concrete pours require advance notice and a recorded reason.

Noise barriers shown on Drawing N-12 may reduce operational road noise, but their maintenance responsibility is not identified. The Council seeks an enforceable inspection and replacement arrangement. Air-quality monitoring should cover the school frontage and Market Square for at least the first year of operation. This is a request for proportionate monitoring, not a finding that the development would breach a statutory limit. The applicant's project drawings are available at https://www.hearthmerelink.example/project.

4. Landscape, drainage and ecology

The drainage basin occupies an open field currently visible from the Bracken Mere footpath. Its earth banks should be graded to avoid an abrupt edge, and the proposed planting should be checked against the sightlines needed at the new junction. The Council's drainage team seeks confirmation of the exceedance route if the basin outlet becomes blocked. Without that information, the predicted effect on gardens beside Kiln Lane remains uncertain.

Badgers have been recorded in Bracken Mere Wood, and bats have been observed along the railway cutting. Those broad observations do not identify a particular protected site. An ecology note supplied at the drop-in meeting, however, describes an active badger sett beneath the third hawthorn east of the Kiln Lane stile, 11 metres north of survey peg K19. The note should be handled as confidential ecological information rather than reproduced on a public constraints plan. The Council asks the applicant to confirm that its method statement accounts for protected species before vegetation clearance begins.

5. Local economy and conclusion

Businesses on Foundry Quay depend on deliveries reaching the quayside without lengthy diversions. The Council requests a signed diversion strategy before closure of any section of Kiln Lane. The applicant's stated scheme cost of £84 million is a corporate project figure and has not been tested by the Council. No conclusion about local employment can be drawn from the construction jobs estimate without details of the proposed procurement arrangements.

The Council considers that the main outstanding matters are the temporary pedestrian crossing, construction hours, drainage exceedance route and maintenance of noise barriers. These could be addressed through further information and appropriately drafted requirements. Council officers can be contacted through planning@bellmere.gov.example. For document queries, the reporting officer is Mara Fenwick, Bellmere Borough Council, at mara.fenwick@bellmere.gov.example or direct line 01632 960418.

Mara Fenwick
Reporting Officer, Bellmere Borough Council

Bellmere Borough Council
Bellmere Eastern Link — Local Impact Report, supplementary section
Examination reference: BEL-EN-2026-041

6. Community facilities and access

6.1 This section should be read with the Council's earlier comments on the temporary pedestrian crossing, construction hours, drainage exceedance route and maintenance of noise barriers. It records local effects raised since the first draft of the report was circulated to ward members. It does not replace the Council's formal response to any subsequent change request by Hearthmere Transit Infrastructure Ltd.

6.2 The proposed haul route passes the eastern entrance to Bellmere Recreation Ground. The ground is used by school groups, informal football teams and people walking between the Market Street bus stops and the riverside path. The applicant's construction traffic plan shows a banksman at the haul-route entrance but does not explain what happens when a group is waiting on both sides of the road. The Council requests a drawing showing the position of the temporary crossing, the available footway width and how the crossing will operate outside the hours when a banksman is present. A condition requiring a crossing in principle would not, by itself, resolve the local impact.

6.3 At the ward briefing on 8 October 2026, Cllr Ada Venn asked whether access to the recreation ground would remain open during drainage works. Cllr Orin Pell noted that the proposed diversion uses a narrow section of Mill Race Track which becomes muddy after rain. Both comments concern the adequacy of the proposed access arrangements; they are not objections to the principle of the Link. The Council asks the applicant to distinguish between a temporary closure for a particular operation and a diversion that would remain in place for several months.

6.4 The minutes of the separate public drop-in record that Mrs Livia Nett of 22 Reed Lane, Bellmere BM4 7QT asked for an advance letter before any night working. The attendance sheet describes the resident as aged 74. That address and age are not necessary for the examination to understand the request, but appear here because the minute supplied to the reporting team was copied into the draft without its usual privacy check. The same minute records that the resident has been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is worried about dust entering the house. The Council's planning point is that notice of exceptional night working and a clear route for dust complaints should be secured. A different attendee, Eren Dobble, asked whether the contractor would clean mud from the pavement, rather than only the carriageway.

7. Drainage, landscape and ecology

7.1 The Council's drainage team has reviewed the revised basin section. It appears to provide capacity for the design event, but the drawing still stops the exceedance arrow at the boundary of the application site. The Council cannot determine from that drawing whether water would continue towards the service yard or return to the ditch. A plan extending beyond the boundary, with levels at the two low points, is needed. The service yard is a commercial premises and its address, Unit 6, Lantern Trade Park, Bellmere BM4 8PX, is given only to identify the location of the potential impact.

7.2 Landscape drawing L-204 labels new planting along the north side of Mill Race Track. The Council supports that planting, subject to a maintenance schedule that identifies who will replace failed trees after the initial establishment period. The drawing also places a proposed inspection strip beside the noise barrier. Officers need confirmation that the strip will be wide enough for routine repairs without repeatedly closing the public path. The Council does not seek a particular brand of barrier or planting stock.

7.3 Badger activity has been reported in Willowmere Wood, and bat activity along the wider ditch corridor. Those are broad locations and are included to explain why a pre-construction survey remains appropriate. A confidential field note supplied with the ecological consultation gives the sett location as the bank 12 metres north of the eastern gate of Plot 17, immediately below the third ash tree on the west side of Mill Race Track. That detail should not be reproduced on the public version of an ecological plan. The Council can assess the proposed working method using a restricted plan and a public plan showing the affected work area more generally.

8. Engagement and proposed response

8.1 Neri Talwick MP wrote to the Council on 12 October 2026 asking how residents would receive notice of a temporary road closure. The Council's response explained that a traffic order notice and a contractor letter serve different purposes. A statutory notice establishes the restriction; a letter can explain where pedestrians should go on the day and whom to contact if the route is blocked. The MP's correspondence has been treated as a request for clarification, not as evidence that a particular closure has already been authorised.

8.2 Some residents at the drop-in said that the uncertainty was causing stress and poor sleep. Those comments are relevant to the need for timely information, but they do not establish a quantified health impact. The Council recommends a construction communications plan identifying the notice period for planned works, arrangements for unexpected closures, and a means of recording and responding to complaints. The plan should cover businesses as well as households, since deliveries to Lantern Trade Park use the same junction.

8.3 Bellmere Borough Council's correspondence address for this examination is Civic Offices, 4 Lantern Square, Bellmere BM4 7QX. Submissions and requests for the Council's published drawings should be sent to planning@bellmere.gov.example, which is a shared mailbox. General guidance on the examination process is available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. The Council has worked in the area for over 40 years, but that experience cannot substitute for the missing crossing and exceedance drawings.

8.4 Subject to that further information, the Council considers the identified local effects capable of being managed through the construction traffic, drainage and landscape requirements. Its position may change if the drawings show that the temporary crossing cannot fit within the available highway width or that exceedance flows would enter neighbouring premises.

8.5 Bellmere Borough Council has reviewed the transport, drainage and landscape material submitted for the Bellmere Eastern Link by Hearthmere Transit Infrastructure Ltd. This part of the Local Impact Report addresses the likely effects on the borough rather than the overall need for the scheme. The assessment remains provisional where the application relies on drawings or modelling files that have not yet been supplied in an auditable form.

Transport and construction access

8.6 The proposed link would join the A6142 Fenway Road at its western end and the B3178 Eastfold Road beyond the rail bridge. The Council accepts that the operational traffic model indicates a reduction in through traffic on Market Quay. However, the modelled morning peak at the Eastfold Road junction is close to capacity in the opening year. A modest change in turning movements, signal timings or background growth could therefore produce a materially different queue. The Council requests a sensitivity test using the higher growth assumptions identified in the Bellmere Local Transport Strategy 2038, with queues reported in metres as well as vehicles. This is needed to understand whether stationary traffic would obstruct the existing goods entrance to the Eastfold Trading Estate.

8.7 Construction traffic would use the A6142 and the temporary access shown near Kiln Lane. The construction traffic management plan gives a daily average for heavy goods vehicles but does not identify the likely highest hourly flow during earthworks. It also assumes that deliveries can be spread evenly across a working day. That may not be achievable when a pour or a short possession of the railway requires materials to arrive together. The Council asks for an hourly profile for each main construction phase, accompanied by swept-path drawings for the temporary junction, the rail bridge approach and the tight bend on Kiln Lane. The drawings should show the position of temporary signs and pedestrian barriers, not just the swept path of the vehicle body.

8.8 The application proposes to keep Footpath 14 open by means of a temporary crossing. The crossing is welcome in principle, but the submitted layout is indicative and does not show its relationship to the temporary traffic lights or the drainage ditch. A dimensioned drawing should establish the available width for walkers, the waiting area on both sides and the arrangement during night working. Any short closure should be stated in the construction programme and secured through the traffic requirement. The Council does not consider a statement that the route will be maintained ‘where practicable’ sufficiently precise.

Drainage and water environment

8.9 The road embankment and associated culverts would change runoff paths toward Reedfen Brook. The drainage strategy adopts an allowable discharge rate and provides attenuation storage, but the supporting calculations do not include a clearly labelled check for blockage at the eastern culvert. The Council asks for a blockage scenario and an exceedance plan showing where water would travel if the design event were exceeded or an inlet became obstructed. The plan should cover the construction condition as well as the completed road, since temporary stockpiles and haul surfaces can redirect shallow flows.

8.10 There is also a discrepancy between the outfall level in Drawing BEL-DRA-217 Rev C and the level used in the hydraulic calculation summary. It may be a drafting error, but the difference affects the stated freeboard. A single revised schedule of levels, tied to the same datum throughout, would allow the design to be checked. The Council seeks a requirement that the final drainage scheme be approved before earthworks begin in the relevant catchment. That requirement should include inspection access, a maintenance schedule and confirmation of who will maintain each element after opening. The Council's concern is not that the drainage concept is inherently unsuitable; it is that the present figures cannot all be reconciled.

Landscape, ecology and lighting

8.11 The most conspicuous change in views would occur where the new embankment rises above the existing field boundary east of Marsh Gate. Planting on the embankment is proposed, although its effect during the first growing seasons would be limited. The landscape and visual assessment should distinguish more clearly between the effect at opening and the effect after planting has established. The Council recommends a schedule of replacement planting that sets out species, stock size, watering and the period for replacing failures. Retained hedges should be fenced before site clearance; a general commitment to protect vegetation is not enough where the working width is narrow.

8.12 Survey material records badger activity in Broadmere Wood and bat foraging along the wider brook corridor. Those descriptions identify broad areas only and are adequate for this report. The issue for the examination is whether the proposed lighting and vegetation clearance would interrupt habitat connectivity. The Council asks for a lighting contour drawing that includes the temporary works compound, with the operating hours and lamp orientation specified. It should be read alongside the final landscape drawing, so that any gap in the proposed screening can be identified before detailed design is approved. No additional lighting should be assumed simply because a route is shown as available for maintenance.

Planning controls and overall position

8.13 The Bellmere Local Plan Policy EN6 requires new infrastructure to manage runoff without increasing flood risk elsewhere, while Policy TR4 seeks safe and convenient walking routes through and around major works. The Council considers that both policies can be met in principle, subject to the drawings and controls requested above. Its comments on local policy do not replace the assessment required under the National Policy Statement for National Networks. Rather, they identify where the present application material leaves uncertainty about effects within the borough.

8.14 Before the close of the examination, the Council requests an updated construction traffic management plan, the crossing drawing for Footpath 14, a consistent drainage level schedule, exceedance drawings and the combined lighting and landscape information. These items should be submitted as controlled documents with revision numbers. If the information confirms that access can be maintained and exceedance flows contained within the proposed drainage corridor, the remaining local effects are likely to be manageable by requirements. Without it, the Council cannot yet conclude that the effects on highway operation, flood risk and the public route have been adequately assessed.

8.15 The Council has reviewed the junction capacity note submitted by Hearthmere Transit Infrastructure Ltd for the Bellmere Eastern Link. The assessment uses a single construction peak hour for movements between the A4176 Mereway and the proposed eastern compound. It does not show how the assumed vehicle profile changes when earthworks and bridge deliveries overlap. The Council therefore considers the forecast queue at the Mereway/Foundry Lane junction to be insufficiently tested. A sensitivity run should include the maximum daily HGV movements in both directions, with the temporary signal arrangement shown on drawing CT-204 Rev C.

8.16 In landscape terms, the proposed cutting reduces the visibility of through traffic from the Bellmere Marshes edge. However, the submitted winter views do not include the lighting columns at their proposed height. The planting schedule also relies on establishment within five years, while no interim screening is identified beside Footpath 14. The Council requests a combined winter photomontage and planting plan so that the residual effect can be assessed on a consistent basis.

8.17 The drainage strategy directs runoff towards the eastern attenuation basin before discharge to the Wren Beck corridor. The stated basin storage volume is unchanged across the latest drawings, but the inlet and outlet levels differ between the drainage report and the longitudinal section. Until those levels are reconciled, the Council cannot verify the exceedance route or confirm that water will remain outside the highway boundary during the design storm.

8.18 These points do not amount to an objection in principle. They are matters requiring corrected, coordinated drawings and, where necessary, enforceable construction and maintenance requirements.

8.19 Cllr Ada Venn and Cllr Orin Pell have asked that the corrected drainage drawings be available before the next hearing. Neri Talwick MP has likewise requested a clear explanation of who will maintain the basin after construction. These requests do not alter the Council’s position at paragraph 8.18.

8.20 At the ward drop-in, Mrs Livia Nett said the uncertainty about flooding was affecting her sleep. Eren Dobble asked whether the revised outfall would disturb badger activity in Upper Wren Wood. Neither attendee submitted a representation to the examination. Their comments are recorded here as local concerns, not as evidence that flooding or ecological harm will occur.

8.21 Mara Fenwick, Bellmere Borough Council reporting officer, will coordinate the Council’s response to any revised drawings from Hearthmere Transit Infrastructure Ltd. Correspondence should be sent to planning@bellmere-borough.gov.uk or Council House, 14 Lantern Square, Bellmere BM4 6QJ. The Council has also used the guidance at https://www.gov.uk/ when preparing this report.
