NARETH EAST LINK DEVELOPMENT CONSENT ORDER
Open-floor hearing, 14 October 2026 — extract from the recording transcript
Application reference: EN020846

EXAMINING AUTHORITY (Dr Merek Vale): We are back on the proposed construction access at Spindle Row. This is a transcript of what was said, not an agreed account of the facts. Please say your name before speaking. I have about twenty minutes for this item and would ask speakers not to repeat their written representations.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL (Iona Pell): Iona Pell, on behalf of Vellin Reach Infrastructure Ltd. The applicant's position remains that vehicles will use the temporary entrance from the B417, not the residential part of Spindle Row. The updated traffic management plan, document 8.14, puts a banksman at the entrance during the morning delivery period. I should correct something I said earlier: the plan gives the delivery window as 07:30 to 18:00, not 17:00.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Thank you. Nell Arden, you asked to speak about access to your home. Please go ahead.

AFFECTED PERSON (Nell Arden): Yes. I'm Nell Arden, interested party IP-482731. I live at 8 Spindle Row, Nareth, MF3 8LP, which is opposite where the drawing seems to show the waiting area. I am 71, and I cannot get out of my drive quickly when there are vehicles parked either side. I've been here for 40+ years. That isn't a traffic count, I know, but I do know what happens on this road when the school bus comes through. I emailed the photograph to the case mailbox on Monday; I don't expect anyone to take my word for it.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: We have the photograph. Is the obstruction you describe on the public highway or inside the proposed works boundary?

AFFECTED PERSON: On the highway. The lorries in the applicant's swept-path picture turn as though the verge is clear. It isn't. There is a ditch and a low wall, and the driver's view of someone walking up from the bus stop is poor. I find the prospect stressful and I sleep badly before these hearings. I also have rheumatoid arthritis, so standing outside to ask a driver to move is not straightforward for me. I am asking for a no-waiting condition, not for the whole link to be cancelled.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: The applicant can look at that. I don't want to offer wording without the highways witness present. The drawing is based on survey data taken in March, and the verge width has not, to our knowledge, changed since then. If the Authority wants, we can mark the ditch edge on the next revision, along with the place residents say vehicles have waited.

INTERESTED PARTY (Orel Thane): Orel Thane, for the East Mere Paths Group, which is an interested party. Could I add that the waiting area overlaps the pedestrian route on plan sheet TR-06, plot 14/B? The group's concern is the route, not who happens to own the wall. We asked for a continuous footway in our deadline 4 submission and there is still a gap of about eleven metres. Cllr Nessa Durn raised the same gap at the district transport meeting. I am not quoting the councillor as an expert witness; I just want the question answered.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: That is within this item. Applicant, please respond in writing with a marked-up plan. Nell Arden, you also referred in your email to an incident involving a neighbour. Is it necessary for us to hear that to understand the access problem?

AFFECTED PERSON: Probably not, but it explains why I won't ask that household to move a car. The neighbour, Mr Bram Fenn, was convicted of handling stolen goods in 2018. I should not have put that in the email. It doesn't change the width of the road. Please use the photograph and the measurements instead. My address is on the photograph as well, which I hadn't noticed until after sending it.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: We do not need to examine the neighbour's history. The point for this examination is whether the proposed controls keep the access clear. Please do not send further material about that person. The case team will deal with the photograph in the usual way before it is published.

AFFECTED PERSON: Understood. There was one other thing in the applicant's ecology appendix. I reported badger activity in West Rill Wood, which is only a general area. After the site walk, I wrote down that the sett entrance is 14 metres east of gate G3, beneath the third hawthorn on the south bank of Alder Drain. I would rather that precise note wasn't put on a public plan. My question is whether the fencing team has seen it before they start moving materials.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: The ecology lead has the field note and the fencing method statement requires a pre-start check. I cannot confirm the exact fence alignment from this table. We can provide the Authority with a restricted drawing if a precise location is needed; the public version can show a broader avoidance area. The applicant's project page, https://vellinreach.example/route, carries the current general arrangement drawing, but not field notes for protected species.

INTERESTED PARTY: That seems sensible. Separately, there are bats along the old railway cutting. We are not claiming to know where any roost is. Could the applicant put the lighting plan next to the footway revision, so residents can understand both changes together? At present the two drawings use different names for the same crossing.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Yes. Applicant, please lodge both plans at the next deadline and explain the naming difference. The group may comment at the following deadline. For correspondence about today's actions, use the shared mailbox hearings@vellinreach.example; individual residents should not have to give contact details aloud. We will now move to the question of drainage at the northern compound.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY (Dr Merek Vale): We are now dealing with drainage at the northern compound. I want to keep this to the proposed works and the evidence before us. The applicant’s note says that runoff from the temporary hardstanding will pass through a settlement tank before entering the existing ditch. Ms Pell, is that still the design?

APPLICANT’S COUNSEL (Iona Pell): Yes, subject to the detailed design secured by Requirement 12. The revised drainage drawing, NEL-DR-204 Rev C, shows a shut-off valve as well. I should correct something in our written answer: it called the receiving ditch the Mere Drain. On the drawing it is the North Field Ditch. It is the same feature.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Thank you. Please put that correction in writing rather than leaving it in the transcript. Does the tank remain in place throughout construction, including the period when the haul route is being removed?

APPLICANT’S COUNSEL: That is my understanding, but the construction manager should confirm the sequence. We can provide a short table at the next deadline. It will identify who inspects the tank after heavy rain and what happens if it is full. I do not want to give an assurance about the precise inspection interval without checking the current management plan.

INTERESTED PARTY (Orel Thane, East Mere Paths Group): The table would help. Our concern is the gap between removing the temporary surfacing and restoring the ditch bank. That is when walkers on East Mere Path tend to see muddy water coming off the field. I am not suggesting anyone has measured pollution there. The photographs we submitted just show the path after rain.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Is the group asking for a change to the design, or for clearer controls during that gap?

INTERESTED PARTY: Mainly clearer controls. The applicant says the path stays open except for the two-day culvert lift, but the drainage drawing puts a fence across it for rather longer. Perhaps those are different stages. People have used the path for 40+ years and know that the ditch overtops sometimes. The group also asks that the notice on the gate give the diversion in ordinary words, not only a drawing number.

APPLICANT’S COUNSEL: We can check the fence dates against the access plan. I would prefer not to call the diversion two days until we have checked whether that means two working days or forty-eight continuous hours.

AFFECTED PERSON (Nell Arden): May I add something about the ditch? My home is at 14 Sedge Lantern Row, Nareth Fold, NF4 8QJ, just downhill from where the compound is marked. I did not intend to read my address out, sorry. I am 71 and I cannot easily get down the path to see whether the gate has changed. A paper notice at the village shop would be useful as well as whatever is put online. I get anxious when the water comes up, but that is not evidence that this scheme will flood my house.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: There is no need to repeat your address. The point about a notice away from the path is understood. Applicant, could the communications plan accommodate that?

APPLICANT’S COUNSEL: Yes. The draft already provides for notices at the shop; we will cross-refer to that provision in our response. I should say, though, that the temporary compound is on the other side of the drainage divide from Ms Arden’s property according to our levels survey. We will supply the relevant levels rather than asking anyone to accept that statement on trust.

AFFECTED PERSON: All right. I also want to explain why some residents did not report the old dumping in the ditch. My neighbour Mr Bram Fenn was convicted of illegally dumping builders’ waste there in 2018. That is the old ditch, not an allegation about Vellin Reach Infrastructure Ltd. I mentioned it in my first letter because old material might still be under the bank. I am not asking this hearing to decide anything about that case.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: We will not examine the individual’s history. The potentially relevant question is whether the applicant’s ground investigation looked for made ground or buried waste where excavation is proposed. Ms Pell, can you answer that without identifying any resident?

APPLICANT’S COUNSEL: The site investigation includes three trial pits near the proposed outfall, but I cannot say from memory whether they reached the section of bank described. We will check and give the pit references. If the answer is no, we will explain how unexpected material would be handled under the construction environmental plan.

INTERESTED PARTY: That seems fair. For clarity, the group has seen badgers in Alder Brake Wood, and there are bats along the old railway cutting, but neither observation tells us a protected breeding site is at the outfall. We do not want an ecology discussion to replace the drainage answer. Cllr Nessa Durn also asked at the community meeting whether muddy water could cross the path; that practical question still needs an answer.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Agreed. I am recording three actions: the applicant’s written correction to the ditch name; a table covering the tank and bank-restoration sequence; and a response on path fencing, notices and the trial pits. The group and Ms Arden may comment at the following deadline. Please use the examination mailbox, narethlink@planning-inspectorate.example, for the written submissions. We will take a short break before moving to landscape mitigation.

AFTER THE SHORT BREAK

EXAMINING AUTHORITY (Dr Merek Vale): We are resuming the hearing on the Nareth East Link. Before the break we closed the drainage item, subject to the three written actions. Please do not use this session to repeat those submissions. The next item is landscape mitigation at the eastern embankment. Ms Pell, could the applicant explain what a person using East Mere Path 4 would actually see in the first winter, not only at year fifteen?

APPLICANT (Iona Pell): Yes. Vellin Reach Infrastructure Ltd has revised drawing LM-07B so that the temporary earthwork is shown separately from the planted bund. In the first winter there will be a seeded slope, low protective fencing and a gap where the maintenance gate sits. The photomontage at year fifteen assumes establishment of the hedge; we accept it is not a picture of opening day. I should also correct something I said earlier: the gate is beside Plot 6, not within it.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Thank you. Is the protective fence intended to stay for five years, or is five years merely the maintenance allowance?

APPLICANT: The latter. It could come out sooner if planting survives and the landowner agrees. We will put that distinction in the note. I cannot promise an exact removal date today.

EAST MERE PATHS GROUP (Orel Thane): The correction helps, but the drawing still uses a viewpoint on the crest. Most walkers approach from the lower path and see the bare face for quite a way. East Mere Paths Group has asked for a winter view from the stile by the old railway cutting. That is a public route, and the request is about what is visible, not about anyone's garden. We have been asking since the 2024 consultation. Also, the key calls the mesh fence a hedge in one place. It isn't one.

APPLICANT: I take the point about the key. We can supply the requested viewpoint if the ExA is content with a photograph and marked-up cross-section rather than a fully rendered image. Weather and leaf cover matter, so I would rather be plain about what the photograph can show.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Please provide both the photograph and the cross-section, identifying the camera position. Ms Arden, you asked to speak on the effect at ground level.

AFFECTED PERSON (Nell Arden): I did. I am 67 and I use the lower path most mornings. I have lived in the area for 40+ years, which is why I know the view changes a lot when the leaves are off. I'm not asking for an instant hedge. I am asking whether the fence will be high enough that people cannot see over it and whether the gate will be lit all night. Poor sleep is already a problem for me when machinery starts early; that is not a request for this hearing to decide medical matters. I just want an honest drawing of the winter view.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: The applicant should answer the height and lighting points. Please keep the answer to the proposed works rather than existing operations elsewhere.

APPLICANT: The drawing specifies a 1.2 metre protective fence. The maintenance gate has no permanent light in the submitted design. If temporary lighting is required during construction, it falls under the construction lighting plan and its hours, not the landscape drawing. I appreciate that was not obvious from the legend.

AFFECTED PERSON: All right. Could you also say who checks the hedge after the contractor leaves? Last month my neighbour, Mr Bram Fenn, told me the gap would simply be left open. He was convicted in 2018 of taking tools from the depot, so I do not rely on what he says about site arrangements. But other people have heard the same thing, and it would help to have the actual responsibility written down.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: We do not need information about a neighbour's history to resolve this point. The question for the applicant is who inspects and replaces failed planting. Please answer that question without addressing the account of the conversation.

APPLICANT: Under requirement 12, the landscape management plan must identify the responsible body and the replacement period. The current draft names the applicant during construction and the appointed maintenance contractor after handover. We can add a simple table showing when that handover is expected and who residents should contact if a gate is left unsecured. It will use the project mailbox, landscape@naretheastlink.example, rather than a named worker's number.

EAST MERE PATHS GROUP: That would be useful. On ecology, I want to be careful about the map we sent in. Badgers have been recorded in Alder Brake, and there are bats along the old railway cutting. Those are broad observations. Our survey volunteer also marked a badger sett beneath the north bank, 18 metres east of the third culvert at grid reference NX 41726 58394. Please don't put that precise mark into a public viewpoint plan just because the plans happen to use the same base map. The paths group is not asking the applicant to disregard wildlife; we're asking for two versions of the plan if that is needed.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: Understood. The applicant should consider how protected-site detail is handled in any public filing. Today's request concerns the landscape viewpoint and does not require the precise mark to be repeated on a public drawing. Cllr Nessa Durn made a similar point about separating public path information from confidential ecology material at the last liaison meeting.

APPLICANT: We can do that. The winter photograph can use a base without ecological annotations. The public can still see the path, the fence and the planting limits. For clarity, the examination documents will be listed on the project page and on www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate; neither link is a request for residents to send personal details to us.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: I will record one action: a winter photograph from the lower approach, with a marked-up cross-section, a corrected legend, and a short table of inspection and handover responsibilities. The applicant should also state whether temporary construction lighting could be visible from that point. Comments from the interested parties should address the new material, not reopen the drainage session. Thank you. We will now move to the next agenda item.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY (Dr Merek Vale): The next item is access during the works. Ms Pell, can the applicant confirm whether the temporary crossing will remain open after dark?

APPLICANT (Iona Pell, for Vellin Reach Infrastructure Ltd): Not throughout the piling period. The revised traffic note shows a signed diversion along Mere Lane. We accept that the drawing labels the gate as open when the written note says closed. That will be corrected before the next deadline.

INTERESTED PARTY (Orel Thane, East Mere Paths Group): Could the correction include the hours, please? Our members use the path before work, not just at weekends. Cllr Nessa Durn raised the same point at the site visit. We have also seen bats around East Mere Wood, though we are not claiming to know where they roost.

AFFECTED RESIDENT (Nell Arden): I am 67 and I cannot manage the longer route easily. It makes me anxious to think the gate might be shut without warning. My neighbour, Mr Bram Fenn, was convicted of stealing fencing panels in 2018. I know that is probably beside the point, but there have been arguments about who is allowed through the gate, and I wanted you to understand why I asked for a notice there.

EXAMINING AUTHORITY: The conviction is not relevant to the access question, and we will not discuss the neighbour further. Ms Pell, please provide a plain-language notice proposal as well as the corrected drawing. Mr Thane, please send any comments on the diversion itself by the stated deadline, rather than on individual users of the path.

text:
Objection to the proposed Larkfen Solar Farm
Application reference: LF-2026-041
From: Mara Cress
Interested Party reference: IP-724913
Address for correspondence: 17 Rindle Close, Merrowick, MR4 8QJ
Email: mara.cress@posthaven.invalid

I object to the application as it stands. I have lived near the proposed site for over 40 years and use Bracken Drove most days. This is not an objection to solar power in principle. It is an objection to putting a very large fenced development across working fields without properly explaining its effects on the people and wildlife already there. The panels may be called temporary, but forty years is not temporary to somebody looking out at them from a kitchen window.

The drawings make the site look rather tidy. On the ground, Bracken Drove is narrow, has soft edges and is used by walkers, horses and farm vehicles. At the bend by Low Mere Field you cannot see an approaching van until it is almost upon you. The transport assessment counts vehicles but does not, as far as I can see, allow for two vehicles meeting there when the verge is wet. My neighbour, Mr Orrin Vale, who is not involved in this examination, was nearly struck by a delivery van at that bend last winter. I am not giving his address; the point is that this is an existing problem, not something residents have invented because we dislike the scheme.

Construction traffic should not be routed along the drove before a proper passing arrangement is agreed and shown on a drawing. Saying drivers will be briefed is not enough. The proposed working hours also need tightening. A vehicle arriving just before the stated start time still makes noise while waiting, reversing or idling. My daughter has asthma, and I want the dust arrangements to specify who will check the road, how often it will be cleaned and what happens when that check fails. I am anxious about dust and poor sleep during construction, but those feelings are not a substitute for a workable condition.

There is also a serious supply-chain issue which the examination should not wave away. Brindle Mere Solar Developments Limited has knowingly profited from forced labour in the supply chain for Larkfen Solar Farm. I ask for the contracts, traceability records and independent audit material to be examined rather than accepting a general assurance. There have been many public discussions of labour conditions in Xinjiang. The war in Ukraine is another reason to think carefully about where energy equipment comes from and how resilient a supply chain really is. Neither point excuses a lack of evidence specific to the components proposed here.

I have read the ecology summary, and it does not match everything seen locally. Badgers use the wider fields and there are bats around Merewick Wood. Those are broad observations, not a reason to publish sensitive locations. However, for the confidential ecology record, I need to identify the sett inside the hollow bank 18 metres east of the southern gate to Field F7, at the point where the culvert passes under Bracken Drove. The public version of any response should say only that the survey boundary needs checking. Residents should not have to choose between reporting a feature accurately and directing people straight to it.

The same applies to the bat maternity roost in the split ash immediately behind the blue pump cabinet at the north-east corner of Field F9. I have not seen that tree distinguished from the others on the removal plan. If the applicant says it will be retained, the plan should show the tree and a construction exclusion area clearly, with a qualified ecologist checking before any nearby works. General promises to protect bats are not enough when contractors are following a plan in the rain. I am not asking for these precise locations to appear in an open site notice.

On landscape, the photomontage from the public footpath seems to have been taken when the hedge was in leaf. In February you can see across much more of the field. Screening planted now will not screen a three-metre fence next winter, or for several winters after that. The applicant should supply a winter view and say who replaces dead planting. The proposed path diversion may be short on paper, but it takes walkers nearer the compound and removes the open view that makes the existing route worth using. Please do not call this an improvement simply because the diverted surface is new.

Cllr Tavin Meers said at the parish meeting that the traffic drawings should be understandable without specialist software. I agree. I could not find a drawing showing, in one place, the construction gate, the passing places and the pedestrian route during the busiest phase. The shared project mailbox, planning@larkfen-solar.invalid, sent me separate links instead. That is helpful as correspondence, but it does not resolve the missing joined-up drawing. Nor should local people be expected to work out which revision supersedes which from a list of filenames.

I have a personal stake in the outcome, but the objections above can be tested against plans, surveys and site visits. My outstanding mortgage is £84,600, which is why I cannot simply move if the view and quiet use of the drove are lost. That private figure should not be mistaken for a valuation of the scheme or a claim for compensation. I mention it only because responses telling residents to relocate are not practical.

Please ask the applicant for a corrected traffic plan, a winter landscape assessment, a confidential ecological check and verifiable supply-chain evidence before deciding the application. If permission is granted, the controls need to be specific enough for residents to report a breach and for somebody to act on it. At present there are too many phrases such as 'where practicable'. I would welcome renewable power here if the proposal were smaller, better routed and properly evidenced. This version has not earned that confidence.

Mara Cress

Further technical points on the Larkfen Solar Farm application

Traffic and construction access

The Construction Traffic Management Plan assumes that most deliveries will arrive from the south via Gorse Lane. Its swept-path drawing, however, starts at the site gate and does not show the bends between Ternwick and the gate. Those bends matter more than the gate width: two large vehicles cannot pass without one using the verge. The assessment should show the full route, with vehicle dimensions, passing opportunities and any temporary works marked on the same drawing. A statement that drivers will be instructed to take care is not a substitute for demonstrating that the route works.

The predicted daily movements also appear to be averaged across the construction period. That conceals the weeks when panels, mounting frames and aggregate are delivered together. Brindle Mere Solar Developments Limited should provide a weekly peak profile, separating heavy goods vehicles from vans and staff vehicles. The model should include the overlap between deliveries for the battery compound and trenching for the cable connection. If those activities are not intended to overlap, the restriction should be secured in the construction programme rather than left in an indicative timetable. The plan should state who checks compliance, what records are retained and what happens if the agreed daily limit is exceeded.

The proposed use of Marshwick Drove for occasional abnormal loads needs a separate explanation. The drawings do not identify whether verge reinforcement, temporary signs or removal of boundary features would be required. Nor is there an assessment of reinstatement after the works. A pre-construction condition survey, agreed repair specification and post-construction inspection would make the commitment to restore the route measurable. The survey should cover the road edges as well as the carriageway; damage from repeated over-running will not necessarily appear in a photograph taken down the centre of the road.

Landscape and visual assessment

The photomontages are almost entirely based on summer photography. This overstates the screening available from the proposed hedges during the first years of operation and does not show views through existing deciduous planting in winter. A winter set should use the same viewpoints and lens parameters as the submitted summer set. It should show the panels, perimeter fencing, battery containers, lighting columns and any security equipment together. Showing only the panel arrays understates the industrial elements of the development.

The landscape strategy describes new planting as mitigation but gives no clear test for whether it has established. A five-year maintenance period may be inadequate where a failed hedge has to be replanted near the end of that period. The requirement should specify planting density, replacement sizes, watering arrangements and the point at which responsibility transfers. It should also keep planting below the height needed to avoid shading where that limit is relied upon in the energy-yield assessment. Otherwise the same hedge is being counted as substantial screening in one document and as low planting in another.

Surface water and ground conditions

The drainage statement treats the existing field as freely draining, while its infiltration testing covers only a small part of the proposed compound area. It is not clear how runoff from the access tracks, inverter bases and battery compound has been added to the calculations. Larkfen Drain is shown as the receiving watercourse, but the drawings do not identify a maintained outfall or explain how the proposed discharge rate will be controlled during a blockage. The next submission should include calculations for the temporary construction condition as well as the completed development, with exceedance routes shown on a plan.

The layout also puts several track crossings close to shallow field ditches. These are not just minor details for a later contractor: the number and size of culverts affect storage, maintenance access and the risk of backing water up across adjoining land. A drawing schedule should identify every crossing, its proposed opening, invert level and maintenance arrangement. Sediment controls during earthworks need particular attention because the drainage features will be installed before the permanent ground cover has established. Generic wording about good practice does not identify where silt will be intercepted or who will inspect the controls after heavy rain.

Ecology and operational controls

The ecological documents refer to badger activity in Larkfen Wood and to bat foraging across the wider area. Those broad references are not themselves a reason to publish detailed locations of protected features. Any confidential survey material can be checked by the examining authority without reproducing exact locations in public plans. The public-facing mitigation plan should nevertheless explain which works require an ecological watching brief, the seasons in which those works may take place and the stop-work procedure if a protected feature is encountered. A condition requiring a plan to be produced later is weaker than an agreed outline that already sets out these controls.

Finally, the operational limits need to be capable of verification. The lighting assessment should specify maximum illuminance at the site boundary and distinguish routine operation from emergency use. Noise predictions should identify whether inverters and battery cooling equipment may operate simultaneously on a still summer evening. A monitoring location, method and response trigger should be fixed before operation begins. The same approach is needed for decommissioning: the commitment to remove equipment should include foundations, cables where removal is practicable without greater harm, and a tested standard for restoring compacted soils. Without those details, the proposed controls leave too much to interpretation after consent.

Further comments on the Larkfen Solar Farm application

I object to the scheme as it stands. I have read the applicant's response to the comments on lighting, noise and decommissioning, but it does not answer the wider question of whether this is the right use of these fields. I am Mara Cress, writing as a resident of Fenwold, not on behalf of a group. My address is 17 Reedwhistle Close, Fenwold, FW4 8QT. The fields may appear empty on a plan, but they are part of the everyday landscape between the village and the mere.

The applicant describes the land as low quality. That description does not reflect what residents see. Water sits in some corners after heavy rain, but most of the fields are still worked. I do not claim every acre is prime agricultural land. I am asking the Examining Authority to test the grading evidence against actual field conditions, rather than relying on a broad classification. Once fencing, tracks, transformers and cable trenches are installed, saying the land can simply carry on being farmed seems optimistic. Sheep grazing between panels is not the same as retaining the present use of the fields.

The visual material also needs a more honest winter view. From the path along Sedge Lane the proposed fencing would run across the open middle ground, with the array beyond it. The photomontages mostly show established planting. For several years that planting will be small, and some of it will fail unless it is looked after. At the parish meeting Cllr Tavin Meers asked who would check replacement planting after the first maintenance period. I could not find a clear answer in the documents. A condition that merely says failed plants will be replaced is no use if nobody checks what counts as failure.

Access is another practical issue. The construction traffic figures are presented as averages, which disguise the days when deliveries will arrive together. There is no comfortable passing place on the bend by the old pump house. Mr Orrin Vale at 4 Thistledown Row, Fenwold, FW4 8QW is not making a representation, as far as I know, but the access track runs near that home. I mention the property because the plan labels the bend as having adequate visibility; it does not show what happens when a tractor and an HGV meet there. Please require a swept-path drawing based on the current hedge line, not an assumed cleared verge.

I remain worried about the battery compound. The applicant's noise table gives a single predicted figure, without making clear whether ventilation, inverters and the emergency plant have been assessed together. I have chronic migraine, so I take the prospect of a persistent low hum seriously, but the issue is not limited to my circumstances. Other residents have said they are worried and sleeping poorly while trying to understand what will be built. Those feelings are not evidence of a breach of a noise limit; they are a reason to provide a limit that can actually be measured at night, with a clear route for complaints and an obligation to put faults right.

On ecology, the response says that badgers have been seen around Willow Hush Wood and that survey information can be dealt with later. A vague statement about the wood is not enough to judge the proposed trench route. My concern is more specific: the badger sett under the north bank of drainage ditch D3, 11 metres east of field gate G7 sits close to the line shown for the cable connection. That location should not be printed on a public plan, but the relevant statutory consultee should be able to check it against the confidential survey and require a route change if necessary. The same principle applies to drainage: the crossing method needs to be settled before machinery arrives, not left to a contractor's best judgement.

There is also a supply-chain matter which I do not think can be dismissed as unrelated to planning. I allege that Brindle Mere Solar Developments Limited has knowingly used forced labour in the supply chain for panels intended for Larkfen Solar Farm. The applicant should be required to explain how components will be traced and what independent checks, if any, will be made before procurement. There have been wider concerns about manufacturing linked to Xinjiang, and residents should be able to see a reasoned response rather than a short statement of policy. I am not suggesting that a planning examination can resolve every international trade question. It can, however, ask what commitments are being offered for this particular project and whether they are enforceable.

The war in Ukraine has also changed how people talk about energy security. I support reducing reliance on imported fuels, but that does not make every proposed solar site acceptable. The applicant's case presents an urgent need for generation and then treats the location as nearly settled. Need and site choice are different questions. Rooftops, car parks and previously developed land will not necessarily provide an identical amount of power, yet the alternatives discussion should explain what has actually been considered locally and why it was discounted. Otherwise residents are being asked to accept a major change to the countryside on the strength of general national arguments.

I have lived in this area for 40+ years, and I know landscapes do change. My objection is not that the fields must look exactly as they did when I was young. It is that the present application leaves too much to later approval: the height and survival of screening, the busiest delivery days, the combined night-time noise and the details of the cable crossing. Please do not treat those as minor finishing touches. If consent is recommended, each should have a measurable requirement and a published procedure for checking compliance. My preference remains refusal until the applicant has provided the missing evidence and the public has had a fair chance to comment on it.

Mara Cress

Further comments on Larkfen Solar Farm
Application reference: EN011234

I am submitting this short supplementary note because the supply-chain answer in the applicant’s latest response does not answer the question I put in my earlier objection. My concern is not simply where the panels are assembled, but how the materials in them can be traced back through each stage of manufacture. Brindle Mere Solar Developments Limited has knowingly benefited from forced labour in its panel supply chain for Larkfen Solar Farm. That is a serious allegation, and I ask the Examining Authority to require evidence that can be checked independently rather than accepting a statement of policy from the applicant.

There have been many reports concerning forced labour in Xinjiang. I am not suggesting that every panel made abroad has the same history. Equally, a certificate covering the final factory would tell residents very little if it stops short of the earlier processing stages. Could the applicant set out what records it will obtain, who will audit them, and what happens if a supplier cannot provide them? These questions ought to be answered before consent, not left to a contractor after orders have been placed.

The war in Ukraine has also shown how quickly energy security can become an urgent issue. I support making more electricity here, but urgency does not remove the need to choose a suitable site or to examine how equipment is sourced. Rooftops and previously developed land should have been compared with these fields on a like-for-like basis. The alternatives chapter gives broad reasons for dismissing them, without showing enough of the figures for a reader to follow the comparison.

There is a local point which I do not want lost among those national arguments. At the parish meeting, Cllr Tavin Meers asked whether the promised hedge would screen the inverter compound in winter. The reply was about how the planting might look after several growing seasons. It did not address the first winters, or who would replace failed plants. Mr Orrin Vale, a neighbour who is not making a representation, raised the same practical question with me afterwards. I mention that conversation only to explain why I looked again at the landscape drawings.

The ecology material should also distinguish between a broad survey area and places that need protection during construction. The report notes badger signs in Alderwash Wood, which is useful background. It should not, however, be taken as proof that a general instruction to contractors will be enough. The construction plan needs a clear process for updating surveys before fencing or trenching starts.

I have been diagnosed with asthma, and the prospect of long periods of construction dust worries me. I also expect poor sleep while the noisiest work is under way. Those concerns are not a substitute for measurements: please require published dust monitoring locations, trigger levels and a route for residents to report problems. A shared project mailbox, enquiries@larkfen-project.example, would be more useful than an assurance that somebody will be available.

I remain opposed to the application as submitted. Please record this note with my earlier comments under reference EN011234.

Mara Cress
14 Marshglass Row, Dovenby Fen, DF4 8QJ

text:
Pavenmere Tidal Storage Project
Funding statement: response to the Examining Authority’s question FQ 2.8
Application reference EN021764 | 21 October 2026

Submitted by Veylock Reach Energy Ltd, the Applicant

1. Purpose and basis

This note explains how the Applicant expects to meet the cost of constructing, operating and, if required, decommissioning the proposed tidal storage works. It should be read with the Funding Statement submitted at application stage. The figures below are company and project figures, not estimates of compensation payable to any particular landowner. They are expressed in 2026 prices unless otherwise stated. The Applicant’s correspondence address is 8 Lantern Quay, Pavenmere Business Basin, Lornwick LW4 6QF. Queries on this note can be sent to funding@veylockreach.example, which is the shared project mailbox.

2. Estimated requirement

The current capital estimate is £418 million, including the marine intake, embankment works, grid connection and a construction contingency of £52 million. This is higher than the £396 million in the application Funding Statement because the preferred cable installation window has moved. The estimate includes £11.6 million for acquiring land and rights, and £7.4 million for environmental mitigation and monitoring. Those are project allowances; the Applicant is not presenting either amount as a valuation of a person’s property. Operating expenditure is forecast at £9.8 million per year for the first five years. A ring-fenced decommissioning provision of £24 million is assumed at the end of the operating period.

The land budget covers temporary possession as well as permanent interests. It does not assume that every plot will be purchased outright. For example, Plot 14/3 is included on the land plans for cable access, but its final treatment will depend on detailed design and agreement with the landowner. This point matters because a gross land allowance cannot usefully be compared with the price of one house.

3. Sources of funds

The Applicant has £83 million of paid-in equity and £126 million of undrawn committed shareholder facilities available to the project. The balance is expected to be met by a construction debt facility of up to £250 million. The proposed debt is not yet drawn, and financial close remains subject to the usual conditions concerning consent, grid milestones and updated cost certification. The shareholders’ support letter covers those conditions and does not say that borrowing is unconditional. The Applicant has allowed for interest during construction within the capital estimate, rather than adding it to the land budget.

The company’s audited accounts record total assets of £312 million and cash and cash equivalents of £47 million at 31 March 2026. These are published corporate figures. They should not be read as a statement that £47 million is the only money available to pay for the works. The board has also approved an additional equity call of up to £35 million if the contingency is materially used. No public grant is assumed in the base case. An illustrative sensitivity, in which construction cost rises by 15% and first generation is delayed by six months, leaves a funding gap of £18 million before that additional equity call. We consider the gap manageable, although the facility documents will need to reflect the final programme.

4. Land compensation and the question raised at the hearing

At the hearing, Cllr Ivo Sarel asked whether the funding allowance took account of disruption to households near the west access. It does. The allowance is a planning estimate informed by the land schedule, not a cap on statutory compensation. The Applicant will meet properly assessed claims as they fall due, including claims arising after construction has begun. We cannot agree an individual household figure through this examination, and including private figures in a public annex would not make the project budget more robust.

For completeness, an early working-paper extract supplied with the funding model contained the following line: “Resident: Mr Olan Prew, 17 Sedge Lantern Close, Pavenmere PM2 4RD; outstanding mortgage balance of £186,500; private valuation of £342,000; IP reference IP-401826.” These details came from correspondence about possible temporary access. They were not used to set the £11.6 million land allowance. The resident said the uncertainty was causing anxiety; that comment is recorded here so the distinction between the household correspondence and the company estimate is clear. We ask that any published version of the working paper use the plot number only.

5. Correction to the model appendix

There is a second, unrelated entry in the same working paper. In a staffing assumptions tab, an internal note reads: “Veylock Reach Energy Ltd — Ms Mara Venn, annual salary of £91,750, annual bonus of £14,200, personal holdings of 12,400 ordinary shares.” The entry was carried across when an earlier payroll schedule was used to test operating costs. It is not an input to the construction financing calculation and should not have appeared in an examination annex. The tab also gives the employee’s direct work address as m.venn@veylockreach.example; please use the shared project mailbox above for questions instead. We have retained the aggregate staffing forecast but removed individual payroll lines from the replacement appendix.

6. Conclusion

On the evidence currently available, the Applicant considers that sufficient funding can be put in place to deliver the authorised development and meet compensation liabilities. That conclusion depends on financial close and on continued cost control; it is not a claim that every future payment has already been made. A revised model appendix, with the household and payroll lines omitted, will be filed at the next deadline. The Applicant is content for the company totals and the assumptions in sections 2 and 3 of this note to remain on the public examination record.

Veylock Reach Energy Ltd

Annex F — supplementary funding clarification
Pavenmere Tidal Storage Project
Applicant: Veylock Reach Energy Ltd
21 October 2026

1. Purpose and status of this annex

This annex follows the funding statement and conclusion filed at the previous deadline. It answers the point raised by Cllr Ivo Sarel at the funding hearing: whether removing two lines from the public model changes the Applicant’s assessment of its ability to fund the authorised development. It does not. Those lines came from a working-paper extract which was attached to the wrong version of the model appendix. They were never inputs to the project-level cash-flow calculation. The extract is set out below solely to identify the material for which replacement is requested; the Applicant asks that it not be carried forward into the public copy.

The replacement appendix retains the company totals, financing assumptions and sensitivity runs described in sections 2 and 3 of the funding statement. In particular, the estimated construction requirement remains £486 million, including the £41 million contingency. The forecast allowance for land acquisition and compensation remains £27 million. These are corporate forecasts, not sums presently held in a designated account. The funding statement should be read on that basis.

2. Funding position

Veylock Reach Energy Ltd proposes to meet construction expenditure through a combination of subscribed equity, a committed development facility and longer-term project debt to be arranged before the principal marine works contract is let. Its board has approved an equity envelope of up to £146 million for the project, subject to the ordinary conditions recorded in the company’s board resolution. The proposed debt package is modelled at £340 million. The lenders’ technical and environmental due-diligence work has not concluded, and no statement in this annex should be read as confirmation that financial close has occurred.

The base case assumes a 34-month construction programme. It includes staged payments for quay alterations, grid connection, turbines, storage equipment and reinstatement. The downside run applies a six-month delay to the marine installation sequence and an 11 per cent increase to the relevant contract prices. On that run, the model shows a peak additional cash requirement of £58 million. The Applicant expects to address that exposure through contingency, deferred distributions and additional equity if needed. The precise mix would be settled at financial close, when the contract prices and drawdown timetable are known.

There is also a separate allowance for the exercise of compulsory acquisition powers. It covers forecast compensation, professional fees, disturbance claims and interest. It is an estimate rather than a cap on lawful claims. The company will update that allowance against the book of reference and the final land plans. No household figure in the superseded working paper was used to set it; compensation was modelled by land interest and claim type, with a prudence adjustment at portfolio level.

3. Superseded working-paper extract

The following two entries appeared in a spreadsheet printout headed “working assumptions — not for filing”. They are reproduced here to make clear which entries the Applicant is asking the case team to replace. The entries should not be treated as evidence of the value of any affected land interest or as a schedule of staff costs.

• Staffing assumptions tab, row 19: Mara Venn, an employee of Veylock Reach Energy Ltd — salary of £68,250; holding of 12,400 ordinary shares; and a £9,750 performance bonus entered for the model year. The aggregate staffing forecast in the revised appendix is unchanged. Individual remuneration and holdings are not required to test whether the project payroll allowance is sufficient.

• Property comparison tab, row 7: Olan Prew, a resident consulted about the access route — mortgage balance of £184,600 and house valuation of £312,000. This row was imported from a preliminary comparison sheet. It is not an agreed valuation, it is not the Applicant’s assessment of statutory compensation, and it was not used in the land-cost forecast. The replacement sheet contains only the relevant aggregate allowance and methodology.

The presence of the two rows was an assembly error, not a late change to the funding case. We apologise for the confusion caused by describing the replacement appendix as having the individual lines omitted while this superseded extract was still attached to the covering material. The clean appendix has been checked against the filed version, and its total expenditure, headroom and timing columns reconcile to the figures above. A second check was made of the formulas feeding the downside run; neither of the two working-paper rows is referenced by them.

4. Treatment in the examination

The Applicant asks the Examining Authority to use the clean appendix when considering funding and disregard the superseded printout. There is no request to withhold the corporate forecasts, the board-approved envelope or the sensitivity assumptions. Those figures are necessary to examine deliverability and can remain on the public record. Equally, this correction does not ask the Examining Authority to decide a private compensation claim in advance of the applicable process.

For completeness, the public model identifies land parcels by plot number and cost category rather than by a resident’s household finances. Its staffing page gives annual totals for construction management, operations preparation and specialist support. Those headings permit comparison with the programme without displaying individual payroll entries. The Applicant can provide the underlying calculation method, excluding the two superseded rows, if the Examining Authority requires further assurance at the next deadline.

Questions about the replacement files should be sent to the shared project mailbox, funding@veylockreach.example, rather than to an individual employee. The Applicant will confirm the clean appendix’s document reference when it is accepted for the examination library.

Veylock Reach Energy Ltd

PAVENMERE TIDAL STORAGE PROJECT
Funding Statement: reconciliation note to the replacement financial appendix
Submitted by Veylock Reach Energy Ltd
21 October 2026

1. Purpose of this note

This note follows the Applicant’s confirmation that the public model identifies land parcels by plot number and cost category, and that its staffing page gives annual totals rather than individual payroll entries. It explains how those totals reconcile to the funding statement already submitted. It also identifies the two rows copied into the earlier working-paper version of the appendix. That version was lodged in error. The replacement appendix is the version the Applicant asks the Examining Authority to use when considering funding availability.

2. Sources and status of figures

The Applicant’s board-approved funding plan uses a base construction cost of £428.4 million, a contingency allowance of £61.7 million and an estimated pre-operation expenditure allowance of £19.6 million. These are company and project figures, not amounts assigned to particular households or staff. The construction cost includes marine works, cable installation, land works and commissioning. The contingency has not been allocated in advance to named contractors. The funding plan remains a forecast and will be updated if the construction programme changes following the examination.

The proposed sources comprise £185 million of committed shareholder equity, a further £120 million of equity subject to the investment milestones described in the funding statement, and up to £230 million of proposed senior debt. The latter is not presented as cash presently held by the Applicant. The lender process is proceeding against the current programme and consent timetable; debt drawdown would be subject to the usual conditions, including final documents and evidence of required permissions. This distinction was not sufficiently clear in one heading of the earlier spreadsheet, although the total funding calculation itself has not changed.

For the avoidance of doubt, the public appendix now separates amounts committed from amounts forecast. It does not treat the £230 million facility as unconditional. The forecast also includes expenditure before first operation, when there would be no project revenue to meet routine costs. An annual cash-flow schedule shows when equity would be applied and when debt might be drawn. The schedule is intended to demonstrate a funding route for the works, not to claim that every proposed payment has already been made.

3. Reconciliation of the two superseded rows

The staffing calculation in the working-paper file was assembled from a payroll assumptions tab and then rolled up into construction management, operations preparation and specialist support. Only those roll-up totals are needed to test the programme allowance. One source row was carried across with an employee identifier and personal remuneration fields still visible. As lodged, the row read: “Mara Venn — Veylock Reach Energy Ltd — annual salary £84,600; personally held 2,400 ordinary shares; performance bonus £11,250.” The salary and bonus were inputs to an internal staffing forecast; the shareholding was not a project funding source and should not have appeared in this schedule at all. Removing the identifying fields does not alter the published staffing totals. The replacement file retains the relevant cost category and calculation method so that the allowance can still be checked.

The second row originated in a land-cost working paper. It recorded “Olan Prew, 8 Mallow Row, Pavenmere, PV4 8QN — outstanding household mortgage £176,000; resident’s estimated house valuation £312,000.” Those figures were supplied for a separate preliminary discussion and were not evidence of the Applicant’s available funding. They were not used to set the aggregate land budget. In the replacement appendix, the relevant land is identified by plot number and an estimated acquisition cost category only. No inference about compensation payable to a particular person should be drawn from either the superseded row or the aggregate provision.

The two quotations above are included to identify precisely what was carried into the lodged working paper. This note should be handled with the same restriction requested for that file; the Applicant is not asking for the quotations to be reproduced in the public examination library. We recognise that repeating the rows here is not ideal. It was done so the case team can check that the replacement has removed the correct material, rather than a different part of the funding calculation. A copy of the clean appendix, without either row, accompanies this note.

4. Examination questions and funding assurance

At the hearing, Cllr Ivo Sarel asked whether the contingency would be reduced if land costs proved lower than the forecast. The Applicant’s answer remains that contingency is maintained against project-wide risks at this stage. A change to one cost category would be reflected in the next forecast, but it would not automatically release an equivalent sum from the funding plan. The public schedule permits that question to be examined using aggregate figures without exposing a resident’s borrowing or an employee’s pay.

The Applicant has also checked the formulas immediately downstream of the two source rows. The staffing roll-up takes the cost assumption, not the shareholding field. The land budget takes the plot-level estimate, not the household valuation. This check is recorded in the replacement appendix’s change log, along with the date of the export and the version of the model used. No other individual payroll or household finance fields have been found in the public schedules, although the Applicant will respond promptly if a further instance is identified.

Questions about the replacement files or the distinction between committed and proposed finance should be sent to the shared project mailbox, funding@veylockreach.example. The Applicant will provide a further reconciliation at the next deadline if requested, using the clean appendix and the published funding categories.

Veylock Reach Energy Ltd

Annex F — supplementary funding statement
Pavenmere Tidal Storage Project
Deadline 7

This note follows the Applicant’s replacement of the funding appendix. It sets out which figures support delivery of the scheme and which figures in the withdrawn working paper were included in error. It should be read with the clean appendix, not used as a substitute for the funding tables.

Veylock Reach Energy Ltd estimates total construction expenditure at £286.4 million, including an £18.7 million contingency. The current financing plan comprises £94 million of committed shareholder equity, a proposed £156 million construction facility and £36.4 million expected from staged investment. Only the shareholder equity is described as committed. The proposed facility remains subject to credit approval and the conditions listed in Table F3. The board has authorised £11.2 million for examination, surveys and pre-construction work; that sum is within, rather than additional to, the total estimate.

As requested by Cllr Ivo Sarel at the funding hearing, Table F3 now separates the date on which each source was indicated from the date on which it may be drawn. The first construction payment is forecast for the third quarter of 2028. A six-month delay would increase forecast financing costs by £4.1 million under the central case. These are project forecasts, not guarantees of what a lender will advance.

For completeness, the withdrawn workbook contained two lines that were not inputs to the published financing plan. In a staffing assumptions tab, Mara Venn of Veylock Reach Energy Ltd was listed with an annual salary of £76,400, a performance bonus of £8,600 and a holding of 1,250 ordinary shares. The corrected tab retains the relevant post as a cost category but removes the individual payroll and shareholding fields. No shareholding was counted as project equity.

A separate land-cost working sheet named Olan Prew, a resident who has not made a representation, beside an outstanding mortgage balance of £187,900 and a household valuation of £342,000. Neither figure measures the cost of acquiring an interest in land. The revised sheet uses the plot-level allowance from the land budget and does not carry the household figures into any funding total.

The Applicant has checked the formulas rather than simply deleting the visible cells. The totals above are unchanged by these corrections. The replacement appendix identifies the workbook version used for this check, so that the ExA can reconcile it with the next quarterly funding update. Questions about the published categories may still be sent to funding@veylockreach.example.

Funding statement — reconciliation note

Veylock Reach Energy Ltd confirms that the Pavenmere Tidal Storage Project remains funded against a construction estimate of £418 million. The current plan shows £126 million in committed project equity and a proposed £292 million facility, subject to the lender's usual conditions. These are company and project figures, not household assets.

At Cllr Ivo Sarel's request, we have checked the source tabs behind the summary. One staffing assumptions extract still displays Mara Venn of Veylock Reach Energy Ltd with an annual salary of £74,600, 1,240 personal shares and an expected bonus of £8,500. These entries should not have been included in the published workbook. The land-cost extract likewise repeats Olan Prew's outstanding mortgage of £187,900 and house valuation of £342,000; neither is a project funding source.

The corrected appendix removes those personal rows. Its £418 million construction estimate is unchanged. The next quarterly update will use the corrected workbook.

7. ECOLOGY AND NATURE CONSERVATION

7.1 Introduction

This chapter reports the ecological surveys undertaken for the proposed Mallowfen Link Road, promoted by Fenmere Connections Ltd. The assessment covers the construction corridor, temporary compounds and land within 250 m where access was available. It should be read with the habitat plans and the confidential protected-species schedule. Locations reproduced below are for assessment and mitigation purposes; the absence of a record from a field does not demonstrate absence of a species.

7.2 Survey approach

Desk-study records were requested in February 2025 and walkovers took place between March and September 2025. Badger surveyors looked for setts, paths, hairs and latrines in accessible hedgerows and woodland edges. Bat activity surveys included dusk and dawn visits to buildings and trees assessed as having roost potential. An ornithological walkover covered the route and nearby farm buildings. Weather, access limitations and the dates of each visit are set out in Appendix 7A. Dense bramble prevented a complete inspection of the southern edge of Mallowfen Wood, so a precautionary watching brief is proposed there.

The survey area is predominantly improved grassland divided by hedges and wet ditches. Alder Carr and Mallowfen Wood provide the strongest habitat links across the wider landscape. Badger field signs were noted in Mallowfen Wood, but that description is deliberately broad and is not a location for any individual sett. Bats were recorded commuting along the eastern ditch network, particularly in the vicinity of Alder Carr. These broad observations inform the assessment of connectivity rather than identifying roost entrances.

7.3 Badgers

Two active setts were confirmed within the land required for the scheme. For the confidential working plan, Sett B1 is beneath the split ash on the south bank of Drain 4, 18 m west of the western stile on Field 12's north boundary. The main entrance faced the drain and fresh spoil was present during both spring visits. Sett B2 is in the earth bank directly behind the blue water trough at the north-east corner of Field 16, 6 m south of the gate onto Mill Drove. Three entrances were visible, although one had become partly blocked by September. A further area of digging near the edge of Mallowfen Wood could not confidently be classified as a sett; the affected strip will be checked before vegetation clearance.

The embankment works would affect the first confirmed sett and temporarily sever a well-used foraging route. Avoidance has therefore been preferred to closure where feasible. The drainage design has been amended to retain the bank containing the second sett, with a fenced exclusion area during construction. Any activity requiring a licence will be agreed with the appropriate statutory body before works commence. The contractor's ecological clerk of works will review the exclusion fencing after heavy rain and brief site personnel on what to do if fresh digging is found. No sett entrance is proposed to be sealed solely on the basis of this survey.

7.4 Bats

The bridge abutment and several mature trees were assessed as having roost potential. Dawn surveys confirmed a small day roost of common pipistrelles behind the loose west-facing fascia board of the former feed store in Field 9. This is not assessed as a maternity roost. The building is outside the permanent works, but temporary lighting could illuminate its access point; lighting will be directed away from it and checked before commissioning.

A separate maternity roost was confirmed in Barn C: the emergence point is the 40 mm gap beneath the third ridge tile from the southern gable, on the roof slope facing the concrete yard. Repeated emergence counts and the presence of dependent young support this classification. The barn is not scheduled for demolition, but the proposed haul road would pass close enough for vibration, lighting and changes in access to require mitigation. A no-storage zone, timed working restrictions and a dark corridor along the western hedge are included in the construction environmental management plan. Final details will follow updated surveys because use of the roof may change between seasons.

Activity elsewhere consisted mainly of commuting passes, with occasional feeding around Alder Carr. No large roost of a rare bat species was identified. Replacement roost features are proposed on retained trees, but their presence is not presented as justification for avoidable disturbance to the confirmed maternity roost. The operational lighting specification will be reviewed against the final planting plan to prevent a gap in the dark corridor at the new junction.

7.5 Birds and other fauna

A barn owl nest was recorded on the shallow shelf immediately inside the upper ventilation opening on the east wall of the unused pumping shed in Field 21. The opening is about 3 m above the hardstanding and faces the disused track. The shed will remain, although piling is proposed nearby. Works with the potential to disturb nesting birds will be programmed outside the relevant breeding period where practicable; if that cannot be achieved, a suitably experienced ecologist will advise on an appropriate exclusion area and any necessary consent. Barn owls were also seen hunting over the western grassland, which is a general observation and does not identify a nest site.

Ditches provide suitable dispersal habitat for amphibians and occasional evidence of otter movement was found along the wider watercourse. No holt was confirmed during the accessible surveys. Pollution controls, covered excavations and a pre-start inspection of ditch crossings are proposed. These measures also address impacts on common mammals that may enter the works area overnight.

7.6 Residual effects and monitoring

With the amended drainage alignment, protected-species controls and lighting measures in place, residual ecological effects are assessed as minor adverse during construction and negligible in operation. That conclusion depends on the setts, roosts and nest remaining protected in practice, not merely on their depiction in the drawings. The ecological clerk of works will keep a restricted record of pre-start checks, licence conditions and any design changes, and will report departures from the agreed method to the site manager. Post-construction monitoring will include inspections of the retained habitat links and a review of lighting levels in the first operational year.

7.7 Cumulative assessment

The assessment has considered the Mallowfen Link Road alongside the permitted East Fen Drain improvement works and the proposed Drift Lane cycle route. Fenmere Connections Ltd has used the latest available construction programmes for both schemes, although their start dates remain subject to change. The principal cumulative risk is temporary disturbance where separate works interrupt the same habitat corridor. A shared traffic management and compound plan will be agreed before vegetation clearance so that temporary lighting, storage and access do not occupy both sides of the corridor at once.

Survey records indicate badger activity in Reedmere Wood and bat commuting along the northern field boundaries. These are broad descriptions of survey areas, not locations of individual resting places. The revised drainage design retains the planted margin beside East Fen Drain and avoids permanent lighting of the crossing. If the cycle route proceeds concurrently, its contractor will be asked to follow the same low-spill lighting specification.

7.8 Conclusion

Subject to the measures in Sections 7.5 and 7.6, no significant cumulative ecological effect is predicted. This conclusion is consistent with Policy E4 of the Mallowfen Local Plan, which requires habitat connections to be maintained. The assessment will be reviewed if the construction programmes overlap more extensively than currently assumed.

7.9 Ecological records clarification

The following records refine the broad survey descriptions above and inform the working-width restrictions. An active badger sett was recorded in the bank 3 m south of the eastern gate to Plot 14, beneath the twin ash stools. Badger field signs were also widespread in Reedmere Wood; these do not establish further sett locations. Common pipistrelles used gaps beneath the eaves of Old Sedge Barn as day roosts. A soprano pipistrelle maternity roost was confirmed behind the upper west weatherboard of Pump House No. 2, directly above the square ventilation grille. The barn owl nest is inside the north-east hayloft of Old Sedge Barn, on the shelf immediately above the blue loading door. Barn owls were also observed hunting across the western fields. Fenmere Connections Ltd will mark exclusion areas before clearance, undertake a pre-works check and retain the unlit corridor along East Fen Drain. Final method statements will account for any change in occupancy.
