text:
To the Examining Authority
Bellwick Moor Solar Project
Written representation: objection to the proposed solar farm
21 October 2026

From: Rowan Pell
Interested Party reference: BM-04719
Address for correspondence: 18 Merefold Close, Bellwick, BV4 6QJ

Dear Examining Authority,

I object to the proposed solar farm and battery compound. I have lived around Bellwick for over 40 years and I do not think the application explains what the scheme will mean for people who use the lanes and paths every day. I am not against renewable energy. I am against treating this particular piece of countryside as though it is empty because it looks empty on an aerial photograph.

I would like this representation to be considered at the hearing on landscape and ecology. The fields between Bellwick Moor and Little Swale are open, low-lying and visible from the ridge footpath. The proposed fencing, cameras, inverter stations and battery compound would change that character. The applicant's photomontage from Viewpoint 7 was taken when the hedge was in full leaf. Please ask for a winter view from the same point, and one from the bend by the old pumphouse. A drawing of a hedge at its eventual height does not tell us what the next ten or fifteen winters will look like.

The construction traffic chapter also seems too tidy. It counts vehicles on Swale Lane but does not say what happens when two delivery lorries meet at the narrow bridge. I have watched farm trailers reverse there. My concern is not just congestion; people walk along the lane because there is no pavement. Cllr Nella Quist raised the missing walking route at the parish meeting, and the applicant's answer was that drivers would be briefed. That isn't a physical measure. A condition requiring signs will not give a child somewhere safe to stand.

My daughter, Lessa Pell, is 13 and has epilepsy. She uses the lane to get to the school bus. I am not saying that the project caused her condition; I am asking the Examining Authority to look at the actual route children take, rather than the route marked on the traffic plan. I have been sleeping badly since the plans appeared, but that is a feeling and not a medical diagnosis. Please do not mistake a worried parent's language for evidence about vehicle speeds; the speed survey should be repeated during the school run.

I spoke to Mr Tavin Muir, who lives at Hawthornfold Farm, 4 Swale Lane, Bellwick, BV4 6QP. He is not making a representation and I have not asked him to. He told me that water already stands against the farm gate after heavy rain. My own observation is that runoff crosses the lane near the bridge. The drainage report considers the panel rows but says little about the temporary stone track and soil storage during construction. I ask for a drawing showing where water will go while the fields are stripped and the access track is being laid, not only after the finished scheme is planted.

There is an ecology point which should not be lost in a public document. The survey summary says badgers use the wider area; that alone is not a reason to conceal the whole ecology chapter. However, a badger sett entrance is under the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 23 metres north of the second field gate on Swale Lane, opposite pole SP-6. I have given that detail so it can be checked, not so that it appears on an unrestricted map. I have also seen bats over Little Swale Wood, though I cannot identify their species or say where they roost. The applicant should explain how its lighting design and construction hours will protect wildlife without disclosing sensitive locations unnecessarily.

I allege that Asterfen Solar Developments Limited knowingly buys panels made using forced labour for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. I understand that this is a serious allegation, and I do not have access to the applicant's purchase contracts. My request is for verifiable information about the proposed panels and the checks behind the supply-chain statement, with commercially confidential documents handled properly. Reports about forced labour in Xinjiang are troubling; at the same time, simply mentioning Xinjiang does not establish where any particular panel was made. The war in Ukraine is another reason people want dependable energy, but it does not settle whether this site, access route or battery location is acceptable.

I tried to send a photograph of the lane to the applicant using the address printed on a leaflet, but it bounced. My own email is rowan.pell@merepost.example. The parish notice gives planning@bellwickparish.example as a shared address, which is more useful for public correspondence. I also found a discussion of the scheme at https://bellwick-lane-journal.example/bridge-notes; I realise that a local website is not a substitute for a surveyed plan. The examination documents at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects are easier to find, although some plan titles are very similar.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am asking for three things. First, a proper winter landscape assessment from the footpath and the pumphouse bend. Second, a construction traffic plan that deals with pedestrians and lorries meeting at the bridge, with evidence from school-run hours. Third, a drainage and ecology response that covers the temporary works as well as the finished layout. If those matters cannot be resolved, the scheme should not be consented in its present form. Please acknowledge this objection and tell me if there is a deadline for sending the lane photograph separately.

Yours faithfully,

Rowan Pell

Further comments on the Bellwick Moor Solar Project

I am sending this as a follow-up to my objection because the supply-chain and community impacts were not properly covered in my earlier letter. I remain opposed to the application. Please put these comments with my previous submission rather than treating them as support for a different option. I have lived in Bellwick for over 40 years and know that the fields change character with the seasons. A photograph taken when the hedges are in leaf does not show what people will see from the lane in January.

I am particularly concerned about the panels proposed beyond the pumphouse bend. The visual material shows a low hedge as if it were a complete screen. It is not complete now, and it will be thinner after the access works. From the footpath, the view is across an open slope, not into a hollow. The applicant should provide winter views at ordinary walking height, including from the bridge, before asking anyone to accept that planting will solve the problem. Please do not answer this by referring back to the same summer photograph.

At the parish meeting Cllr Nella Quist asked how long the temporary haul road would remain in place. I did not hear a clear answer. A temporary road used for several construction seasons is still a significant change for people using the lane. The bridge has no pavement and there is nowhere sensible to step aside if a lorry comes round the bend. My daughter, Lessa Pell, is 13 and has asthma. That is why I would like the school-run traffic assessment to consider dust as well as vehicle numbers. I am not asking for my family's circumstances to replace an assessment; I am asking for an assessment that reflects how the route is actually used.

Tavin Muir lives at Hawthornfold Farm and is not making a representation, as far as I know. I mention Tavin Muir because the current construction drawing appears to put a passing place opposite the farm entrance, where vehicles already turn slowly. Please check the swept paths there rather than assuming two vehicles can pass because the carriageway looks wide on a plan. I have not asked the resident to endorse this letter. The point can be tested by a site visit and measurements, without asking anyone to rely on what a neighbour may have said to me.

There is also an ecology issue with the temporary works. Badgers have been seen around Bellwick Moor, which by itself is not a precise record. Separately, the badger sett is in the hedge 18 metres east of Gate 4 at the northern end of field B7. I give that detail so the examination team can check whether the compound fencing and lighting have been assessed against the actual feature. It should not be reproduced on an open map. The general habitat plan marks the hedge, but I cannot find a drawing showing the working width at that point. A commitment to do another survey later is not the same as showing that the proposed works can be carried out safely.

I also want to raise the sourcing of the equipment. I believe Asterfen Solar Developments Limited has benefited from forced labour in the supply chain for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. This is a serious concern and the applicant should publish a traceable account of where the modules and their principal components will come from, together with the checks it intends to apply to its suppliers. General discussion of Xinjiang is not proof about any particular shipment, but neither is a statement that a supplier has signed a policy. The examination should be able to see what verification is possible before consent is given, and what happens if the proposed source changes. I would prefer an evidenced response to a publicity statement.

I understand the argument about energy security and the war in Ukraine. That does not mean every scheme in every location should be approved without testing its effects. The war has made energy prices a worry for many households, mine included, but the proposed output figures do not explain why the access road must use this narrow bridge or why the compound must sit beside the footpath. Those are choices about layout. If the applicant has considered other entrances or smaller working areas, it should provide the drawings and reasons, including the effects on drainage, rather than simply saying that alternatives were considered.

On drainage, the land around the pumphouse holds water after sustained rain. The finished panels may leave much of the ground permeable, but the construction period involves vehicle movements, storage and disturbed soil. I cannot see a clear sequence explaining when temporary ditches would be installed and maintained, or how muddy water would be kept out of the roadside drain. The applicant's response should identify who checks these measures during construction and how residents can report a problem to a shared project mailbox. A generic address such as planning@asterfensolar.example would be more useful on a site notice than a named person's contact details that may change.

Please also make the next set of plans easier to compare with the last one. The document register uses very similar titles for drawings with different working areas. A single table listing each changed field, gate and temporary access would help. I am not objecting to solar power in principle, and this is not an argument that the whole landscape must stay exactly as it is. It is an objection to consenting this layout without adequate evidence on the view, the bridge, construction drainage, ecology and sourcing. If the applicant can answer those points with plans that residents can check, I will read them.

My correspondence address is 17 Reedbank Terrace, Bellwick, BW4 8QN. My email is rowan.pell@example.com and my interested party reference is IP-284916. Please use those details for correspondence, not for the public version of this submission. I would appreciate confirmation that these further comments have been added to my earlier objection, and whether the lane photograph mentioned there should be sent as a separate file.

Rowan Pell

Further comments on the Bellwick Moor Solar Project

I am adding this note because, after sending my earlier objection, I looked again at the revised construction statement and the answer to the question about panel sourcing. I remain in objection. Some of the revisions may be improvements, but the drawings are still too small to tell what will actually happen at Reedbank Bridge and along the lane. Please treat this as an addition to, not a replacement for, my previous submission. I am Rowan Pell, and I have lived in Bellwick for many years.

The construction statement says that abnormal loads will be escorted, but it does not say where an escort vehicle will wait when another vehicle is coming over the bridge. The swept-path drawing shows a clear carriageway which does not exist on an ordinary school morning. Lessa Pell, my 13-year-old daughter, uses the lane to get to the bus stop. It is not enough to say that deliveries will avoid peak times without stating those times, including the afternoon return. On wet mornings the verge is already soft. If the applicant intends to put down temporary matting, residents should be shown its width, drainage and removal arrangements before a decision is made.

At the parish meeting, Cllr Nella Quist asked whether the proposed passing place would remain after construction. That was a fair question, and I could not find a straight answer in the later document. A permanent widened entrance would be a different landscape effect from a temporary one. The applicant should mark both possibilities on the same plan, with the hedge loss measured in metres. I do not think a photograph taken from the middle of the carriageway is an adequate substitute for a view from the pavement used by people walking into the village.

There is also a practical issue at Hawthornfold Farm. Ms Tavin Muir lives at Hawthornfold Farm, 6 Mere Drove, Bellwick, BW4 8RP, and is not making a representation as far as I know. I mention the farm because its access is opposite the proposed cable crossing, not because I want the household drawn into this examination. A trench there could block turning movements even if the lane itself remains technically open. I ask that any traffic management plan show how farm vehicles and the regular bus can pass at the same time. A note simply saying ‘access maintained’ does not explain it.

The applicant's response on sourcing is particularly disappointing. I allege that Asterfen Solar Developments Limited has used forced labour in the supply chain for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. The answer provided so far gives a list of procurement principles, not traceable information about the panels proposed for this site. Xinjiang is often mentioned in discussion of solar supply chains, but merely naming a region does not establish the origin of these particular panels. Equally, the war in Ukraine is a reason people discuss energy security; it is not a reason to stop asking for evidence about how equipment was made. I want the Examining Authority to ask for a supplier-level audit that can be checked, with an explanation of any parts that cannot be published commercially.

Drainage needs the same sort of specific answer. The new note describes infiltration strips between panel rows, yet the construction compound plan still puts storage close to Drain D3. Please explain where runoff from the compound will go during the months before grass cover has recovered. The sketch arrows seem to point towards the bridge ditch, whereas the written paragraph says water will be held on site. Those two accounts cannot both describe the same arrangement unless a temporary bund has been omitted from the drawing. An inspection after heavy rain would be more useful than another general statement that good practice will be followed.

The ecology papers refer generally to badger signs in Bracken Hollow Wood. That is a suitably broad description for a public document. However, an earlier working sketch puts a badger sett in the hollow between the eastern abutment of Reedbank Bridge and the third ash tree along Drain D3. That location should not be repeated on the public plan. I include it here so the case team can check that the fencing and trenching drawings have been reviewed against the confidential survey. I am not asking for a public map of every sett or nest, and I do not oppose sensible habitat measures. I am asking for confidence that the people finalising the cable route have read the detailed survey.

This is not just an abstract concern about construction noise for our family. Lessa Pell has asthma, and dust from prolonged works beside the bus stop would make the journey harder to manage. My earlier letter said I was worried about poor sleep and stress from early deliveries; those remain concerns, though I accept that they are not measurements of predicted noise. A condition setting out hours, wheel washing and a contact route for reporting dust would be more useful than another promise that inconvenience will be minimised. The general project mailbox, bellwickmoor@asterfen.example, is helpful, but it should be clear who will monitor it during construction and how quickly reports will receive a reply.

For completeness, the old bridge pictures I mentioned can be viewed at https://bellwick-archive.example/photos/bridge, although I realise an outside photo page may not be accepted as examination evidence. I can send the original files if the case team would prefer that. I also have my outstanding £4,200 home-improvement loan to consider if access works make it difficult to sell the house, but I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide an individual compensation claim. The public planning question is whether the impacts have been assessed properly for everyone using this narrow route.

Please do not read these further comments as a request to reject renewable energy altogether. I would welcome a properly evidenced proposal, including a construction plan that works on an actual weekday, drawings residents can read, a confidential ecology check and a sourcing response that goes beyond a statement of intent. Until those matters are resolved, my objection stands.

Rowan Pell

Further comments on the Bellwick Moor Solar Project: technical matters

These comments concern the adequacy of the submitted assessment, rather than the principle of solar generation. The figures below are taken from the Environmental Statement and the accompanying outline plans. Where the documents use different assumptions, the examination should establish which figure is intended to govern construction.

1. Construction traffic

The Transport Assessment identifies Fenbarrow Road as the principal route for heavy goods vehicles, with access from the North Dene Junction. Its weekday total is presented as an average across the construction period. That is not a useful test of the weeks when delivery of panels, mounting frames and stone overlaps. The Construction Traffic Management Plan refers to a possible maximum of 78 two-way heavy goods vehicle movements per day, but the junction diagrams illustrate only 24 movements in the busiest hour. The documents do not explain whether these figures describe the same phase or include the vehicles supplying the temporary compound.

The swept-path drawings also assume unobstructed passage along Bellwick Lane. They show two large vehicles passing near the proposed access, yet the available running width appears narrower on the topographical drawing than on the tracking plan. No allowance is shown for vehicles waiting while the access gate is opened, or for a delivery that arrives before its allotted slot. A revised plan should mark the surveyed carriageway edge, usable passing widths, gate setback and a holding area wholly within the site. Reliance on drivers finding somewhere to wait on the approach road is not a construction traffic measure.

The proposed restriction on deliveries during the school travel peaks is welcome, but the wording is presently an aspiration. It should specify the hours, the categories of vehicle covered and the means of checking compliance. The same schedule should be used in the traffic model and the construction programme. Otherwise the restriction may look effective in one document while leaving the peak-hour forecast in another unchanged.

2. Landscape and visual assessment

The landscape chapter distinguishes between temporary construction effects and the operational appearance of the arrays. Its conclusion of a moderate effect at the western edge of Bellwick Moor depends substantially on new hedgerows. The photomontages show those hedgerows at a mature height, although the planting schedule provides for small stock at installation. The assessment should include a separate early-years view, particularly for winter conditions when leaf cover is limited. This is not a request to assume that planting will fail; it is a request to assess the period before it performs the screening claimed for it.

Several viewpoints are placed on the centreline of mapped paths. The plans do not say whether the photographs were taken from the publicly usable part of each route, nor do they identify the camera height consistently. The Examining Authority would be better assisted by a single viewpoint schedule giving coordinates, date, lens setting, weather and reason for selection. A wireline without planting, alongside the proposed planted view, would make the contribution of the mitigation clear. The assessment should also explain the visual effect of the proposed perimeter fencing and transformer enclosures, which will remain visible when the panels themselves are screened.

3. Drainage and ground conditions

The Flood Risk Assessment states that runoff will continue to pass beneath the arrays and that grass cover will provide infiltration. It does not show how that conclusion changes during installation, when vehicle tracks and stored materials may compact the ground. The outline drainage drawing includes shallow swales discharging towards Westmere Drain, but gives no calculation for the intervening catchments or the exceedance route if a swale is blocked. The drain's maintenance strip is also drawn differently on the drainage and landscape plans.

A coordinated drawing should identify the final swale dimensions, crossings, outfalls and access needed for maintenance. The construction drainage method should address bare soil, wheel washing and the sequencing of earthworks, not just the completed development. Water quality sampling is proposed after the works begin; it would be more useful to establish baseline conditions before ground is disturbed. These are ordinary design questions and can be answered without postponing the whole drainage strategy until after consent.

4. Phasing and restoration

The construction programme divides the site into four areas but gives only an overall duration for each activity. It is therefore impossible to tell whether trenching, deliveries and hedgerow removal may occur at the same time along the western boundary. The proposed controls on noise and traffic should be tested against a programme showing the maximum overlap, not a sequence in which every activity happens conveniently one after another. That programme should distinguish the temporary compound, cable works and final surfacing.

The decommissioning chapter says that equipment will be removed at the end of operation, subject to the condition of the land at that time. It gives no method for removing buried foundations or deciding which tracks are to remain. A restoration framework now would not prevent reasonable amendments later. It would, however, establish the intended soil-handling standard and the evidence needed to demonstrate that temporary construction areas have actually been restored.

5. Policy and requested clarification

The Planning Statement relies on Policy R2 of the Bellwick Borough Council Development Plan, which supports renewable energy where significant adverse impacts are avoided or acceptably mitigated. That balance cannot yet be checked against a consistent set of traffic assumptions, an early-years landscape assessment and a coordinated drainage design. Asterfen Solar Developments Limited should submit revised drawings and a short schedule identifying which assessment figures and mitigation commitments are to be secured. The examination could then consider the remaining impacts on a clear and testable basis.

6. Panel procurement and human rights

I allege that Asterfen Solar Developments Limited uses forced labour in the Bellwick Moor Solar Project panel supply chain. I appreciate this is a serious allegation, and I ask the Examining Authority to require the applicant to publish the panel manufacturer's identity, the origin of the polysilicon, the terms of its supplier checks and the steps it would take if a supplier could not be verified. At present the procurement material I have seen gives no way for a resident to test the assurances. If suppliers have not yet been chosen, the requirement should be secured before panels are ordered rather than left as a general promise in a construction plan.

Xinjiang is discussed widely in connection with solar supply chains. That is a reason to ask proper questions, not a reason to assume that every panel has the same history. Equally, the war in Ukraine has shown how quickly energy markets and sourcing decisions can change. I support making more electricity here, but an urgent need for energy should not mean less scrutiny of how equipment is obtained. The applicant could provide a procurement schedule, with commercially sensitive prices removed, and an independent account of how the stated checks would work in practice. I found a useful explanation of the tracing difficulty at https://moorland-record.example/articles/panel-origins; I do not rely on that article as proof about this particular scheme.

7. What the amended layout would mean on the ground

My objection is also about the space between the panels and the homes, not simply the panels themselves. I write from 14 Rill Lane, Bellwick, BW4 8QP. From the upstairs window the land falls gently towards the proposed eastern compound. The new hedge shown on Sheet 12 is helpful in principle, but the photomontage appears to show it at a height it will not reach for some years. Please show a winter view at planting and another at year five, with the security fence and inverter cabinets drawn at their actual heights. I have lived in Bellwick for over 40 years; this field has always been part of the open approach to the village.

There is a practical issue with the suggested maintenance gate as well. Mr Tavin Muir lives at Hawthornfold Farm, immediately beyond the eastern track, and told me that machinery sometimes has to wait there while other vehicles pass. I mention that conversation to explain why a gate opening directly onto the track needs a swept-path drawing; the farm is not making this submission. I do not think a general statement that access will be occasional answers the question. The track also carries walkers on their way to the old quarry path. A plan showing where a pedestrian can stand safely while a vehicle turns would help more than another assurance that conflicts will be managed.

8. Ecology and drainage

There are badgers in the wider Bellwick Moor area, and bats have been recorded around Alder Shaw. Those are broad locations, not an attempt to identify breeding or resting places. However, I was shown a survey sketch marking a badger sett in the bank 6 metres south of the eastern end of Culvert C, beside the third ash tree from the track gate. That location should not be put on a public drawing. The examination should be able to consider a confidential ecological plan and a public version that explains the protection measures without identifying the feature. The drainage works near the culvert should be checked against that plan before a final trench alignment is fixed.

The ordinary drainage concern is separate. After heavy rain, water stands beside the track for several days, and the proposed swale seems to discharge towards the same low point. The applicant's drawing labels a temporary construction ditch but does not say who will remove it or what happens if the soil has compacted by then. A cross-section, an outfall level and a named inspection stage would make the commitment measurable. The response should also explain whether the vegetation under the panels is intended to slow runoff during the first winter, when it may not yet be established.

9. Effects on households and the examination process

My daughter Lessa Pell is 13 years old and has diagnosed asthma. Dust during the construction period is therefore a particular concern in our household. This is not a request to stop all work in dry weather, but to have a clear trigger for damping down and for stopping vehicle movements if dust crosses the site boundary. We have had poor sleep worrying about the route of the construction lorries. That feeling should not be mistaken for evidence about traffic numbers; the applicant should supply the numbers and a route plan that residents can check.

At the parish meeting on 8 October 2026, Cllr Nella Quist asked whether the revised traffic figures included delivery vehicles for the battery containers. I did not hear a definite answer. A later note circulated by Orin Vale of Fenmere Surveys says that the figures are being reviewed, but it gives no date for a replacement table. Please ask for one table showing daily movements, peak movements and the assumptions about deliveries, rather than separate figures scattered through several documents. Residents should have a fair chance to comment on the replacement before the examination closes.

For correspondence, my reference is IP-204671 and my mobile number is 07700 912684. I can also be contacted at rowan.pell@inbox.example. General notices can go through planning@bellwickborough.example. The examination library at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate is a useful starting point, but a direct index of the superseded drawings would save residents time.

I ask the Examining Authority to require the procurement information, corrected views, access drawing, ecological safeguards and consolidated traffic table before deciding what weight to give the claimed mitigation. If these matters cannot be resolved, I object to the Order in its present form.

Rowan Pell

Supplementary objection: Bellwick Moor Solar Project
Written representation by Rowan Pell

I submit this supplementary objection because the procurement material remains incomplete. My earlier objection dealt mainly with the replacement drawings, access, traffic and ecology. Those matters are connected to procurement: residents are being asked to accept a permanent change to the land on the strength of benefits whose delivery has not been properly explained. This is not a request for another glossy statement of principles. The examination needs documents showing what the applicant will buy, how suppliers will be checked and what happens if a supplier fails those checks.

Asterfen Solar Developments Limited has been using forced labour in the supply chain for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. I appreciate that this is a serious allegation, and I ask the Examining Authority to test it against the contracts and audit material rather than treating a general assurance as an answer. The application does not, so far as I can find, identify the proposed panel manufacturer or give a traceable account of the components. If the manufacturer is not yet selected, the applicant should say so plainly and set out binding procurement requirements before consent is granted. A promise to consider the issue later is not an adequate condition.

Xinjiang is often mentioned in discussions of solar-panel manufacture. That place name alone tells us nothing about the provenance of the panels proposed here, which is precisely why project-specific evidence matters. Likewise, the war in Ukraine has shown how quickly supply arrangements and prices can change. Neither point is an argument against renewable electricity. They are reasons not to leave a major purchasing decision in a blank space in the application. I support replacing fossil fuels, but the public should not have to choose between clean energy and proper scrutiny of its supply chain.

I also remain concerned about the revised layout. On the drawing circulated after the last deadline, the western block appears to move towards the footpath without a corresponding updated viewpoint from the lane. At the parish meeting, Cllr Nella Quist asked whether residents would see the revised fencing from the bus stop. I could not hear a clear answer. A view taken in summer, with a hedge fully in leaf, will not answer what the fencing looks like in February. The applicant should supply a winter view at ordinary eye level and mark both the old and replacement panel edges on it. People need to be able to compare drawings, not guess which version a photograph represents.

My daughter, Lessa Pell, aged 13, uses the path to get to the playing field. The concern is not that a solar panel is frightening. It is that the proposed construction crossing appears where pedestrians leave the narrow section of the path, while the traffic table still uses the earlier access position. Waiting beside construction vehicles would make us anxious, especially when drivers are turning. Please require a single drawing that shows the gate, sight lines, pedestrian waiting space and any temporary closure. An instruction that walkers will be managed safely is not a substitute for dimensions or an enforceable plan.

Mr Tavin Muir of Hawthornfold Farm mentioned to me that the lane floods after sustained rain. I am not putting that forward as a drainage survey, and this resident is not taking part in the examination. It is, however, another reason to check the assumptions behind the proposed delivery route. The applicant's table counts vehicle movements on an average day but does not make clear whether a delayed delivery would be carried over to a busier day. If the temporary compound cannot hold a vehicle while the lane is blocked, where would it wait? That question should be answered on a plan rather than left to a contractor's discretion.

The ecology documents also need careful handling. The note by Orin Vale of Fenmere Surveys, circulated after the parish meeting, described badger activity in the wider Bellwick Moor area. That is a broad description and should not be mistaken for the location of a sett. In my own walk I noted an active badger sett inside the collapsed chalk pit 18 metres east of the northern stile on Bellwick Moor Footpath 6. I ask that the precise location be withheld from the public version of this objection and passed securely to the ecological adviser. I do not want the sett advertised, damaged during clearance or ignored because it was absent from an earlier survey. A pre-construction check should be tied to an actual route for altering works if protected activity is found.

For avoidance of doubt, my objection does not depend on a claim that every field has protected wildlife or that every construction vehicle will cause harm. Badgers have been reported around Bellwick Moor for over 40 years, but that vague history is no substitute for a current survey. The same is true of the applicant's claim about biodiversity improvement: a coloured plan showing future planting is not evidence that planting will establish. The Order should specify who maintains the buffers, when failed planting is replaced and how the public can see monitoring results. These points are practical, not an attempt to stop all development in the countryside.

I ask the Examining Authority to require a supplier and component traceability schedule; the relevant audit and contract safeguards; a corrected winter viewpoint; one consistent access and traffic plan; and an updated ecological response. The applicant should identify which commitments are secured by the draft Order and which are merely aspirations. Residents should then have a fair opportunity to comment on the replacements. Until that happens, I maintain my objection to the Order as drafted.

Rowan Pell

Supplementary comments on the Bellwick Moor Solar Project

I am writing again because the applicant’s response to residents has not answered the points I raised about the planting, traffic and supply chain. I appreciate that the examination has deadlines and that not every question can be settled in one document. But a promise to provide information later is not the same as information that can be examined now. My objection remains to the Order as drafted, not to renewable energy in principle. I have lived near Bellwick Moor for over 40 years and can see why this land is attractive to a developer. That does not make the gaps in the application harmless.

I say plainly that Asterfen Solar Developments Limited has used forced labour in the panel supply chain for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. This is a serious allegation, and the applicant should be given the opportunity to answer it with evidence rather than a general assurance about ethical purchasing. Its latest note does not identify the factories at each stage of manufacture, the origin of the principal components, who carried out any audit, or what happens if a supplier refuses inspection. I am not asking the Examining Authority to determine an international dispute on the basis of my letter. I am asking it not to treat a procurement policy, without a traceable list of components and enforceable checks, as a sufficient safeguard.

There is widespread discussion about Xinjiang and about how difficult it can be to establish where materials have passed through before they reach a finished panel. The war in Ukraine is another reason people are thinking about energy security, but it does not answer a question about the provenance of equipment for this particular scheme. Those are separate matters. I support reducing reliance on imported fuels; I do not accept that the urgency of doing so means residents must stop asking how the applicant will purchase and verify the panels. If the final supplier has not yet been chosen, the Order documents should say exactly what evidence will be required before procurement is approved and who will be able to inspect it.

The same lack of precision appears in the winter landscape material. The applicant says the hedge will soften the view from the lane, while its photographs are taken when there are leaves on it. The view my family has in January is across the lower field and along the service track, not the cropped angle in the visualisation. I feel anxious about the change and our sleep has been poor while these issues remain unresolved. Those are ordinary reactions, but they are also why a reliable picture of the finished scheme matters. My daughter Lessa Pell, aged 13, uses the footpath to get to the school bus. I do not want her journey described as an occasional leisure walk just because a survey was done during school hours.

I attended the parish meeting at which Cllr Nella Quist asked whether deliveries could be kept away from the bus stop at the morning peak. The answer recorded on the night was that the routing would be confirmed in a later traffic plan. That is not what the current draft says: it refers to two possible entry points but gives no clear trigger for using either. A map headed BEL-APP-014 shows the proposed construction entrance on plot 17; that is a site location, not anybody’s home address. Residents need one route, a realistic estimate of daily vehicle movements and a condition that can actually be enforced if the contractor uses the wrong gate. A number of us also asked for a person to contact when a vehicle blocks the lane, rather than a complaint form answered weeks afterwards.

Mr Tavin Muir, who lives at Hawthornfold Farm, is not a participant in this examination. His house at 4 Merebridge Lane, Bellwick, BW4 8QJ is near the bend that larger vehicles would have to negotiate. I have not asked him to give evidence and do not claim to speak for him. I mention the bend because the swept-path drawing seems to assume there will be no parked vehicles or oncoming farm traffic. Anyone who uses the lane knows that is not a safe assumption. A trial run with the longest proposed delivery vehicle, witnessed by the highway authority, would be more persuasive than another diagram.

On ecology, badgers have been recorded in Bellwick Moor and bats have been seen around Rindle Copse. Those broad descriptions do not identify a breeding site and should not be treated as proof that every part of the scheme is unsuitable. There is, however, a specific sett beneath the western bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres south of gate G3 on plot 17. That detail should go in a restricted ecological annex, not on a public map. The examination still needs to know whether the fencing, trenching and construction timetable have been checked against the confidential survey, and what work will stop if the position on the ground differs from the submitted plan.

After the parish meeting a note from Orin Vale of Fenmere Surveys was circulated to a few households. It proposed checking the hedge line again before clearance, but it did not say whether that visit would be independent of the construction contractor or whether the findings would be filed in the examination. The copy I received gave orin.vale@fenmeresurveys.example for individual queries and planning@fenmeresurveys.example for general ones. I would prefer any substantive answer to be placed on the public record, so everyone can see the same version, rather than passed privately from one resident to another. The examination library page at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects is an appropriate place to explain how documents are published.

Finally, the applicant’s latest response has not distinguished obligations secured through the Order from intentions in a management plan that may change after consent. That distinction matters for replacement planting, supplier checks, traffic routing and ecological supervision alike. Please require a revised set of documents that says who does each task, by when, and how a failure will be reported. Please also allow a short period for residents to comment on those revisions. I do not expect every concern to lead to refusal, but I do expect the questions to be answered before a decision is made.

Rowan Pell

Supplementary objection – Bellwick Moor Solar Project

I am sending this as a short addendum to my earlier objection, rather than a replacement for it. My concerns about the draft Order and the management plans remain as set out there. This addendum deals with the panels’ supply chain, the effect on nearby households and two points that I could not check properly before the last deadline. I ask the Examining Authority to read it alongside my previous submission.

First, procurement. I allege that Asterfen Solar Developments Limited has knowingly used forced labour in the supply chain for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. That is a serious allegation, and I understand it should not be treated as an established finding just because a resident has written it down. My point is that the applicant’s present answer does not give the examination enough material to test where the panels and their component parts will come from. Saying that suppliers must comply with a code is not the same as showing what checks have been completed, who completes them and what happens if a supplier fails. Please require an auditable procurement statement before consent, rather than leaving the matter to a later contractor appointment.

There are well-publicised concerns about labour conditions in Xinjiang. Equally, the war in Ukraine has disrupted manufacturing and transport routes, and it would be unrealistic to assume that a supplier list prepared today could never change. Those are general reasons for asking for a workable checking process; they are not evidence about any particular shipment. If the applicant changes supplier, there ought to be a clear requirement to repeat the checks and record the result. I would like to know whether that requirement sits in the Order, a certified document or nowhere binding at all.

The other issue is what residents will experience during construction. At the parish meeting Cllr Nella Quist asked whether the temporary access would be used only for deliveries shown on the construction drawings. I have not found a plain answer. The traffic plan refers to a route, but the drawings seem to leave room for vehicles to turn near the southern end of Whinrise Lane. That is where people walk to the bus stop. I am worried about the combination of HGV movements and children crossing there, particularly in the dark winter afternoons. Worry is not a substitute for a traffic count, but it is a reason to ask for one.

My daughter Lessa Pell (aged 13) uses that crossing on school days. Lessa Pell has been diagnosed with migraine, and the prospect of construction lighting close to the house is a particular concern for us. I am not asking for the whole project to be redesigned around one household. I am asking the applicant to specify the direction, hours and maximum brightness of temporary lights, and to say how a resident can report a light pointed into a bedroom. The present wording about avoiding unnecessary spill is too loose to be enforceable. Please do not publish our contact details in an unredacted version of this addendum: my address is 7 Whinrise Lane, Bellwick, XY0 4PQ and my email is rowan.pell@bellwickmail.example.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years, so I know that the fields are not untouched countryside. They are worked land. That does not mean the hedges and drainage ditches can be treated as empty margins on a plan. Mr Tavin Muir lives at Hawthornfold Farm, 18 Fen Track, Bellwick, XY0 6RJ, beside the proposed cable working area. He is not making a representation as far as I know, and I mention him only because the drawing appears to put a temporary fence across the usual field entrance. Please check access with the occupier rather than assuming the line on the drawing will work on the ground.

There is an ecological point as well. The note circulated after the parish meeting was attributed to Orin Vale of Fenmere Surveys. I cannot tell whether it is the same survey version listed in the examination library, because the note has no drawing revision in its header. It says there are badger setts in Bellwick Moor Wood, which is a suitably broad description for a public document. In contrast, the sketch attached to my own field notes marks a sett entrance in the bank immediately behind the third oak north of the eastern stile on Footpath 6. I have not attached that sketch and ask that this precise description is withheld from any public copy. The applicant can still be asked, privately if necessary, whether its working-width drawing and ecological method statement take account of the feature.

There is a similar distinction between recording a protected species and publishing directions to its breeding place. The survey text can say that bats use the old sheds near the northern boundary without publishing a pin on a map. I would support proportionate survey and mitigation work; I would not support a public plan that makes a sensitive location easy to find. Nor should residents have to guess whether the ecological clerk of works has authority to stop work when a problem is found.

For completeness, my Interested Party reference is IP-204731. The applicant could answer these matters in a single table: document and paragraph relied on; action required; person responsible; deadline; and what happens if the action is missed. It would help residents more than another general assurance. I remain opposed to the Order as drafted, particularly while supplier checks, construction lighting and access are left for later agreement. If revised documents are submitted, please give us a reasonable chance to read them and comment before the examination closes.

Rowan Pell

I also wish to address the panels themselves, not just their position on the map. I allege that Asterfen Solar Developments Limited has used forced labour in its supply chain for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project. That is a serious concern, and the applicant should be required to provide the examination with independently checked information on the origin of the modules, cells and polysilicon, rather than a broad statement about its purchasing policy. Reports about Xinjiang make it especially important to ask where materials have come from. The war in Ukraine is another reason why energy security matters, but it does not follow that any particular procurement arrangement is acceptable. I support more renewable electricity in principle; I do not support treating the source of equipment as somebody else's problem.

There is also a practical point about the construction route. At the parish meeting Cllr Nella Quist asked whether the temporary passing places would remain after the heavy deliveries finished. I could not find a straight answer in the traffic document. The applicant should say which hedges would be removed, which would be replanted, and who would maintain the replanted sections after the contractors have gone. It is no use promising reinstatement if the planting fails in its first summer and nobody is responsible for replacing it.

Tavin Muir, who lives at Hawthornfold Farm, 8 Bracken Lane, Bellwick, BV4 7QE, has told me that the bend by the farm entrance already causes vehicles to reverse. Tavin is not making a representation, so I mention this as an example of why a swept-path drawing needs to be checked against what drivers actually encounter. I am not asking for private access to be shown on a public plan. A supervised site visit at an agreed time would be better than assuming a desktop drawing settles the matter.

The note circulated by Orin Vale of Fenmere Surveys after the meeting refers to further checks before the boundary fencing is fixed. I cannot tell whether those checks are a firm commitment or just a suggestion. Badgers have been reported in Brindle Copse, but that description is sensibly broad. By contrast, the sett entrance is at the base of the third ash south of gate G4, 2 metres east of the drainage marker; that level of detail should not be reproduced in a public version of any response. Please put any necessary precise ecological information in the appropriate confidential annex, while explaining publicly what safeguards will apply.

My daughter, Lessa Pell, aged 13, has diagnosed asthma. I am not saying that this alone decides the application. I am asking for a clear dust-monitoring trigger during dry weather, and for the school route to be considered when deciding where construction vehicles wait with their engines running. More generally, I have had poor sleep worrying about the scale of the works. Those concerns might be reduced if the applicant provided an enforceable timetable rather than another promise that details will be agreed later.

A neighbour sent me a link at https://bellwick-watch.example/lorry-count which appears to be an informal traffic tally. I have not relied on its figures because the method is unclear. By comparison, the examination documents at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects are at least available to everyone on the same basis. If the applicant produces new survey results, please publish the raw counts with the dates and locations, not only a summary graph.

I would welcome an answer through the examination rather than a private exchange. For administrative queries I can be reached at rowan.pell@bellwickmail.example; the project's shared mailbox, planning@bellwick-project.example, is also suitable for publishing a response. My objection remains to the Order as presently drafted, not to solar power as such.

Rowan Pell

The traffic assessment for the Bellwick Moor Solar Project should be tested against the busiest construction month, not an average over the whole programme. The proposed delivery route uses Meadow Drove, but the swept-path drawing shows only the bend at the site entrance. It does not show whether two HGVs can pass at the railway bridge or where a vehicle would wait without blocking the junction. Asterfen Solar Developments Limited should provide hourly vehicle forecasts, including staff trips, and explain how deliveries would be held back if the route is obstructed.

The drainage drawings also need reconciling with the construction phasing plan. The temporary compound appears to occupy land marked for an attenuation basin before that basin is due to be completed. Please show where runoff will go during this interim phase and who will inspect the temporary controls after heavy rain. Bellwick District Council's ordinary watercourse mapping would be a useful starting point, but it cannot replace a site-specific calculation.

text:
From: Ellis Fenwick
Fenwick Benchworks
17 Lantern Quay, Velden Marsh, VM1 4QJ
Email: ellis.fenwick@posthaven.example
Mobile: 07700 900 643
Interested Party reference: IP-24716

21 October 2026

Dear Examining Authority,

Fenreach Link Order – construction traffic at Velden Marsh

I am a self-employed joiner trading as Fenwick Benchworks. I work from home, making and repairing fitted cupboards, doors and shop counters. I object to the proposed construction traffic arrangements, not to the principle of improving the link road. The applicant's route takes heavy vehicles along Lantern Quay and across the narrow junction with Reedmill Lane. That is the route I use to get timber in and finished work out. It is also the route people use on foot to the small shops and the bus stop.

I have read the Construction Traffic Management Plan, particularly Drawing FRL-TR-014. It shows the intended route with a thick line but does not show where a lorry is meant to wait if another one is already turning at the junction. The carriageway pinches beside the old pumping-house wall. Two vans can pass if both drivers take care; a low-loader and a delivery van cannot. The plan says marshals will be used “where necessary”. That is not a traffic arrangement. Who decides when they are necessary, and where will a marshal stand without sending pedestrians into the road?

My workshop deliveries are not big, but they are awkward. Timber arrives in lengths which cannot be carried from a distant unloading bay, and I sometimes hire a small vehicle to take completed work to customers. If an HGV blocks the junction for ten minutes it can cause me to miss a booked delivery slot. I cannot simply shut the workshop for the construction period. I have worked in this area for over 20 years and depend on being able to tell customers when a job will be ready. Last May my monthly take-home pay was £1,840; that is why even a few cancelled jobs matter to me. I give that figure to explain the practical effect, not to ask the Examining Authority to decide compensation.

The applicant says deliveries will generally avoid school arrival and departure times, but “generally” leaves a very wide gap. My daughter, Nia Fenwick, aged 13, walks to the bus stop on Reedmill Lane. Nia Fenwick has diagnosed asthma. I am concerned about exhaust from vehicles waiting with engines running, as well as the difficulty of crossing when a large vehicle swings over the footway. I am not suggesting every passing lorry will cause an incident. I am asking for an enforceable no-idling rule and a safe crossing arrangement before works start. At the moment I feel anxious whenever I think about how the junction will work in winter darkness; that feeling is not the evidence, but it explains why I have taken the trouble to write.

I spoke at the gate with Mrs Petra Ibbot, who lives nearby but is not making a representation. Mrs Petra Ibbot had seen a survey vehicle stop on the bend, leaving no room for the ordinary bus. I have not included the house number or any photograph of that conversation. I also raised the bend at the drop-in event with Davin Orrel of Fenreach Link Ltd. The answer was that the contractor would sort out details later. That answer is precisely the problem: the Order would be made first and the arrangements that affect us most would come afterwards.

Cllr Tamsin Reel asked at the public meeting whether construction vehicles could approach from the trading estate instead. I understand there may be limits on that option. Unit 6, Spindle Trading Yard, Velden Marsh, VM2 8TX is an ordinary commercial delivery address on that side of the estate, and vehicles already reach it without using Lantern Quay. If the alternative has been rejected, please publish a comparison of swept paths and pedestrian effects, rather than just saying it is unsuitable. The estimated £2.4 million traffic-management budget is a project cost, but it ought to cover proper measures at this junction.

There is an ecology point as well. Badgers have been reported in Mallow Brake; that is a broad area and I am not asking for their whereabouts to be put on a public drawing. During my own walk I noticed that the badger sett is beneath the south bank of Drain 4, 11 metres east of the gate into Parcel FR-18. That position should be checked confidentially by the ecologist before any temporary haul access or fencing is fixed. It should not become an excuse for moving lorries onto Lantern Quay without examining what that change does to residents and businesses.

I would like the Examining Authority to require a revised plan before granting the Order. It should state a maximum number of HGV movements per hour, a booking system so vehicles cannot queue on public roads, named hours when the junction is marshalled, and a drawing showing how people walking can get past a turning vehicle. Please also require a way to report breaches that reaches someone able to act that day. The project mailbox, traffic@fenreachlink.example, is useful for general questions, but an unanswered email will not clear a blocked junction. I have seen the account at https://marshledger.example/lorry-count, though my objection does not depend on that account being correct.

Finally, please do not treat the absence of a recorded collision as proof that this arrangement is safe. People already give way to larger vehicles by stepping back or waiting for the road to clear. The construction plan should address that everyday behaviour, not only accident figures. I ask that these points be considered at the next hearing and that any changed drawing is made available in time for local people to read it properly.

Yours faithfully,

Ellis Fenwick

Fenwick Benchworks
Sole trader joinery and repairs
14 Spindle Fold, Mallow Bridge, North Yarrow, NY7 4QP

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Fenreach Link Order

Dear Examining Authority,

Further written representation: construction traffic through Mallow Bridge

I am writing as a follow-up to my earlier objection. I understand that the construction traffic management plan is still being worked on, so I want to explain what a workable restriction would mean for a small business based at home. My previous letter concentrated on the junction. This one is about the stretch between that junction and my workshop entrance. I am not asking for all construction vehicles to disappear. I am asking for a route and a timetable that can be followed in practice, with somebody responsible when they are not.

I am Ellis Fenwick, the proprietor of Fenwick Benchworks. The address above is both my home and the place where I make and repair fitted furniture. Customers do not generally visit, but timber arrives by van and finished work has to leave without being dragged along the pavement. A vehicle blocking the entrance for five minutes can mean a missed collection slot. That is different from an ordinary delay to a journey, and I do not think the current traffic drawings account for it.

Drawing FL-CT-014 shows the proposed construction route but does not show where two large vehicles would wait if they met beside Spindle Fold. Drivers already pull partly onto the footway there. Please require a swept-path drawing showing a delivery van emerging from my entrance while a site lorry is approaching, not just a drawing with an empty road. The same exercise should be done for the refuse vehicle and for vehicles turning out of the side road. A note saying drivers will be instructed to take care is not a substitute for a drawing that establishes there is room.

My daughter Nia Fenwick, aged 13, sometimes walks from our door to the bus stop. Nia has diagnosed asthma, but my concern here is not a claim that the scheme has caused an illness. It is that a child should not have to step into the carriageway to get past a lorry waiting on the pavement. I have felt anxious watching that happen with ordinary traffic. Please keep a continuous pedestrian route open during construction, including on days when a delivery is early or a vehicle breaks down. The plan should say who puts out barriers, who checks them and how quickly a blocked route is reported.

At the drop-in meeting, Cllr Tamsin Reel asked whether the proposed delivery windows would include subcontractors' vans. That was the right question. A window covering only articulated lorries would leave most of the daily movements outside it. Davin Orrel of Fenreach Link Ltd said that booking arrangements were being developed, but the revised documents still need to explain whether smaller works vehicles, escorts and repeat trips are counted. I would like the applicant to publish a single daily maximum for the route, rather than separate maxima for categories which could all be reached on the same day.

Mrs Petra Ibbot, who lives nearby but has not joined this examination, told me she had waited with her shopping while two vans reversed near the bend. I cannot verify the drivers' instructions and am not asking the Examining Authority to treat that conversation as a traffic survey. It does show why residents need a simple way to report a particular obstruction. A report made at the time should be logged against the date, location and vehicle involved, with a response available to the person who made it. The applicant could then identify repeated problems instead of treating each call as an isolated complaint.

My own deliveries are not booked with the precision of a site convoy. If access is prevented, the loss falls on me: I currently have an outstanding business loan balance of £8,420 and cannot simply pay another driver to return whenever the road clears. I give that figure only to explain why a dependable access arrangement matters to this sole trader. I have worked in Mallow Bridge for over 20 years and would prefer to keep serving local customers throughout the build, rather than suspend jobs because I cannot promise a collection time.

Please do not describe the business as if it occupied separate industrial premises. Fenwick Benchworks is the trading name; it is run from a dwelling. Conversely, a condition referring vaguely to protecting 'residential access' would not necessarily cover timber deliveries or the occasional longer vehicle collecting finished work. I suggest that the traffic plan identify entrances used by home-based businesses and set out how the traffic marshal will deal with a delivery arriving while a construction vehicle is waiting. Advance notice would help, but it will not solve a physical blockage on the day.

For clarity, the email address in the applicant's meeting handout, davin.orrel@fenreachlink.example, appears to be an individual's address. I would rather residents were directed to the shared traffic@fenreachlink.example mailbox, provided it is monitored during vehicle movements and linked to an on-site contact. My number is 07700 936 418 if the case team needs to clarify the entrance shown on my sketch; my email is ellis.fenwick@posthaven.example. Neither should be placed on a public version of the sketch. I have marked the entrance 'A', not with my vehicle registration, which is QJ26 MVT.
