Technical matters arising from the revised construction information

This section concerns the construction assessment for the Fenreach Link Order. It does not depend on any particular occupier's arrangements. The points below could be resolved through drawings, model outputs and enforceable limits, rather than assurances that details will be settled after consent.

Traffic modelling

Fenreach Link Ltd has compared the proposed construction traffic with an average weekday flow on Mereglass Lane. That is not the most useful comparison for a lane with a single running width at two bends. The relevant test is whether the forecast vehicles can pass the bends, the field entrances and the temporary signal stop lines during the same hour. The transport note gives daily HGV totals but no arrival profile for the busiest fortnight of earthworks. It is therefore not possible to tell whether the stated maximum of 26 two-way HGV movements is spread evenly or concentrated around a shift change. An hourly profile should be supplied for each construction phase, including spoil export, aggregate import and abnormal loads.

The swept-path drawing labelled FL-TM-07 shows a rigid vehicle passing the entrance to Compound B with the opposing lane clear. It should also show a vehicle waiting to turn into that entrance while a second construction vehicle approaches from the north. If simultaneous movements are to be prevented by booking, the booking limit and the means of checking it need to appear in the Construction Traffic Management Plan. A booking system is not a substitute for enough physical waiting space. The drawing should identify the usable carriageway width, not simply the highway boundary, and should show the position of any temporary barriers, signs and drainage works. Those features can materially change the available turning space.

The baseline count should be repeated outside the school holiday period and presented in 15-minute intervals. A daily average conceals short queues at the Mereglass Lane and Alderbank Road junction. The assessment should include a sensitivity run using the highest observed 15-minute background flow with the maximum permitted construction arrivals added. It should report queue length and delay separately for each arm of that junction. A statement that the junction operates within capacity over an hour would not answer the narrower question of whether a short construction convoy blocks access from Alderbank Road.

Construction phasing and controls

The draft programme describes the northern cutting, Compound B and the drainage outfall as separate activities. The works drawings, however, allow all three to be active during Phase 2. A consolidated phase plan should identify the maximum number of crews, vehicles and open work fronts at any one time. Otherwise each topic assessment may rely on a different, less demanding version of the programme. The plan should also distinguish a working day from a day when deliveries are permitted: those are not necessarily the same thing.

The proposed requirement refers to a traffic plan being approved before commencement. It does not say whether a revision is needed when the haul route, compound entrance or permitted daily movements change. Those matters should be defined as material changes requiring approval before they are put into use. The same requirement should oblige the contractor to retain daily arrival records and provide a monthly summary to the relevant highway authority. This would make the limit capable of being checked against actual activity rather than existing only as a forecast.

Drainage and ground levels

On plan FL-DR-12, the temporary ditch along the eastern edge of Compound B ends at the point where the access crosses the existing watercourse. The drawing does not show how water from the ditch passes beneath the access, or where it goes if the crossing is blocked by sediment. A cross-section, invert levels and a maintenance access should be provided. The temporary works must be sized for the period when stripped ground is exposed, which may produce a faster runoff response than the completed landscaped site. A permanent drainage calculation cannot simply be treated as the temporary works calculation.

The submitted flood note assumes that runoff from the stockpile area is kept separate from clean water. That separation needs to be shown on a plan with falls, bunds and discharge points. The proposed check dam is drawn immediately upstream of a bend, where access for removing accumulated silt appears restricted. Moving it a short distance, or showing a workable access strip, may solve the problem. The detail should be fixed before stripping starts; once the compound is occupied, moving drainage across the haul surface would be considerably harder.

Landscape and ecology

The visual assessment uses a winter view from the public footpath at Bracken Rise but a summer view from the approach to Alderbank Road. For a consistent comparison, both viewpoints should have a winter baseline and a photomontage showing the first full winter after construction. The proposed hedge is a reasonable long-term measure, but the assessment should not assign it its mature screening effect on opening. The schedule should specify replacement planting where establishment fails and a minimum period of aftercare.

The ecology documents refer generally to badger setts in Mereglass Wood. That is a broad habitat reference, not a reason to omit the construction boundary from public drawings. The boundary can be shown without marking individual protected-species features. The Environmental Management Plan should explain how surveys immediately before vegetation clearance will alter the method of working if required. This is particularly important where the programme allows clearance and ditch excavation in the same phase.

Policy and requested changes

The draft assessment against the Fictional Regional Transport Statement 2025 says the scheme will maintain local access during construction. That conclusion needs the hourly traffic test, a buildable passing arrangement and an enforceable revision process described above. For examination document FL-2026-0041, a useful update would be one coordinated set of phase drawings, with the same compound layout and maximum vehicle movements carried through the traffic, drainage and landscape assessments. This is a request for a checkable construction envelope, not a request to rule out construction traffic altogether.

Further points on the construction envelope

The point about one coordinated set of drawings is not just tidiness. At present the traffic note assumes the western compound is entered from Brindle Mere Road, while the surface-water drawing appears to show the same entrance shifted east to make room for a settlement basin. The landscape section then assesses the compound boundary in its earlier position. Fenreach Link Ltd should confirm which arrangement is actually proposed, or assess both as alternatives. Otherwise a change made to solve one problem may simply move the problem into another chapter of the assessment.

Traffic modelling

The hourly construction traffic figures should be supplied for each main phase, not only as a daily total. A daily total can hide two concentrated delivery periods that coincide with ordinary use of the road. The figures should distinguish heavy goods vehicles from vans and other construction vehicles, identify empty return journeys, and show whether movements to the western and eastern compounds could occur at the same time. If the programme assumes that they cannot, that assumption needs to appear in the construction management requirements.

The junction test at Brindle Mere Road and Larkspur Cut should use the busiest credible construction hour. It should include the time taken for a long vehicle to turn where opposing traffic has to wait, rather than treating each movement as though it passes through without delay. A simple drawing showing the swept path is useful, but it does not by itself establish how the junction works when two vehicles arrive close together. The temporary signals, if required, should also be included in the delay calculation. It is difficult to see how the conclusion of no material disruption can be checked without those inputs.

There is a similar gap in the explanation of passing places. The draft refers to 'local widening where necessary' but does not say how many places are needed or whether they remain available while drainage works occupy the verge. Phase drawings should mark their chainages, usable lengths and the periods when they can be used. This matters particularly during the ditch excavation phase mentioned above. If a proposed passing place is also the working area for a ditch gang, it cannot perform both functions on the same day. The revised information ought to show a workable sequence rather than rely on a later contractor to find one.

Drainage and temporary works

The permanent drainage design is easier to follow than the arrangements during construction. Drawing FL-D-218 shows the completed carrier ditch and outfall, but the construction sequence appears to interrupt the existing ditch before the new one is connected. Please show the temporary flow route for each stage and the point at which the completed system takes over. The drawings should state what happens if a heavy rainfall event occurs while a trench is open. Saying that pumps may be used, without identifying where water would be discharged and how silt would be retained, is not an assessment of that stage.

The proposed settlement basin also needs to be tested against the compound layout used in the traffic assessment. Its access for emptying should not block the vehicle waiting area. The basin should remain within the assessed limits of land disturbance, including any bund formed from excavated material. I am not suggesting a particular size or method: the concern is that its location, capacity and maintenance access must be compatible with the other temporary works. The inspection schedule in the outline construction plan should make clear what triggers cleaning and who records it. Any change to the outfall or temporary discharge point should be shown on an updated phase drawing before that phase starts.

Landscape and ecology

The visual assessment considers the finished earthworks and planting but gives less attention to the temporary stockpiles. In some views a stockpile beside Larkspur Cut would be higher than the permanent embankment. A maximum stockpile height, duration and location should therefore be part of the assessed envelope. The same information could be used in the dust controls, avoiding two different descriptions of the same temporary feature. Where a stockpile would be moved between phases, the worst-case location in each phase should be shown rather than averaged across the programme.

The habitat note mentions badger activity in Alderwash Wood. That general observation is useful context, but it is not a reason to omit the effect of lighting and overnight storage along the work corridor. The lighting plan should show the maximum extent and operating hours of temporary lighting, including at compounds and vehicle holding points. Its assessment should use the same compound boundaries as the traffic and drainage drawings. The proposed dark corridor can then be checked against the actual construction layout, not only against the completed scheme.

Policy and control of revisions

The Fictional Regional Transport Statement 2025 asks that access effects be addressed at the design stage where practicable. The current material identifies mitigation in principle, but leaves several items to be fixed after consent. A later approval process is sensible for minor adjustments; it should not be used to decide the first workable position of a compound entrance, basin or passing place. Those features affect whether the assessment's conclusions hold. The examination should have enough detail to establish the limits within which later adjustments can safely be made.

For that reason, the outline construction management plan should include a schedule of phase-specific limits: maximum hourly vehicle movements, approved access points, passing-place availability, temporary drainage routes, compound boundaries, stockpile heights and lighting hours. Each limit should refer to a drawing revision. If a later method statement proposes to exceed a limit or move a feature outside the assessed area, the change should require a fresh assessment and an identified approval, not merely a note in a site diary.

These are practical requests for consistent drawings and numbers. They do not require every item of plant to be chosen now. They do require the principal temporary arrangements to be credible at the same time and in the same space. A short reconciliation table alongside a revised FL-2026-0041 would allow the examination to see what has changed in each technical document and whether any assumption has been carried forward incorrectly.

Further technical comments on the Fenreach Link Order

Traffic and construction access

The reconciliation table suggested above should include traffic assumptions, not only the physical limits of the compounds. Fenreach Link Ltd uses a peak construction vehicle figure in the transport assessment, but the construction programme shows earthworks, culvert installation and haul-road formation taking place in overlapping periods. The figures may each be reasonable on their own. What is missing is a check that the same delivery has not been assigned to a different period in the traffic model simply because a work package changed name.

The proposed access from Mirebank Road needs a drawing showing the largest vehicle expected during the culvert works. The swept-path drawing presently illustrates a standard articulated vehicle, whereas the construction description refers to abnormal loads for bridge sections. If those loads will use another access, that route and its operating period should be stated. If they will use Mirebank Road, the drawing should show how a vehicle can enter and leave without waiting across the junction with Ternfold Lane. The assessment should also identify where vehicles wait when a delivery slot is missed. A booking system does not, by itself, provide space to stop.

The highway tables should distinguish daily totals from peak-hour movements and should use the same construction phases as the noise assessment. A total spread across a long day can conceal a short queue at the start of a shift. The proposed monitoring would be more useful if it recorded vehicle arrivals by hour and by access, with a clear trigger for reviewing delivery times. It is not necessary to prescribe every future delivery, but the Order documents should contain a tested upper case that can be enforced.

Landscape and lighting

The landscape drawings show planting on the permanent embankment, while several construction drawings show that area serving as a working strip. That may be a sensible sequence, but the landscape assessment appears to count some of the planting as screening before the strip is released. The planting schedule should therefore identify the earliest realistic season for each area, following reinstatement and soil preparation. It should not treat a proposed plant symbol as an existing screen.

The visual material for the Brindle Rise viewpoint should also be checked against the temporary stockpile heights in drawing FL-2026-0041. The photomontage shows a relatively clear view across the works, yet the construction layout places stored material in the foreground. Either the material is below the illustrated sightline or it is not; a section with both levels on the same datum would settle the point. This matters because temporary effects can persist through more than one planting season.

Lighting deserves a similar cross-check. The construction description allows mobile task lighting, and the ecology measures call for unlit margins near Gorsewick Wood. Both can be achieved if the relevant working areas and hours are fixed consistently. A condition requiring lighting to be directed away from the wood would be difficult to interpret without a plan showing the boundary to which it applies. The general reference to bats in Gorsewick Wood is useful background for the assessment; it is not a substitute for a workable lighting layout.

Drainage and ground levels

The drainage strategy relies on temporary channels during the earthworks, but the channels do not appear on every phase plan. The plans should show where runoff goes while the permanent outfall is unavailable, particularly during the period when the eastern cutting is open and the basin is still being formed. Saying that temporary drainage will be provided leaves unanswered whether it has space beside the haul road and whether it can operate when material is stored nearby.

The proposed discharge control should be shown against the same catchment area used in the flood calculations. Drawing DR-14 appears to take the northern strip into the permanent basin, while the earthworks plan grades part of it towards a temporary ditch. That may only be a difference in construction sequence. A short table giving the contributing area and outfall for each phase would confirm it. Brackenmere Borough Council and the fictional Holmefleet Drainage Board should then be able to assess the relevant phases from one set of figures rather than reconstructing them from separate plans.

For the permanent works, the maintenance plan should identify access to each silt trap without relying on land reserved for the finished planting. Where a maintenance track and proposed trees occupy the same strip, the track width and planting offset need to be resolved now. Otherwise an apparent benefit on the landscape plan could disappear when a workable maintenance route is provided later.

Securing the assessment

These issues are related. Moving a stockpile can alter a view, block a drainage channel or change the distance travelled by a lorry. The construction environmental management plan should therefore refer to a controlled set of phase drawings, rather than reproduce separate commitments that may have been taken from different revisions. It should specify the maximum stockpile envelope, the access arrangements, the temporary drainage route and the lighting zones for each phase. Those are parameters, not a request for a final contractor method statement.

I suggest that the examination asks for a single schedule of assumptions alongside a revised FL-2026-0041. It should say which assessment uses each assumption, identify any limit secured through the draft Order, and flag any matter left for later approval. The schedule would also make it easier to see whether a proposed change remains within the assessed case. At present, the individual documents describe a scheme that may be deliverable, but they do not yet demonstrate that the busiest construction period, the available working space and the mitigation measures all fit together.

Enclosure: technical note on construction access, drainage and landscape measures
Fenreach Link Order

This note follows the letter above and sets out the points I think need to be shown on the drawings before the construction arrangements are approved. It does not propose a different route. The issue is whether the proposed route can be built while keeping the adjoining road network and drainage working.

1. Construction traffic

The Construction Traffic Management Plan uses a daily total for heavy goods vehicles, but the junction assessment appears to use an hourly arrival profile. Those are not interchangeable. Fenreach Link Ltd should provide a table for each construction phase showing the maximum arrivals and departures in any rolling hour, the number of abnormal loads, and the assumptions about vehicles waiting off site. A daily cap alone could still allow most deliveries to arrive in the same hour.

The drawing for the Brindle Lane / East Mere Road junction should show swept paths for two vehicles meeting, not just a single vehicle turning through an empty junction. The current tracking line crosses the centre of East Mere Road at the point where the road narrows beside the culvert. If temporary signals are proposed there, their stop lines, visibility and effect on the queue back towards Merefold Cross should be modelled. The figures should include the busiest construction week, as the letter requests, rather than an average week across the programme.

There is also an apparent difference between the traffic chapter and the draft Construction Traffic Management Plan over the use of Mill Sward Road. One describes it as an emergency diversion; the other permits deliveries when Brindle Lane is unavailable. The latter is a routine alternative route in practice, and needs a junction assessment and a stated limit. It should not be left to the contractor to decide what “unavailable” means. A closure for a planned utility crossing is foreseeable and can be included in the phase programme.

A short-duration count should not be treated as a reliable baseline for this junction. The September 2026 survey was taken before the harvest movements identified in the applicant’s own agricultural access schedule. Either the modelling should include a justified allowance for those movements or a further count should be undertaken in the relevant season. I am not suggesting that harvest traffic determines the whole design; it is simply a foreseeable overlap that the construction plan ought to test.

2. Drainage and water quality

The proposed temporary compound on Plot 14 slopes towards Larkwash Beck. The drainage drawing shows a perimeter ditch and settlement tank, but no exceedance route if the tank is full or isolated for maintenance. A plan should indicate where water goes in that situation and demonstrate that it will not run along Brindle Lane before entering the highway drain. This matters during early earthworks, when the permanent attenuation basin will not yet be available.

The draft requirement refers to an approved drainage scheme for the authorised development. It should expressly cover temporary works and the sequence for bringing treatment measures into use. Otherwise the permanent scheme could satisfy the wording while the highest sediment risk occurs earlier. The plan also needs a named inspection interval for silt controls after heavy rainfall, a trigger for clearing them, and a record available to the relevant planning authority. “As necessary” is too loose to be checked.

The culvert extension beneath East Mere Road has been assessed using the final channel profile. Please confirm whether the temporary working platform reduces the effective opening during construction and, if so, what design storm has been used for that stage. The flood-routing drawing should show both the temporary and completed arrangements on the same level datum. That would make it possible to check whether the proposed bund diverts water towards the road rather than back into the existing floodplain.

3. Landscape, ecology and reinstatement

The landscape figures show the proposed hedge at its anticipated height after establishment. A second view at opening year would help distinguish the effect of planting from the effect of retained vegetation. The cross-section beside Reedmere Wood should also state the width of the maintenance strip. At present the strip is marked on one plan but appears planted on another. Both cannot be implemented as drawn.

The ecological material refers to badger activity across Reedmere Wood. That is a useful habitat-level observation and does not identify a particular protected feature. The practical question for this note is whether the construction lighting design keeps the woodland edge dark while the compound is operating. Please show the lighting columns, maximum mounting heights and the assumed screening, including the period before new planting has grown. A general commitment to directional lighting will not show whether spill reaches the retained edge.

Topsoil storage also needs a firmer specification. The proposed reinstatement areas overlap, on different plans, with haul-road widening and a temporary drainage swale. Fenreach Link Ltd should identify which use comes first, how the soil will be kept separate from subsoil, and when the land will be released for reinstatement. The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan could then use measurable completion criteria, including ground levels, drainage performance and replacement of failed planting, rather than relying only on a statement that the area has been made good.

4. Order controls

These matters can be resolved through drawings and requirements; they need not prevent a decision in principle on the route. However, the approved construction traffic, temporary drainage and lighting plans should be in place before the relevant phase starts. A single approval before commencement of any works may come too early to capture the final compound layout, while approval after works begin comes too late to control the effects discussed above. Please also identify which body will receive monitoring returns and which requirement provides for corrective action if the agreed hourly traffic limit is exceeded. That would make the controls understandable to the contractor and capable of being checked during construction.

5. Construction traffic

The construction traffic assessment uses an average daily figure, but the practical constraint is the short period when deliveries and ordinary traffic use the same junction. The drawings show the temporary access onto Kestrel Lane approximately 140 metres east of the Marsh Fold roundabout. At that point the lane narrows before the railway bridge, and two large vehicles cannot pass without one waiting. The assessment should therefore show hourly movements, not just a daily total, for each construction phase. In particular, it should separate excavation, concrete deliveries and the removal of surplus material. These activities need not occur together, but the draft programme does not rule that out.

I suggest that Fenreach Link Ltd supplies a revised swept-path drawing showing a vehicle waiting within the compound while another turns in from Kestrel Lane. The present drawing appears to assume that the access is clear on arrival. A booking system is useful, but it is not a physical substitute for space to wait off the highway. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should also specify what happens if a delivery arrives outside its slot. Otherwise the hourly limit discussed under paragraph 4 will be difficult to enforce. Monitoring should count vehicles actually entering and leaving, rather than bookings made by the contractor.

The 2025 baseline survey should be checked against the proposed working hours. It was undertaken during a period when the nearby freight yard operated reduced hours, according to the assessment's own survey note. This does not make the survey unusable, but a sensitivity test using the yard's normal operating pattern would help demonstrate that the proposed access remains workable. The results should be reported for the morning and afternoon peaks separately.

6. Surface water and ground levels

The drainage strategy proposes temporary settlement tanks followed by discharge to the Brackenmere Cut. It gives a final outfall rate but not the maximum pumped flow during excavation. That distinction matters where a heavy shower follows several dry days and exposed soil is present. The temporary drainage plan should identify the sequence for installing cut-off drains, tanks and the permanent attenuation basin. It should also state how water will be held if a tank needs cleaning or if a sample exceeds the agreed limit. A drawing of the final drainage layout is not enough to explain that interim arrangement.

Fenreach Borough Council and the Brackenmere Catchment Board should receive the same monitoring returns, with a clear procedure for notifying both bodies of an exceedance. I am not proposing a different final discharge rate. The point is that the Order controls ought to cover the period before the permanent system is available. The Brackenmere Surface Water Note, section 3, already recognises temporary runoff as a separate construction issue, so this would be consistent with the applicant's approach rather than a new assessment topic.

7. Landscape and reinstatement

The landscape drawings show replacement planting along the eastern embankment, but the sections do not show the finished level at the edge of the temporary compound. A cross-section through that edge, with existing and proposed levels on the same datum, would make it possible to check whether the restored slope can support the planting shown. The Landscape and Visual Assessment should also explain whether the winter views from the public footpath were assessed before or after the proposed screening becomes established.

There are general references to badgers in Alderbank Wood in the ecology chapter. This is a broad habitat reference, not a reason to omit the wood from the landscape assessment. The woodland edge will remain visible above the new embankment, and the assessment should describe that combined view without assuming that all planting succeeds immediately. A requirement for replacement of failed plants over the establishment period would make the drawings more dependable.

To the Examining Authority
Fenreach Link Order — construction traffic

I am writing as the proprietor of Fenwick Benchworks, which I run from my home at 14 Rillcut Lane, Brackenmere, BK7 3QP. I object to the proposed lorry route past the workshop. The drawings discussed above show the restored embankment, but not how delivery vehicles will pass on Rillcut Lane while that work is being done. My customers collect fitted units there and I cannot ask them to wait in the carriageway.

At the public meeting, Davin Orrel of Fenreach Link Ltd said deliveries would be managed. That is not a traffic plan. Cllr Tamsin Reel also asked about school-time movements. My daughter Nia Fenwick, aged 11, walks that way, and Mrs Petra Ibbot has already told me the bend has poor visibility. Please require timed deliveries and a banksman at the access, with the arrangements shown on a drawing before works start.

Ellis Fenwick
IP-90417

Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey Note
Merevale Link Energy Project | Environmental Statement | October 2026

1. Scope and survey basis

This note accompanies Chapter 8, Ecology. Fenharbour Ecology Partnership carried out walkover and vantage-point visits for Merevale Link Energy Ltd between February and July 2026. The survey area covers the proposed cable crossing of the Alden Brook, the former Merevale Viaduct and the temporary access route beside Rook Fen. The purpose was to record field signs, assess whether construction could disturb protected breeding or resting sites, and set out measures to be secured in the Outline Ecological Management Plan (OEMP).

Locations are presented at different precisions deliberately. A two-figure reference identifies a broad survey square; a ten-figure reference for a field sign records where a surveyor stood. Precise locations of protected resting and breeding sites are included only for examination and should not be reproduced in the publicly accessible version of the drawings. The broad survey squares TL 47 71 and TL 48 71 are sufficient for the discussion in Chapter 8. All locations and records in this appendix relate to the fictional project survey, not to records for the wider county.

2. Methods and limitations

The brook banks were checked from publicly accessible ground and land made available to the applicant. Surveyors looked for spraint, feeding remains, prints, slides and potential holts. Birds were watched from fixed points without approaching ledges or reedbeds during the breeding season. Visits included a dawn watch on 14 May 2026 and an evening watch on 9 June 2026. Water was high after rain on the second visit, so the absence of prints at that time is not evidence of absence. No burrow was opened, and no nest was climbed. The full visit log and weather sheets are retained by Fenharbour Ecology Partnership.

A local resident, Ms Nola Venn, of 14 Tern Row, West Merevale, MV4 2QH, sent a photograph showing a large bird over the viaduct. This was useful context but was not treated as a confirmed nesting record. Ms Nola Venn is not an Interested Party in this examination as far as the survey team is aware. Tavi Rell, a field ecologist at Fenharbour Ecology Partnership, checked the photograph against the survey notes. Queries about the survey should go to ecology@merevalelink.example rather than tavi.rell@fenharbour.example; no direct number is provided in the public copy.

3. Results: otter

Spraint was recorded on an exposed stone at TL 48126 71490. A second deposit and several footprints were found at TL 482 715, approximately 300 m farther upstream. These are field signs, not resting places. The banks within the broad square TL 47 71 also contain roots and cavities that could provide cover. Otter activity is therefore considered regular, although the survey cannot estimate the number of animals using the brook.

One active holt was confirmed at TL 47982 71344, beneath the east-bank root plate of the split willow 18 m downstream of the old sluice. Fresh bedding and a well-used entrance were visible from the opposite bank; the surveyor did not enter the feature. This location is supplied for design and licensing purposes only. The location should be held in the restricted ecology layer, not on the general construction drawing. A note saying only ‘otter signs along Alden Brook near Rook Fen’ is adequate for public-facing route information, but would not be adequate for setting the site-specific exclusion zone.

4. Results: Schedule 1 birds

Peregrine activity was observed around the former Merevale Viaduct on three visits. An occupied nest was confirmed at TL 48236 71629, in the north-facing recess of Pier 3 above the eastern maintenance track. The feature was identified from a distant watch point; no close inspection was made. The public mapping should show only ‘peregrine recorded within TL 48 71’. An old, unoccupied stick structure on the west abutment was also noted, but its ownership by any species is uncertain and it is not relied upon in the assessment.

Marsh harrier was seen hunting over Rook Fen on 14 May. The observation was made from the access track at TL 48317 71942; this is an observer position and does not identify a nest or breeding site. There was no evidence of breeding in the surveyed part of the fen. References elsewhere in the OEMP to birds using Rook Fen, or to habitat roughly north of the village, are intentionally broad. They should not be read as plotted nest records.

5. Effects and conservation measures

Without controls, piling at the viaduct and night working by the brook could cause disturbance. The cable alignment does not require removal of the confirmed holt or the occupied viaduct feature, but temporary compounds could bring lighting and people closer than indicated on the current general arrangement. The applicant will mark restricted buffers on a controlled plan issued to the ecological clerk of works and construction manager. The plan will be revised after a pre-start check, since a bird may change nesting position and otter resting sites can be used intermittently.

The OEMP requires directional lighting, no materials stored on the brook bank, and a stop-work procedure if fresh evidence is found outside the controlled area. Any work within a restricted buffer will await the necessary specialist advice and, where required, a licence. Vegetation clearance near the viaduct is to be programmed outside the relevant breeding period unless a competent check demonstrates that the work can proceed lawfully. An annual review will compare monitoring records with the baseline and record any change to access arrangements.

The applicant's published mitigation allowance is £84,000; this is a project budget, not a personal payment. Some residents have reported poor sleep because of the proposed works, but that concern is not a clinical finding in this ecology survey. The project document index is available at https://merevale-link.example/ecology. A volunteer's unrelated sightings page, https://marshwatch-notes.example/map, was not used to locate protected sites and is not part of the examination evidence.

APPENDIX E-7: OTTER AND SCHEDULE 1 BIRD SURVEY — CONTINUED
Merevale Link Energy Project

7.4 Baseline records and survey limitations

This appendix should be read with the confidential constraints drawing, not used as a public guide to wildlife locations. The survey corridor included the Culden Beck crossing, the viaduct approaches and land at Larchmere Farm. Fenharbour Ecology Partnership undertook walkovers in February, April and June 2025 for Merevale Link Energy Ltd. Tavi Rell of Fenharbour Ecology Partnership checked the original field sheets against the photographs before the records below were entered into the constraints schedule. The April visit followed heavy rain, so an absence of tracks at that visit has not been treated as evidence of absence.

Records supplied by others were screened separately. Ms Nola Venn, a local resident who is not participating in the examination, supplied a photograph of an animal on the beck bank. Its date could be checked, but the photograph did not establish a resting place. The volunteer sightings page at https://marshwatch-notes.example/map was not used to place a protected-site marker. Survey method and the non-confidential drawings are indexed at https://merevale-link.example/ecology. The licence guidance referred to by the survey team is at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/wildlife-licences.

7.5 Otter evidence

Otter footprints and spraint were recorded intermittently along Culden Beck. The broad survey area can be described as grid square NX 43 67; that square is not a location for any particular resting place. Two spraints on exposed stones below the viaduct had washed away by the following visit. No conclusion about the number of animals using the beck is drawn from those signs. The banks elsewhere included old root cavities and several dry shelves, most of which showed no evidence of regular use.

One feature was assessed as an active holt on the combined evidence of repeated fresh spraint, bedding material and a clear entrance beneath roots. Its location is NX 43827 67294, beneath the second alder on the west bank immediately downstream of Culden Footbridge. The point is retained here solely to explain the avoidance area shown on the restricted drawing; it must not be transferred to a public-facing works plan. A second root cavity farther upstream was recorded as a possible lie-up, not a confirmed holt. It would be misleading to give that uncertain feature the same status as the confirmed record.

The proposed temporary culvert lies upstream of the confirmed feature. Although no permanent loss of bank habitat is anticipated, piling noise, lighting and personnel on the bank could cause disturbance. The construction environmental management plan will therefore establish a fenced exclusion area before compound set-up, prohibit night working beside the beck and retain an unlit passage along one bank. Its precise dimensions will be checked against the final construction method and, where required, a licence. Vegetation clearance near the viaduct is to be programmed outside the relevant breeding period unless a competent check demonstrates that the work can proceed lawfully. An annual review will compare monitoring records with the baseline and record any change to access arrangements.

7.6 Schedule 1 birds

Barn owl activity was recorded around the open grassland and farm buildings. A nest containing young was confirmed at NX 44163 66982, in the north-facing loft opening of the easternmost stone outbuilding at Larchmere Farm. This is a breeding-site record, not merely a record of a bird hunting over the fields. The building is outside the permanent land take but is close enough to the proposed construction route for disturbance to be considered. The name Larchmere Farm is used on the land plans; no occupier details are needed for this assessment.

Peregrine was observed over the viaduct on two visits. On the June visit, food delivery and calling identified a nest ledge at NX 43609 67641, on the inner face of the third viaduct pier counting from the south abutment. Earlier observations of a bird passing over Merevale Wood did not, by themselves, indicate nesting there. The record for Merevale Wood is therefore a broad activity record only. Similarly, the note that badger setts occur in Merevale Wood does not identify a sett and has no bearing on the bird breeding-site assessment.

The two nest locations are included in this controlled version so that the Examining Authority can understand how the construction buffers were derived. Public drawings will show constraints by work area rather than reproduce nest coordinates. The contractor must not assume that a blank area on a public drawing has been surveyed and found clear. A pre-start inspection by a suitably experienced ecologist remains necessary where access, timing or work methods change.

7.7 Conservation and monitoring measures

The barn owl building will be retained. Deliveries past its access track will be routed away from the opening during the relevant breeding period, and lighting will be cowled so it does not illuminate the loft. No replacement box is proposed as a substitute for retaining the occupied structure. For peregrine, scaffold design and the sequence of viaduct repairs will be agreed before mobilisation; work near the occupied pier will be deferred where a check confirms that breeding activity makes it necessary. Any licence requirement will be resolved before, not after, the affected operation starts.

Monitoring will record whether the otter passage remains usable and whether the two bird sites remain occupied, without requiring repeated close approaches merely to demonstrate compliance. Results will be reviewed after the first construction season and at the annual review. A failure of the passage, or evidence of disturbance attributable to the works, will trigger a method review and corrective action agreed through the ecological clerk of works. The applicant's published mitigation allowance of £84,000 is a project budget, not a payment to an individual. Residents' reports of poor sleep are acknowledged in other parts of the Environmental Statement, but are not clinical evidence and do not alter the interpretation of these wildlife records.

8.7 Residual effects, monitoring and reporting

This section draws together the construction and operational ecology assessments for the Merevale Link Energy Project. It should be read with the habitat schedule and the outline Ecological Management Plan (EMP). The assessment has been prepared for Merevale Link Energy Ltd using survey information compiled by Fenharbour Ecology Partnership. It does not treat a record outside the works area as evidence that a species is absent from the works area; equally, it does not assume that every suitable habitat is occupied.

The principal construction effects arise from temporary land take, vegetation clearance, noise and lighting, and the risk of sediment entering field drains. These effects are concentrated around the cable corridor, the converter compound and the temporary access tracks. Much of the corridor will be reinstated following installation, although reinstatement is not the same as immediate recovery. Hedgerow gaps will be replanted during the first suitable planting season, with replacement plants maintained under the EMP. The assessment allows for a lag before they provide comparable shelter and connectivity.

The approach to avoidance is set out as a sequence rather than a single pre-commencement check. Working widths will be marked before clearance; retained vegetation will be fenced where practicable; and the ecological clerk of works will brief the relevant construction teams on the limits of the authorised area. If an unexpected ecological constraint is found, work in that part of the site will pause while the method is reviewed. This hold point is intended to prevent a programme change from being treated as permission to extend into retained habitat.

At Larchmere Farm, the land plan shows an existing field access that can be used for the temporary construction route. Larchmere Farm is the name of the land parcel on the drawings; the ecology assessment does not rely on the identity of any occupier. The access design limits new hedge removal, but soil storage and turning movements still require controls. Topsoil and subsoil will be stored separately, and stockpiles will be kept clear of drainage grips. The proposed drainage measures are described in the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan, document ML-APP-6.4.

Water quality is an indirect pathway for effects beyond the construction footprint. The shallow drains joining Brindle Mere form a connected system, so a spill or a sustained release of fine sediment could travel outside the working area. Silt fencing alone is not relied upon as a complete measure. The contractor will use phased excavation, check dams where appropriate, contained refuelling arrangements and inspection after heavy rainfall. Discharge points will be confirmed through the final method statements. The assessment assumes these controls are in place before ground is opened, not added once a problem has been observed.

Survey records indicate general use of the wider field network by bats, and badger signs have been identified in Merevale Wood. Those statements identify broad survey areas, not individual roosts or setts. The submitted plans therefore show precautionary working zones and retained habitat without publishing sensitive wildlife locations. There is no proposed continuous night working along the corridor. Where short-duration lighting is required for safety, fittings will be directed into the work area and switched off when the activity ends. The final lighting schedule will be checked against the approved construction limits.

For birds, clearance will be programmed outside the main nesting period where reasonably practicable. If that cannot be achieved, a check immediately before the relevant operation will establish whether the activity can proceed. A check is not a standing approval for later clearance: conditions may change between inspection and work. The monitoring described above is similarly proportionate. It tests whether mitigation functions during construction without making repeated visits to sensitive features a routine requirement of the project.

Habitat creation comprises species-rich grassland on reinstated margins, native hedge planting and management of retained ditch edges. The seed mix and establishment regime will be agreed in the detailed EMP. Success will be assessed against measurable establishment criteria, including ground cover, hedge survival and the presence of damaging invasive species. A failed planting area will be reseeded or replanted in the next suitable season. Merevale District Council and Brindle Fen Drainage Board will receive the annual summary so that any proposed changes to ditch maintenance can be considered alongside drainage requirements.

The operational assessment assumes routine inspection of the permanent compound and periodic vegetation management, rather than continual activity across the cable corridor. On that basis, disturbance effects during operation are expected to be substantially lower than during construction. Replacement planting will take time to mature, and a localised, temporary reduction in habitat connectivity remains. No claim of an immediate ecological gain is made for the first year of operation. The longer-term outcome depends on the maintenance and remedial provisions being implemented for the full management period.

On the stated design and secured mitigation, significant residual ecological effects are not predicted. That conclusion is conditional: a material change to access, lighting, drainage or working width must be screened against the ecology assessment before it is adopted. The applicant's published mitigation allowance of £84,000 is a project budget and does not replace the specified measures or their performance tests. General comments about noise and poor sleep are addressed elsewhere in the Environmental Statement; they are not species survey records. The annual report will distinguish observed results from assumptions and will identify any corrective action still outstanding.

8.10 Implementation and verification

This section sets out how the ecological commitments will be checked during construction and operation of the Merevale Link Energy Project. It should be read with the Environmental Statement, the outline Landscape and Ecological Management Plan (LEMP), the Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) and the drainage strategy. The plans show the working corridor, access arrangements and habitat-management areas; they are not a substitute for the pre-commencement checks required below. Merevale Link Energy Ltd will retain responsibility for delivering the measures, including where a principal contractor undertakes the work.

8.10.1 Pre-commencement checks

Fenharbour Ecology Partnership will review the construction programme and the final limits of disturbance before vegetation clearance starts. The review will compare the approved design with temporary compounds, haul routes, lighting positions and drainage outfalls. Any land outside the assessed working width must be treated as a design change, not as spare construction space. The ecological clerk of works will record whether the relevant exclusion fencing, pollution controls and briefing materials are in place before each work area is released.

Survey information has a limited useful life. Checks immediately before works will therefore be proportionate to the habitat affected and the season in which the activity occurs. For example, a check of scrub proposed for clearance does not remove the need to stop work if an active nest is subsequently found. Likewise, the absence of field signs on an earlier visit does not establish that a watercourse crossing can be altered without review. Records will state the date, conditions, area checked and action taken, rather than simply recording that a survey was completed.

The public figures in this chapter refer to broad survey areas. They include badger activity in Willowhatch Wood, bat activity across the Brindle Fen corridor and otter signs along the Merevale Cut. None is intended to identify a resting or breeding site. Detailed confidential survey information will be made available only to those implementing the relevant protection measures and to the appropriate consenting body where required. Construction drawings issued more widely will show necessary work restrictions without reproducing sensitive species-location information.

8.10.2 Construction controls

The CEMP will require clearly marked working limits. Material storage, refuelling and vehicle parking will be confined to designated areas, with no informal widening of access tracks. At watercourse crossings, the contractor will install the specified sediment controls before ground disturbance and inspect them after heavy rain. Pumped water will not be discharged directly to the Merevale Cut. If a control fails, the affected operation will pause while the cause is corrected; adding an inspection entry after the event will not, by itself, satisfy this requirement.

The temporary route near Larchmere Farm is shown on the land plans and is assessed as a construction access, not a permanent road. Its use will be restricted to the assessed width and duration. Reinstatement will include removal of temporary surfacing, treatment of compacted ground where appropriate and replacement of the agreed vegetation cover. The name Larchmere Farm identifies a mapped property; this chapter makes no assumption about its occupier.

Directional lighting will be used only where needed for safe working. Luminaires will face into the active work area, and their hours of use will be recorded. A change from task lighting to continuous overnight lighting would require ecological review, even if the number of columns remained the same. The review will consider light spill towards retained hedgerows and the Brindle Fen corridor, alongside the safety reason for the proposed change.

8.10.3 Habitat establishment

The outline LEMP specifies native planting, grassland establishment and management of retained boundary features. Success will be judged against measurable outcomes: establishment of the planted stock, the extent of bare ground, evidence of erosion and whether invasive plants have become established. A photograph of a newly planted area is useful evidence of installation but not proof that the habitat has established. Failed planting will be replaced in the next suitable season, with the reason for failure considered before the same method is repeated.

Management will not aim to make every area look uniformly tidy. Varied sward height and some standing vegetation are compatible with the habitat objectives, provided access, drainage and safety requirements remain met. Cutting dates may be adjusted in response to conditions recorded during inspection. Any adjustment that reduces the area or duration of the secured habitat provision will be referred back for review rather than treated as routine maintenance.

8.10.4 Monitoring and reporting

Monitoring results will be compared with the baseline and with the performance tests in the LEMP. The annual ecology summary provided to Merevale District Council and Brindle Fen Drainage Board will distinguish completed actions, observed habitat condition, departures from the approved method and outstanding remedial work. It will also explain any survey limitation, including areas that could not safely be entered. A statement of ‘no change’ without supporting observations will not be treated as a monitoring result.

Where a performance test is missed, the report will identify a practicable corrective action, the party responsible for carrying it out and the next opportunity to verify the result. The need for correction does not automatically mean that a significant ecological effect has occurred; equally, a prediction of no significant residual effect is not a reason to defer correction. This approach allows the examination commitments to be followed through for the full management period while keeping the publicly available account focused on outcomes rather than sensitive site detail.

Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 bird survey note (continued)

8.6.4 Basis of this note

This note records the observations behind the monitoring measures described above. It is to be read with the conservation plan for the Merevale Link Energy Project, rather than as a replacement for it. Survey visits were undertaken in March, May and July 2025 by Fenharbour Ecology Partnership for Merevale Link Energy Ltd. Water levels were high on the March visit and access to the southern bank of the Wicker Drain was not safe. A return visit was therefore made in May. The absence of a sign on one visit has not been treated as evidence that a channel is unused.

References beginning MV are positions on the project’s local survey grid, not Ordnance Survey references. A two-digit reference identifies a broad survey square; five digits identify a feature closely enough for a field team to relocate it. The latter should remain in the controlled ecological record. The wider Wicker Drain corridor falls within project-grid square MV 41 69. That square includes several drains and reedbeds and does not, by itself, identify a resting or breeding place.

8.6.5 Otter evidence

Otter spraint was recorded on two exposed stones beneath the old accommodation crossing, with prints in soft silt approximately 30 m downstream. The stones were washed clean by the July visit. Prints and spraint establish use of the watercourse but are not, by themselves, evidence of a holt. Surveyors also checked accessible banks for entrances, flattened vegetation and repeated trails; a narrow trail at the crossing could equally have been made by other mammals.

One active holt was assessed on the north bank: its entrance is at project-grid MV 41783 69426, beneath the third willow stump west of the Wicker Drain footbridge. This is a relocation description for the ecological clerk of works, not a location to be copied into the public works plan. The entrance was not entered or probed. Fresh bedding visible from the bank and repeat tracks informed the assessment, although the number of animals using it is unknown. The proposed temporary access track was moved away from this bank in design revision C. No bank cutting, lighting or material storage is permitted within the protection area shown on the controlled plan.

A resident photograph supplied by Ms Nola Venn shows an otter in the general Larchmere Farm reach in winter 2024. It has no reliable position attached and is used only as supporting evidence of activity in the wider catchment. In particular, the photograph cannot establish which bank feature the animal used. Larchmere Farm is the property name shown on the land plans; this appendix does not identify an occupier.

8.6.6 Schedule 1 birds

A marsh harrier was seen carrying material into the Reedmere reedbed on the May visit. The broad observation square is MV 42 68. Follow-up watches were made from the existing maintenance path, without approaching the birds. The confirmed nest position is project-grid MV 42164 68837, in reed compartment R4, 12 m east of the northern sluice gate. That position is supplied for implementation of the exclusion area and should not appear on public-facing ecological figures. Two fledged young were subsequently observed from a distance; this does not establish that every young bird survived beyond the survey period.

There was also a single little ringed plover displaying over bare gravel in the northern works area. No nest, eggs or dependent young were found there on the two follow-up watches. The works-area record is therefore retained as possible breeding activity, not described as a confirmed nest site. The gravel area lies within MV 43 70, a coarse reference that covers the whole proposed compound and adjacent field margin. Pre-start checks remain necessary if bare gravel is present when works commence. A negative check expires if the ground conditions materially change or works are delayed into another breeding season.

8.6.7 Conservation and checking arrangements

The controlled plan sets out stand-offs around the confirmed features, the permitted access route and the sequence for installing temporary fencing. Fencing will be placed from the landward side under ecological supervision; operatives must not first walk the boundary through the reedbed to decide where it should go. If a marked route cannot be used because of flooding, works will stop at that location while a revised method is agreed. This is preferable to treating an access difficulty as permission to shorten a stand-off.

The pre-start briefing will distinguish signs of otter passage, which may occur along much of the drain, from evidence requiring immediate review, such as a newly occupied resting place in a work area. For birds, the briefing will explain that a quiet watch does not authorise entry into a marked exclusion area. The ecological clerk of works may request a pause and further observation where behaviour changes or a previously unrecorded nest is suspected. No instruction to relocate a nest is made by this appendix.

Tavi Rell of Fenharbour Ecology Partnership checked the field sheets against the mapping before this note was issued. The check identified one transposed digit in an early working copy; the controlled plan and the positions stated here use the corrected entry. This matters because a five-digit reference can appear precise while directing a team to the wrong bank. Field teams will use the controlled plan together with the physical description and will report any discrepancy before fencing is installed.

Annual summaries to Merevale District Council and Brindle Fen Drainage Board will state the survey dates, whether the access restrictions were followed, any interruption to works and the outcome of corrective action. They may identify the relevant broad survey square, but not the precise holt or nest positions. The underlying observations will be retained so that an apparent change in use can be checked against water level, visibility and survey effort, rather than presented without qualification as a gain or loss of habitat.

8.7 Interpretation of monitoring results

The annual summary described above is intended to test whether the mitigation is functioning, not to serve as a simple count of animals. A dry survey season may produce fewer signs along the drains even where habitat remains suitable. Equally, a rise in recorded activity could reflect better visibility after vegetation cutting. Fenharbour Ecology Partnership will therefore compare each observation with water levels, survey effort, weather and the construction programme before recommending a change to the measures. An absence of records for one season will not, by itself, be treated as evidence that a habitat feature is no longer used.

The applicant, Merevale Link Energy Ltd, will keep the monitoring programme aligned with the approved Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) and the Landscape and Ecology Management Plan (LEMP). Where those documents specify different inspection frequencies for the same feature, the more frequent inspection will apply until the discrepancy is resolved through the document-control procedure. This avoids an informal change to the commitment simply because a later drawing uses a different revision number.

8.8 Habitat establishment

The principal permanent habitat measures comprise species-rich grassland on the cable easement where operational access permits, hedgerow reinforcement along field boundaries, and shallow wet margins beside the drainage improvement area. The seed mix will reflect the existing soil conditions rather than assume that a wetland mix is suitable throughout. Topsoil handling, the timing of sowing and the first two cuts will be recorded, since poor establishment can otherwise be mistaken for an unsuitable design. Arisings from establishment cuts will be removed where practicable to avoid enriching the sward.

At Larchmere Farm, the land plans distinguish the operational track from the adjacent planting strip. This distinction is important: a hedgerow planted within the swept path of maintenance vehicles would need repeated trimming and could not achieve the stated structure. The detailed planting schedule will therefore be checked against the final track geometry before installation. Any local adjustment will preserve the committed length and connectivity of planting, and will be shown on the as-built plan.

Replacement planting will be assessed at the end of the first and third growing seasons. Failed plants will be replaced in the next suitable planting window using the approved species schedule. A low survival rate across a whole strip will prompt a review of soil preparation, drainage and browsing pressure rather than repeated like-for-like replacement without investigation. The establishment specification does not require every individual plant to survive; it requires the intended habitat to develop and remain connected.

8.9 Construction interfaces

Ecological controls will be included in the weekly works planning meeting for each active construction area. The relevant plan will show working limits, retained vegetation, temporary fencing and access routes. A pre-start check will confirm that the plan reflects conditions on the ground, including any drain maintenance undertaken since the last walkover. If a previously unrecorded ecological constraint is encountered, work in the affected area will pause while the agreed procedure is followed. The remainder of the works need not stop where it is physically and ecologically separate.

Temporary lighting will be directed into the working area and kept to the minimum needed for safe operations. Lighting near retained hedgerows and drains will be reviewed as part of the compound layout, particularly where a change to working hours is proposed. The assessment assumes that routine night working is not required along the full route. A proposal to extend it would need to be checked against that assumption before implementation.

Excavations left open overnight will be covered or provided with a suitable means of escape, depending on their size and the safety requirements for that activity. Materials will be stored so that they do not encroach on retained margins. These measures apply across the construction corridor; they are not dependent on a species being recorded during a particular survey visit.

8.10 Drainage and water quality

The drainage design retains the broad direction of flow towards the Brindle Fen system. During construction, clean and potentially silty water will be kept separate where reasonably practicable. Discharge points and sediment controls will be checked after heavy rainfall and following changes to the earthworks layout. The inspection record will identify the location by work area and drawing reference, without adding protected-species locations to the general site diary.

Brindle Fen Drainage Board will receive the drainage information required under the relevant consent process. The ecological assessment does not substitute for that process or imply permission to alter a watercourse. Similarly, a monitoring result indicating poor vegetation establishment beside a drain will be considered alongside the Board’s maintenance requirements before a revised planting treatment is selected.

8.11 Residual effects and reporting

With the construction controls and habitat measures secured, the assessment predicts no significant residual adverse ecological effect at the project-wide scale. This conclusion does not mean that each field margin will remain unchanged during works. It relies on limiting the duration and extent of disturbance, reinstating temporary working land, and establishing the permanent measures shown in the LEMP. The conclusion will be reviewed if the final design removes a retained feature or materially changes the assessed drainage regime.

Annual reporting to Merevale District Council and Brindle Fen Drainage Board will distinguish completed actions from actions still in progress. It will include the area of habitat established, broad condition findings, departures from the approved method and the response to those departures. Records of precise sensitive-species locations will remain in the controlled ecological dataset, not in the public summary. General queries about the published summary may be sent to ecology@merevalelink.example. The purpose of this reporting is to make delivery auditable while avoiding false precision in either the ecological conclusions or the public location data.

7.8 Residual ecological effects and verification

7.8.1 This section should be read with the Landscape and Ecological Management Plan (LEMP) and the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP). It sets out how the conclusions for the Merevale Link Energy Project will be checked as detailed design and construction proceed. The assessment assumes that the measures identified as embedded mitigation are delivered in full. It does not treat proposed habitat creation as a substitute for avoiding damage to retained features in the first instance.

7.8.2 Merevale Link Energy Ltd will maintain a design change register covering the working width, access arrangements, drainage outfalls and temporary compounds. Fenharbour Ecology Partnership will review changes against the ecological baseline before the relevant work package is released. A change that remains within the assessed limits of deviation will not automatically require a new field survey; its ecological implications will nevertheless be recorded. A change outside those limits, or one that alters an identified pathway of effect, will be subject to a separate assessment and, where necessary, an amended method statement. This distinction is important because a revised drawing can appear minor in engineering terms while changing the extent of vegetation clearance.

7.8.3 The baseline comprises habitat mapping, walkover observations and the species surveys described in Appendix 7.2. Survey conditions and access constraints are listed in that appendix rather than repeated here. The baseline is appropriate for the current assessment, but it is not assumed to remain current indefinitely. Before clearance in each construction phase, the relevant areas will be checked for material changes in habitat condition and for newly apparent ecological constraints. These checks are a verification measure, not a means of deferring assessment of an otherwise foreseeable effect.

7.8.4 The principal construction risks are temporary loss of field-edge vegetation, disturbance associated with lighting and movement, and the transport of sediment towards receiving ditches. The proposed working sequence retains the established hedgerow network wherever practicable and limits temporary crossings to those shown on the construction plans. Where a crossing cannot be avoided, its width will be restricted to the space required for safe installation. Topsoil will be stored separately from subsoil, and reinstatement will follow the soil-handling specification. The specification is intended to preserve the conditions needed for vegetation to recover; it does not guarantee that every reinstated strip will immediately match its former condition.

7.8.5 Water-management controls will be installed before exposed soil is left adjacent to a ditch. They include clean-water diversion, settlement capacity and the ability to isolate a discharge if monitoring indicates visible sediment. The receiving ditch network forms part of the Brindle Fen catchment, where flow direction can vary during managed drainage operations. For that reason, the contractor will confirm the active drainage route at the start of each work package rather than relying solely on the general arrangement drawing. Brindle Fen Drainage Board will receive the agreed inspection summary under the reporting arrangements described above.

7.8.6 Operational drainage has been assessed on the basis of the proposed attenuation and controlled-release arrangement. Routine maintenance must keep inlets, outlets and vegetated treatment areas functioning as designed. An inspection after a significant storm will consider erosion, standing water outside the intended storage areas and signs that a flow path has been obstructed. If a defect is identified, the remedy will be specified before further habitat works are undertaken in the affected area. This avoids a situation in which newly established planting conceals an unresolved drainage problem.

7.8.7 The lighting design uses directional fittings and avoids continuous illumination of retained boundary vegetation. Construction lighting will be task-specific and switched off when no longer needed for the task. The detailed lighting schedule will be checked against the approved parameters before installation. Records will identify the fitting type, mounting arrangement and operating period so that any complaint about spill can be investigated by reference to the installed scheme, rather than to an indicative drawing alone. The assessment does not depend on an assertion that there will be no light spill anywhere on the site.

7.8.8 Species records have informed the avoidance measures, but the public chapter reports them at a scale suitable for consultation. Badger activity has been recorded in the wider Brindle Fen landscape, and bat activity is associated with the hedgerow network. Neither statement identifies a protected breeding or resting place. Pre-commencement checks and any required working restrictions will be managed through the controlled ecological dataset. Where a check finds a constraint that requires a change to the approved method, the work will pause in the affected work area until an appropriate response has been agreed. The public compliance record will describe the type of response without publishing a precise location.

7.8.9 The proposed habitat works include reinforcement of retained hedgerows, establishment of species-rich margins and management of drainage-side vegetation. Establishment will be assessed by condition as well as by area. A margin counted as planted will not be reported as achieving its target condition simply because seed has been applied. Failed sections will be identified for remedial action in the next suitable planting season, with the reason for failure considered before the same treatment is repeated. This approach should make annual comparisons meaningful despite differences in weather between monitoring years.

7.8.10 With the stated measures in place, the assessment identifies no additional significant residual ecological effect from the assessed construction and operational activities. That conclusion is conditional on retaining the specified features, applying the drainage controls and completing the verification steps. Merevale District Council will receive the annual ecology summary, including any departures and corrective action. The controlled dataset will remain available for the purposes set out in the LEMP. Should detailed design remove a retained feature or materially change the drainage regime, the conclusion in this section will be reviewed before the relevant work proceeds.

7.8.11 The conclusion at paragraph 7.8.10 does not remove the need for pre-commencement checks. The baseline surveys describe conditions during the survey period; they do not establish that every ditch, field margin or structure will remain unchanged until works begin. The construction ecological management plan (CEMP) will therefore set out a check-and-release procedure for each work area. A check will confirm that the relevant exclusion fencing, drainage protection and retained-habitat markers are in place before vegetation clearance or ground disturbance starts. Where conditions differ materially from the baseline, work in the affected area will pause while the implications are assessed and the method statement updated.

7.8.12 This is a precautionary control, not an assumption that protected species are present throughout the Order limits. Records of badgers in Brindle Fen and occasional bat activity along the western hedgerows provide context for the assessment, but those broad descriptions are not intended to identify individual resting places. Construction drawings circulated outside the ecological working group will show the limits of protective measures without reproducing sensitive survey detail. The controlled survey records will be used by the ecological contractor to position any necessary fencing and to brief the workforce before clearance.

7.8.13 Merevale Link Energy Ltd will retain the existing ditch network except at the crossing locations shown on the drainage drawings. The crossings have been sized to maintain ordinary flow and provide a continuous margin where practicable. Temporary diversions will not be opened until the receiving channel is functioning, and no pumping discharge will enter a watercourse without settlement and inspection. The principal pathway for a construction effect is the movement of fine sediment during wet-weather earthworks. The sequence of works, rather than the final layout alone, is therefore important to the conclusion of no significant residual effect.

7.8.14 The proposed construction sequence begins with the installation of clean-water cut-offs on the upslope side of each active work front. Sediment barriers and settlement capacity will then be established before topsoil stripping. Exposed soil will be kept to the minimum area required for the current phase; stockpiles will be set back from ditches and covered or seeded if retained beyond the short-term programme. Following heavy rain, the site drainage lead will inspect the controls before works restart. A failed barrier will be repaired and accumulated material removed without scraping it into the adjoining ditch. These steps are secured through the CEMP and the outline drainage management plan, rather than left to a general commitment to good practice.

7.8.15 At Larchmere Farm, the land plans show a narrow working strip beside existing arable land. The farm name is used here to identify the land parcel; the assessment does not rely on any particular cropping pattern or occupier. The strip will be reinstated to its existing ground profile, subject to the final land-drain connection details. Where a hedge has to be crossed, the opening will be limited to the approved working width and replanted with locally appropriate native species after the temporary access is removed. Replacement planting is not treated as an immediate equivalent to mature hedge habitat. The assessment allows for the intervening period and depends on retaining the longer, connected sections throughout construction.

7.8.16 Lighting is expected only at compounds and at work fronts where a safety need has been demonstrated. Lamps will be directed towards the task area, mounted no higher than necessary and switched off when the area is not in use. The operational compound will use motion-controlled lighting rather than permanent illumination of the boundary. The predicted change in light spill at the western hedgerows is negligible with these controls. If detailed design proposes additional permanent lighting, its effects on the retained dark corridor must be checked against the baseline before installation.

7.8.17 Fenharbour Ecology Partnership has compared the habitat schedule, drainage drawings and construction programme to identify places where commitments could otherwise be lost between documents. Table 7.24 of this chapter records the required action, the document securing it and the point at which compliance can be verified. For example, a retained hedge shown on the habitat plan must also appear as an exclusion area on the contractor’s setting-out drawings. A crossing identified on the general arrangement plan must have a corresponding drainage detail. This cross-check is necessary because a commitment shown only in an illustrative landscape drawing would not provide a reliable construction control.

7.9 Monitoring and reporting

7.9.1 Monitoring will test whether the measures have been delivered and whether the assumptions used in the effects assessment remain reasonable. It is not proposed as a substitute for mitigation. During construction, inspection records will cover the condition of exclusion areas, water-quality controls, hedge crossings and reinstatement. Each record will note the work phase and recent weather so that a change observed after a storm is not automatically attributed to the project.
