7.O.20 On this basis, and subject to implementation of the OLEMP and CEMP, the assessment does not identify a likely significant residual effect on the ecological corridor associated with Merevale Drain. That conclusion relies on retaining the corridor, controlling construction disturbance and completing the monitoring and remedial process described above. It does not depend on assuming that species will remain in fixed positions throughout the project. If the final design or construction sequence changes materially, the relevant ecological assessment and method statements will be reviewed before the affected work proceeds.

7.P Cumulative effects and delivery of ecological measures

7.P.1 This section considers whether the Merevale Link Energy Project, when assessed with other reasonably foreseeable works in the study area, could alter the ecological conclusions in Section 7.O. It addresses habitat loss, disturbance, changes to drainage and interruption of movement along Merevale Drain. It also explains how the measures in the Outline Landscape and Ecology Management Plan (OLEMP) will be carried through detailed design. The assessment uses the project design described in Chapter 3 and does not assume that any optional enhancement is necessary to avoid a significant effect.

7.P.2 The cumulative review draws on the development schedule in Appendix 7.12, updated to the October 2026 examination deadline. Developments were screened where their construction footprint, drainage catchment or operational activity could interact with the habitats affected by the project. Distance alone was not used as an exclusion test: an upstream drainage intervention may be relevant even if it is not adjacent to the Order Limits. Conversely, a scheme separated by built development and without a shared ecological pathway was not taken forward simply because it appears within the wider search area.

7.P.3 The committed surface-water improvement works proposed by Brindle Fen Drainage Board have a potential pathway to Merevale Drain. Those works are intended to improve conveyance through existing channels; their final construction programme is not confirmed. The assessment therefore considers a conservative overlap with the project’s principal earthworks. With both schemes operating their stated pollution-prevention controls, a temporary increase in suspended sediment remains possible during exceptional rainfall, but a sustained change in water quality is not predicted. The construction environmental management arrangements will require inspection after heavy rain and prompt repair of any failed controls.

7.P.4 Merevale District Council has identified a proposed active-travel route near the eastern edge of the assessment area. Its alignment remains subject to design, so this is treated as a reasonably foreseeable rather than a committed scheme. On the available layout it would not remove the retained vegetation strip beside Merevale Drain. The potential combined effect is instead a short period of additional noise and lighting during construction. If the programmes overlap, the project contractor will coordinate working hours and temporary lighting positions with the route promoter. This coordination is a practical control, not a substitute for either scheme’s own consent requirements.

7.P.5 The remaining developments listed in Appendix 7.12 do not create a credible shared pathway for effects on Alderwash Wood or the drain corridor. Some would result in small areas of habitat change within the wider landscape, but the cumulative assessment distinguishes that broad background change from effects which can reasonably be attributed to concurrent works. No numerical habitat gain has been credited twice. Where another scheme proposes planting outside its own red line, that planting has not been counted as mitigation for the Merevale Link Energy Project.

7.P.6 At detailed design, the minimum retained corridor widths shown on Ecology Parameter Plan E-07 will be checked against the setting-out drawings. The temporary works boundary will be marked before clearance begins, and storage, refuelling and spoil placement will be excluded from the retained corridor. A change to a working area shown on E-07 will require an ecological review before it is instructed on site. This is important at narrow crossing points, where a seemingly minor adjustment to plant access could increase disturbance or damage established bankside vegetation.

7.P.7 The OLEMP specifies native planting appropriate to the soils and wetness conditions of each parcel. Replacement planting is not proposed as a line of evenly spaced trees throughout the drainage corridor: open sections are retained where they contribute to the existing habitat pattern and allow maintenance access. Species selection and stock sizes will be confirmed following final ground investigation. Failed plants will be replaced in the next suitable planting season, subject to the establishment thresholds in the OLEMP. Those thresholds apply to the planted area as a whole and do not require every individual plant to survive.

7.P.8 Protected species controls will be set out in the pre-construction method statements. The surveys recorded evidence of badger activity across Alderwash Wood and suitable foraging habitat for bats along the wider Merevale Drain corridor. These broad descriptions are sufficient for the cumulative assessment; sensitive field records are held separately and are not reproduced on the public parameter plan. An ecologist will check that the method statements reflect conditions immediately before relevant works. If new evidence changes the assessed impact, works in the affected area will pause while the design and any necessary permissions are reviewed.

7.P.9 Monitoring will test whether retained vegetation, replacement planting and drainage controls perform as intended. The first inspections will take place during construction, followed by annual checks for the period specified in the OLEMP. The annual summary will report measurable matters, including planting establishment, evidence of erosion and completion of remedial actions. Fenharbour Ecology Partnership will prepare the initial monitoring template for Merevale Link Energy Ltd. The results will be provided to Merevale District Council and Brindle Fen Drainage Board so that the same evidence can inform any agreed adjustment to management.

7.P.10 The cumulative conclusion is necessarily conditional on the controls being delivered, rather than on the absence of all ecological change. Temporary construction effects may be noticeable within the corridor, particularly if two schemes work in the same season. However, the retained habitat connection, pollution controls, timing measures and corrective monitoring provide a reasonable basis for concluding that there will be no likely significant cumulative residual effect on the ecological corridor associated with Merevale Drain. A material alteration to the project layout, construction sequence or known programme of a screened-in scheme will trigger a review of this conclusion before the relevant activity proceeds.

7.P.11 The conclusion in paragraph 7.P.10 does not remove the need for scheme-level checks. Before each construction phase, Merevale Link Energy Ltd will confirm the working boundary, drainage outfalls and retained vegetation against the approved ecological drawings. Fenharbour Ecology Partnership will record any material change in habitat condition along Merevale Drain, including changes arising from the separate surface-water works proposed by Brindle Fen Drainage Board. The check is intended to identify a change in the assessment assumptions, not to repeat the full baseline survey.

7.P.12 Badger activity recorded within Alderwash Wood is described at woodland scale in this chapter; no sett location is needed to explain the cumulative conclusion. If pre-construction surveys identify a new constraint, the relevant method statement will be updated before works begin. Monitoring results will be summarised annually for Merevale District Council and Brindle Fen Drainage Board. The annual summary will distinguish observations attributable to the Project from changes associated with other works, insofar as the available evidence allows.

text:
Written representation on health and air quality
Brindle Fen Freight Interchange (application reference TR050092)

From: Mara Fenwick
Address: 14 Sedge Lane, Wrenford, WF8 4PL
Email: mara.fenwick@post.example
Telephone: 07700 900654
Interested Party reference: IP-472031

I am submitting this as a resident, not as a medical expert. I have lived in Wrenford for over 20 years and our house is on the route used to reach the proposed interchange. My objection is mainly about the extra diesel traffic and the length of time it may continue, both during construction and once the site is operating. I have read the air quality chapter and the non-technical summary, but I cannot find a clear account of what conditions will be like at individual houses on Sedge Lane when lorries are queuing.

My GP has diagnosed me with asthma and chronic migraine. I use a prescribed preventer inhaler each morning and carry a salbutamol inhaler when I go out. I also take propranolol for the migraine. These are not details I would usually put in a public letter, but the question of exposure at our home matters more to me than an average figure across a wider area. Dr Iona Vale at Wrenford Respiratory Practice advised me to keep a note of occasions when traffic fumes appear to make breathing difficult. I am not saying that the interchange has caused my conditions: it has not been built. I am asking the Examining Authority to take account of people who already have health problems when deciding whether the proposed controls are adequate.

My child, Ash Fenwick, is 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Ash attends occupational therapy, and changes to routine can be particularly hard to manage. On school mornings we walk towards the bus stop near the proposed construction access. The route shown in the transport material seems to put delivery vehicles across that walk. A diversion may look minor on a drawing, but it would mean learning a different journey while coping with noise, dust and unfamiliar traffic. I would like the applicant to explain how families are supposed to find out about changes before they happen, including temporary changes lasting only a day or two.

There is also the ordinary business of living here. We open the kitchen window in summer, put washing out and sometimes sit in the small garden. When a vehicle idles outside now, I can smell the exhaust indoors if the window is open. I feel anxious about the possibility of more of that, especially at night, and poor sleep makes the next day harder. I understand that feeling anxious is not the same as showing a breach of an air quality limit. It is, however, part of why a statement that predicted concentrations are compliant does not answer all of my concerns about wellbeing.

The documents appear to rely on traffic being spread across several approach roads. Sedge Lane is narrow in places and drivers already use it as a short cut when the main road is busy. I could not see a firm commitment preventing construction workers or delivery drivers from using it, as opposed to an intention to direct them elsewhere. The applicant should publish a plan that residents can actually use, showing where vehicles will wait if they arrive early, who will check the agreed routes and what happens after repeated complaints. Please do not leave those matters to a document prepared after consent without an opportunity for residents to comment.

I spoke to my neighbour Rowan Peake about the assessment because the monitoring point marked on the map seemed to be well away from our end of the lane. Rowan is not making a representation, as far as I know, and I do not speak on anyone else's behalf. The point is that a single monitor cannot necessarily describe every front door. I would welcome monitoring nearer the homes affected by the access route, with results made available in plain language through the project mailbox, consultation@fenmerelink.example, or another shared contact point. Residents should not need to work out who an individual officer is before reporting a problem.

At the community event Cllr Elin Rowe asked whether the construction programme could be broken down by month rather than by phase. That would help. The present description makes some of the busiest periods sound quite short, but it is hard to tell whether several activities might overlap. I would also like a specific explanation of how the proposed wheel washing, road cleaning and dust checks will work on dry, windy days. These are practical requests, not an assertion that every vehicle will cause harm.

I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide an individual medical claim or to assume that my experience is typical. I ask it to require a clearer assessment of exposure at houses on the access routes, enforceable limits on vehicle movements and idling, advance notice of route changes, and a complaints process with published response times. If those measures are already secured somewhere in the draft requirements, please identify the wording and explain how a resident could check that it is being followed. At present I do not think the application gives us that assurance.

Mara Fenwick

Further note to the Examining Authority
Bracken Mere Freight Link — air quality and health representation
From: Mara Fenwick
21 October 2026

I am sending this further note because the applicant's reply on construction traffic appears to treat the monitoring point at the site boundary as if it also describes conditions beside the access roads. It does not, at least not in any way that I can understand from the documents. My earlier representation asked for an explanation of wheel washing, road cleaning and dust checks on dry, windy days. This note explains why a clear answer matters to my household. I do not suggest that the Examining Authority can predict what will happen to any one person's health.

I have been diagnosed with asthma. I use a beclometasone inhaler each day and carry a salbutamol inhaler for symptoms. I also have chronic migraine, for which I have been prescribed sumatriptan. These details are given to explain why I pay particular attention to dust, exhaust and advance warning of unusually busy periods. They are not evidence that the proposed development caused either condition, and I do not want them treated as a substitute for proper air-quality modelling. Dr Iona Vale at Wrenford Respiratory Practice has not been asked to give expert evidence in this examination; I mention my clinician only to distinguish a diagnosis from my ordinary worries about the scheme.

My child, Ash Fenwick, is 11 and has autism. Changes in routine can be difficult, particularly if they happen without warning. Ash has attended occupational therapy, and I try to plan journeys and school mornings so that unexpected noise and delays do not become the whole focus of the day. If a construction route is changed at short notice, or a queue forms on Rook Lane while engines are left running, we cannot always simply set off earlier. This is a practical point about the usefulness of notice, not a claim that the project will necessarily make the disability worse.

The road is used by people walking to the bus stop and by families going to school. In the morning there can be a line of vehicles on the bend before the site entrance, where drivers seem to wait for a gap. The drawings show the entrance, but I could not find an assessment that sets out where waiting construction vehicles would actually stand if more than one arrives at once. Please ask Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd to show the maximum queue assumed in its assessment, the hours used for that assumption, and what will stop a queue extending back towards the crossing. An average daily total does not answer that question for the half hour in which everyone is trying to get somewhere.

My neighbour, Rowan Peake, has said that there is sometimes dust on the front windows after ordinary traffic goes past. Rowan is not making a representation, as far as I know, and I am not offering that comment as a measurement. I include it because the response to my earlier question seems to rely on people noticing a problem and reporting it afterwards. That leaves open who receives a complaint, how quickly somebody checks the road, and whether the check is recorded when no breach is found. A public log could record the time, location in general terms, weather, action taken and outcome without publishing anyone's personal details.

At the community event Cllr Elin Rowe asked whether residents would see the same traffic information as the contractors. I thought this was a useful question. The proposed notices would be much more helpful if they gave a start and finish time, the reason for a route change, and a number for reporting a vehicle using the wrong route. A generic project mailbox such as airquality@larkhaven-infrastructure.example could also receive photographs, provided the applicant explains who checks it outside office hours. I am not asking for the names of individual drivers or for residents to confront them.

I appreciate that the applicant has committed to a construction environmental management plan. My difficulty is that the commitment is described in several places but the detail seems to be left until later. For example, one document mentions dampening exposed surfaces, while another refers to inspections in suitable weather. What counts as suitable weather? Would an inspection take place before work starts after several dry days, and who decides whether sweeping has actually removed dust rather than moved it to the edge of the carriageway? A requirement to keep records is only useful if the records can be checked and there is a clear response when they show repeated problems.

I have experienced stress and poor sleep while trying to work through the application. I know those feelings are not diagnoses and cannot establish the likely concentration of pollutants beside Rook Lane. Equally, it would be wrong to treat the lack of a personal pollution monitor in my house as proof that there is no issue to assess. Residents should be able to understand the assumptions behind the predicted effects, including the number of heavy vehicles, the proportion using each route and whether an idling vehicle is accounted for. If the applicant says existing background levels make no difference to the conclusion, please ask it to explain that in plain language.

I have lived in this area since 2019 and want the project to be assessed fairly. I am not asking for a guarantee that there will never be dust or a delayed journey. I ask for limits and working arrangements that can be understood before permission is granted, rather than reassurance that everything can be sorted out later. In particular, please clarify the trigger for extra road cleaning, the method for checking vehicle queues and idling, how route changes will be announced, and where the results of complaints and inspections will be published. That would allow residents to judge whether the measures described on paper are happening in practice.

Mara Fenwick

Further health representation — Bracken Mere Freight Link
From: Mara Fenwick

I am adding this note because the applicant's response on air quality treats exposure as an annual average, whereas the difficult days for us are particular days. I am not saying that a short spell of dust proves the scheme is unsafe. I am asking the Examining Authority to look at what residents may actually experience when road works, queuing lorries and dry weather happen together. The tables in the environmental statement do not tell me how that combination will be noticed quickly or what will be done about it.

I have been diagnosed with asthma and chronic migraine. I use a budesonide inhaler every morning and keep a salbutamol inhaler with me. I also take propranolol, as prescribed for the migraines. I give these details reluctantly, not because I want the examination to decide anyone's medical treatment, but because a statement that the predicted change is 'negligible' does not answer my practical concern. If I need to keep the windows shut during construction, that is a real change to how we use our home, even if the annual figure at a modelled receptor remains low. I would prefer this information to be handled with care when the representation is published.

My child, Ash Fenwick, aged 11, has autism and a moderate learning disability. An unexpected change to the walk to school, loud reversing alarms or a long line of stationary vehicles can make the journey difficult. That does not mean the link cannot be built. It means the promised arrangements for deliveries and temporary crossings need to be specific. At present I cannot tell whether a crossing will be staffed at school times, who decides when that is necessary, or how much notice families will get if a footway is closed. A notice placed at the works gate after we have set off would not help.

Our home is at 18 Plover Rise, Wrenford, WF4 8QR. I include the address so that the case team can understand which approach road I mean, not as an invitation for it to appear on a public map. The junction nearest us is already awkward in the morning. Some drivers wait with engines running outside the row of houses while they decide whether to turn back. I cannot measure what comes from those vehicles, and I do not want my observation mistaken for a monitoring result. Please ask Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd to explain whether its traffic assumptions include that sort of waiting during the construction phases, especially if a lane is temporarily narrowed.

At an appointment at Wrenford Respiratory Practice, Dr Iona Vale advised me to keep track of occasions when my symptoms changed and what was happening nearby. I have done that in an ordinary notebook, not with scientific equipment. There are entries about cooking smells and cold weather as well as traffic, so I am not claiming that every bad day was caused by the road. My point is narrower: the proposed complaints process should not require a resident to prove the source of dust before the contractor checks what is happening. A dated report from a resident ought to be enough to prompt someone to inspect the road surface and any vehicle queue.

I spoke to my neighbour Rowan Peake about the plan for road cleaning. This neighbour is not taking part in the examination, and I do not rely on that conversation as evidence of a medical effect. We were simply unsure whether 'as required' means after a complaint, after a visible deposit, or after a measured threshold has been exceeded. Those are quite different arrangements. If the applicant intends to inspect every working day, it should say so in the requirement and say where the inspection record can be seen. If it does not intend that, residents should know before a decision is made.

Cllr Elin Rowe attended the community event in September 2026. I asked there whether the temporary traffic plans would be circulated before each phase rather than only at the start of the project. I understood the answer to be that the contractor would provide updates, but nobody could say how far ahead. I may have misunderstood, which is why a written answer would help. A generic promise to engage with residents does not tell a parent whether tomorrow morning's crossing will be open. It would also help people who do not use social media if notices were available by more than one method.

There is a wellbeing issue separate from the conditions I have described. Even on days when I feel well, uncertainty about access and dust makes it harder to plan ordinary things. I have slept poorly while trying to make sense of the construction timetable. I do not ask the Inspectors to treat poor sleep or worry as a prediction of illness. I mention them because clear, usable information is itself a reasonable mitigation measure. It is cheaper to tell people accurately what will happen than to leave them trying to interpret a technical drawing after the route has changed.

Could the applicant please provide a short table for each construction phase showing the expected HGV route, working hours, any school-time crossing arrangements, the person or team responsible for inspecting dust and mud, and the action that follows a failed inspection? Please also state how a complaint made in the evening is logged and when a reply can be expected. A shared project mailbox would be useful, but it should be accompanied by a way to report an urgent obstruction when the site office is shut.

I support a fair assessment based on evidence. I am not asking for my family's circumstances to replace that evidence, or for the applicant to promise there will be no inconvenience at all. I am asking the Examining Authority to check that the measures relied upon in the air quality and transport assessments are written down clearly enough to be delivered and checked. Without that, residents are being asked to trust an arrangement we cannot yet see.

Further representation on health and air quality — Bracken Mere Freight Link

I am writing again because the practical questions in my earlier representation are closely connected with health. I have lived in Wrenford for more than 20 years, and I know that not every dusty day is caused by the proposed works. My concern is that the assessment treats a short period of disruption as manageable without showing clearly what happens for households where even a short period matters. I ask that this be read alongside my earlier comments about inspections, evening complaints and the proposed route for construction traffic.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma and chronic migraine. I use a beclometasone preventer inhaler every day and keep a salbutamol reliever inhaler for symptoms. This is not a request for the Examining Authority to make a medical judgment about me. It explains why I need to know what the dust controls will actually be, rather than just being told that dust will be minimised where practicable. A lorry leaving mud on the road, or a dry stockpile beside a used footpath, may be a small event in a construction log. For someone trying to get through an ordinary day, it is not necessarily small.

My child, Ash Fenwick, is 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Changes to a familiar journey can be difficult, particularly when they happen without warning. On some mornings the walk past the proposed haul-route junction is the only straightforward way for us to get where we need to go. I am not saying the application must preserve every existing journey unchanged. I am saying that notices of temporary closures should reach residents before a closure starts, should say whether a pedestrian route is still open, and should be understandable without having to search several technical documents. An update posted only after the barriers are in place is too late for a family setting off early.

Dr Iona Vale at Wrenford Respiratory Practice has advised me to pay attention to periods of visible dust and to follow my existing treatment plan. I do not offer that advice as expert evidence on the applicant's modelling: it concerns my own circumstances. I have not asked the practice to take part in this examination and do not expect the Examining Authority to contact anyone there. What I can say from experience is that being told to stay indoors is not a complete answer. People still need to go to school, work, shops and appointments. The assessment should therefore explain how exposure will be prevented at the source, not rely on residents changing their lives around the site.

At the community event, Cllr Elin Rowe asked whether a resident would be able to find out on the same day that a dust complaint had been investigated. I thought that was a fair question. The answer I heard described a complaints process, but I could not tell whether it covered evenings and weekends. I would welcome one project mailbox, such as brackenmere@larkhaven-infrastructure.example, for routine reports, with a separate means of reaching the duty team when a pavement is blocked or mud has made a crossing unsafe. A mailbox by itself is no use if nobody checks it until Monday.

My neighbour Rowan Peake, who is not making a representation, mentioned seeing dust hang over the lane after vehicles used the verge last spring. I cannot verify its source and I am not presenting that conversation as monitoring data. It did make me look more carefully at the proposed wheel-wash arrangements. The applicant should say who records a failure, how long vehicles are stopped while it is fixed, and where residents can see a summary of incidents. If a measure is relied upon to reach an air-quality conclusion, it should be possible to check whether that measure was working on a particular day.

I am also concerned about the distinction between average conditions and the short periods when several activities happen at once. The documents discuss construction traffic, earth movement and dry weather, but I have not found a plain explanation of what changes if those conditions coincide near homes. Would work be paused, or would there simply be another inspection? Please put any trigger levels and the required response together in one accessible place. It would help to explain who has authority to stop an activity and how that decision is recorded. Residents should not have to guess whether an inspector's observation has led to any action.

I have had poor sleep while reading about the scheme, and the uncertainty has made me anxious. I am not asking for those feelings to be treated as a diagnosis or as proof of an air-quality effect. They are part of why timely information matters. If a monitor shows an exceedance, a short public note saying what happened, what was done and whether it is still happening would be more reassuring than a general promise to investigate. Equally, if a complaint turns out not to be related to the works, please say so and explain how that conclusion was reached.

Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd may well be able to carry out this project without the impacts I fear. My point is that the draft arrangements need to be specific enough for residents and the Examining Authority to test that claim. I ask for clear commitments on inspections, vehicle cleaning, temporary pedestrian routes, notification, incident records and out-of-hours contact. That would not remove every inconvenience. It would give affected households a fair way to understand what is planned and what happens when things go wrong.

Mara Fenwick

Health representation concerning the Bracken Mere Freight Link

I am writing separately about health because the practical matters in my earlier representation—vehicle cleaning, inspections, pedestrian routes and complaints—are not just matters of tidiness for my household. I support the request for clearer controls, rather than asking the Examining Authority to decide whether anyone's symptoms were caused by this scheme before construction has even started.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma. I use a beclometasone inhaler every day and carry a salbutamol inhaler for sudden symptoms. I also have migraine with aura and have been prescribed sumatriptan tablets. These are my own circumstances, not a claim that everybody living near the route will have the same response to dust or exhaust. On days when the air seems poor, I find myself checking whether the windows can be opened and whether a walk along the road is sensible. I do not want an answer which simply says that construction effects will be temporary. An effect can be temporary and still be difficult to manage while it is happening.

My child, Ash Fenwick, is 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Changes to a familiar journey can be very hard for Ash, especially where a diversion is announced only after we have left home. Ash receives occupational therapy, and the advice we have been given is to prepare for changes in advance where we can. I am not saying that the applicant must design its whole construction programme around one family. I am asking for notice that is early enough and plain enough for families to use. A map with a coloured line but no indication of when a crossing will actually close is not useful for that purpose.

At the community event, Cllr Elin Rowe asked how residents would hear about short-notice changes. The answer I took away was that updates would be put online. That is helpful as one route, but it should not be the only one. If a delivery or an incident changes the safe walking route that morning, people setting out for school or work need a sign at the relevant junction and a reliable way of checking what has happened. I would prefer a dated weekly notice as well, delivered to affected streets, with a clearly marked section for anything that has changed since the previous issue. Please do not assume that every household will notice a revised document on a project website.

I have spoken to my neighbour Rowan Peake about the proposed access arrangement. That conversation is one reason I think the complaints process needs to distinguish between a report being received and the problem actually stopping. It is easy to picture someone reporting visible dust, being told it has been logged, and seeing the same activity the next day. The published log could give the time of the report, the location in general terms, what was checked, the action taken and the date the matter was closed. It need not identify the household making the report.

I discussed my concerns with Dr Iona Vale at Wrenford Respiratory Practice. I am not submitting a medical opinion from the practice or suggesting that my clinician has assessed the Environmental Statement. I mention the appointment to explain why I have paid attention to what the draft controls actually say. The advice to me was to keep following my treatment plan and to seek medical help if my symptoms changed. That does not tell the Examining Authority what dust level to set; it does explain why an enforceable response to a dust complaint matters to me more than a general statement that good practice will be followed.

The air-quality assessment appears to deal chiefly in averages and predicted concentrations. I understand why those figures are used, and I am not asking for them to be discarded. But I would also like the applicant to explain what happens on a dry, windy day when several activities coincide near homes: vehicle movements, cutting or excavation, and material being taken off site. Who decides that a particular operation should pause? What observation or measurement triggers that decision? Where is it recorded, and how will a resident know that a control has been changed? If the answer is that a site manager exercises judgement, the requirements should say what information that judgement is based on and what minimum action follows a confirmed problem.

There is a difference between my diagnosis and the general worry many of us have about air quality. My sleep has been poor when I think about years of works, and I know other residents feel stressed by the uncertainty. Those feelings are real, but I am not presenting them as additional medical diagnoses. Nor am I claiming that every spell of dust on the existing road comes from Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd. Baseline conditions should be recorded properly so that later complaints can be investigated fairly, including complaints the applicant believes are unrelated to its works.

Finally, please make the out-of-hours contact arrangement usable. A recorded message saying the office will respond on Monday would not help with a Saturday incident. I would like the final documents to identify a staffed reporting route, a response time and an escalation route if the first response does not resolve the issue. The same information should appear on notices at the site entrances and in the weekly updates. Residents should not have to search several management plans to find it.

I am not seeking special treatment. I want the health information above considered alongside practical, testable controls that would help all affected households understand what is happening, report a problem and see what was done about it.

Mara Fenwick

Technical matters relevant to exposure and mitigation

The following comments concern the evidence and controls for the Bracken Mere Freight Link. They are about how the proposed works would operate, rather than any individual circumstances. In particular, the examination needs a clear account of what happens during the busiest construction weeks, not only an assessment of the completed road.

The transport assessment for Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd gives annual average flows and a modelled weekday peak. Those are useful, but they do not show whether a short period of spoil removal, bridge deliveries and ordinary commuter traffic could coincide. The construction traffic management plan should contain a week-by-week forecast of heavy goods vehicle movements for each entrance, split between the morning peak, school opening period, afternoon peak and overnight hours. The forecast should identify whether an empty returning vehicle is counted as a movement. Without that definition, the numbers in the transport assessment and the draft management plan cannot readily be compared.

The routing proposal relies heavily on Merebank Road and the eastern roundabout. The junction modelling should test a temporary lane closure at the roundabout as well as normal operation. A model that assumes uninterrupted access to the compound does not establish what will happen when a delivery is refused or has to wait for a banksman. The applicant should show the space available for vehicles to queue within the site boundary and state the procedure if that space is full. It should also provide the assumed growth factors, turning counts and sensitivity tests in a form that can be checked against the traffic figures in Appendix T3.

The air quality assessment uses monitoring data from before the proposed construction period. I do not suggest that older data must be discarded, but the examination should know how representative it is of present traffic and background concentrations. The assessment ought to show separate construction scenarios for earthworks, haul-road use and the busiest combined traffic period. Dust risk is not adequately described by saying that the contractor will damp down as necessary. The secured plan should specify inspection frequency, the weather trigger for additional controls, wheel-wash operating standards and the point at which work must pause if controls are ineffective. A log of inspections and corrective action should be available for review, with commercially sensitive information removed if needed.

There is a similar issue with noise. A single predicted daytime construction level can conceal a great deal of variation between piling, breaking out hardstanding and routine vehicle movements. The assessment should distinguish those activities and show the plant numbers and utilisation assumptions behind each prediction. It should also explain whether reversing alarms have been modelled and what practicable alternatives will be considered. If quieter equipment is assumed in the assessment, its use needs to be secured in the construction environmental management plan rather than left as an aspiration. Any exception for essential work outside the stated hours should require advance notice, a recorded reason and approval through a defined process.

For the operational scheme, the proposed low-noise surfacing is an important assumption. The documentation should state the specification, where the surfacing starts and ends, and how deterioration will be addressed. The prediction should be tested against a reasonable worn-surface case. Otherwise the headline noise figures may depend on a benefit that reduces during the life of the road. Monitoring after opening would be more useful if the locations, duration, traffic-count method and reporting timetable were fixed before construction starts.

Landscape mitigation also needs to be considered as a maintained feature, not just a drawing showing planting at maturity. The views from the Merebank Road crossing and the public path beside Bracken Mere Wood are particularly relevant to the submitted visual assessment. For each viewpoint, the applicant should provide comparable winter views for the opening year and the design year. The planting schedule should identify minimum stock sizes, replacement periods and who will maintain the screening after the initial establishment period. A requirement to replace failed trees is only effective if failure is checked and recorded.

The drainage strategy says the highway runoff will pass through treatment features before discharge to the reedbed outfall. It would help to see the design storm, climate-change allowance and maintenance assumptions together on one drawing. The assessment should address the effect of a blocked inlet during an intense storm, not simply the performance of a clean system. During construction, temporary drainage and silt controls should be installed before the main earthworks. The final construction sequence should show where water would be held if a treatment feature is not yet available.

Ecology information should be handled carefully without making the design impossible to scrutinise. The submitted material mentions badger signs in Bracken Mere Wood and bats using the wider corridor. Those broad descriptions are sufficient for the public account; exact locations of sensitive breeding or resting places need not be reproduced in a general circulation plan. The public-facing commitments should instead identify the relevant working restrictions, the responsible ecological role and how compliance will be recorded. Any change to a restriction during construction should be documented and justified before work proceeds.

Finally, the draft requirements should make these controls enforceable. Terms such as ‘where practicable’ and ‘as appropriate’ may be unavoidable in places, but each plan should have a named approval stage, measurable actions and a route for reporting departures. The weekly construction update proposed by the applicant could publish planned high-impact activities, traffic changes and monitoring summaries. A shared project mailbox, brackenmere.enquiries@larkhaven.example, could receive questions about those updates; it should not replace the staffed incident route requested above. Taken together, these changes would let the examining authority assess the likely effects on a consistent basis and would give the eventual operator clear obligations to deliver.

Further technical comments on the draft controls

The construction traffic assessment for the Bracken Mere Freight Link relies on a single daily total for heavy goods vehicles. That is not enough to test the busiest period on Ternfield Lane, where the construction access meets the local road. The figures in Environmental Statement Chapter 12 should be broken down by hour, direction and construction activity. An average day could conceal a short period when earthmoving deliveries, staff arrivals and ordinary freight traffic coincide. The assessment should also distinguish vehicles entering the site from vehicles leaving it: the two turning movements have different effects on queuing and visibility.

The junction model in APP-TR-014 uses a background growth allowance but does not clearly explain how traffic displaced from Quarry Bank Road has been assigned. If the model assumes that those vehicles continue on the same route after the new link opens, it may overstate one effect and understate another. Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd should provide a simple comparison of the base case, the construction case and the operational case using the same network boundaries. Each comparison should show the assumed traffic flows, the busiest hour, queue lengths and the extent of any sensitivity testing. This would make it possible to see whether the conclusions depend on a particular routing assumption rather than on the physical capacity of the junctions.

The proposed construction access should not be assessed in isolation from the temporary signal arrangements. A queue reaching the bend north of Bracken Mere would create a different safety issue from a queue contained within the straight section by the site gate. The traffic management plan therefore needs an observable trigger for changing the signal timings or suspending deliveries. It should state where queues will be measured, how often observations will be made during the busiest phases, and who can instruct a change. A commitment merely to ‘monitor traffic’ would be difficult to enforce because it does not identify what happens when the monitoring finds a problem.

There is a similar lack of precision in the landscape material. Viewpoint LV6 appears to have been photographed before the proposed compound levels were fixed. The photomontage shows the completed embankment and planting, but not the compound during the period when stored material and lighting columns could be most visible. A construction-stage visualisation from the same viewpoint would help distinguish temporary effects from those attributed to the finished scheme. The finished-scheme images should also state the assumed planting heights and the year in which screening is expected to become effective. Planting shown at maturity should not be treated as mitigation available on the opening day.

The landscape management plan should describe what happens if planting fails rather than relying only on an initial planting specification. Replacement planting should use an agreed survival threshold and be checked after each growing season. The proposed earth bund beside Ternfield Lane may screen lower-level activity, but the submitted sections do not show consistently whether lighting will be visible above it. Sections at the highest and lowest ground levels would be more useful than a single typical section. The lighting plan should include column heights, aiming angles and a limit for light spill at the edge of the working area.

Drainage is another matter where the drawings and the written assessment need to be read together. Further technical points on the assessment

The same principle should be applied to the highway modelling. The Transport Assessment for the Bracken Mere Freight Link presents a forecast for the opening year and a later design year, but the tables do not make it easy to trace which flows belong to the freight link, which belong to background growth and which arise from development already committed in the area. It should include the junction of Fen Dyke Road and Old Kiln Lane, where a small change in turning traffic may be more important than the change in total daily vehicles.

The modelling should also test a credible busy-day pattern rather than relying only on an average weekday. Freight arrivals are unlikely to be spread evenly through the hour, particularly where vehicles are released from a holding area in groups. Queue lengths reported as averages may therefore conceal short periods when vehicles block an approach or prevent a right turn. The assessment ought to show the maximum modelled queue, the assumed arrival profile and the sensitivity of the result to a modest increase in heavy goods vehicles. If those inputs are not fixed by the proposed operating controls, the model should not treat them as guaranteed.

There is also a distinction between construction traffic and permanent operation which is blurred in the current drawings. The haul route crosses Old Kiln Lane before the permanent access is available, yet the swept-path plans appear to assume the final kerb arrangement. A revised drawing should show the temporary junction as it would actually be used in each phase, including visibility splays, pedestrian space and the position of any waiting vehicles. The location and capacity of temporary settlement measures should be shown on a phasing plan, rather than left entirely to a later method statement. Otherwise the decision maker cannot tell whether the construction footprint can accommodate both the works and the proposed controls.

For the permanent scheme, the discharge calculation should state its rainfall allowance, impermeable area and permitted outfall rate in one place. It should be possible to compare those inputs directly with the drainage drawings. The proposed maintenance schedule needs to identify who will inspect the basins, how sediment will be removed and what access remains available once planting has established. Mere Vale Drainage Board should be consulted on any proposed connection to the Mere Vale Cut, but consultation alone does not establish that the outfall will perform as modelled. They should cover temporary compounds as well as the completed road; a temporary installation operated for many months can still have a material effect. Technical appendix: matters requiring a coordinated design response
Bracken Mere Freight Link — examination representation

The outstanding design choices identified in the preceding representation cannot be assessed reliably as separate matters. The traffic model determines where vehicles are expected to queue; that in turn affects the assumptions used for air quality, the practicality of walking routes and the space available for drainage. Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd should provide one coordinated drawing set and an accompanying schedule of assumptions before the close of the examination. The schedule should identify which parameters are fixed by the proposed development consent order and which are left for approval after consent.

Traffic modelling

The transport assessment uses an opening-year forecast but does not make sufficiently clear whether the same construction traffic assumptions have been carried into the junction assessments, the construction environmental management plan and the air quality calculations. A simple reconciliation table would help. It should show, for each construction phase, the forecast daily heavy goods vehicle movements, the peak-hour movements, the assigned access route and the corresponding model run. If a phase is treated differently in two documents, the reason should be stated rather than left to be inferred.

Particular attention is needed at the proposed connection with Fenwick Bypass and at the eastern end of Merebank Road. A junction can operate within a reported capacity threshold while still producing intermittent queues that obstruct a crossing or delay a bus. The examination would benefit from queue-length outputs, not just average delay figures, for the weekday morning and afternoon peaks. Eastridge County Council should also be given a clear opportunity to confirm whether the proposed sensitivity tests reflect the highway authority's requested growth assumptions. This is a request for a check of the modelling evidence, not an assertion that the predicted flows are necessarily wrong.

The same consistency is needed for abnormal loads and temporary closures. If deliveries are excluded from a peak-hour model because they would be managed by booking slots, the booking restriction should be secured in an enforceable document. A statement that deliveries would 'normally' avoid the peak does not establish what would happen when a delivery is late or when another route is unavailable. The construction traffic management plan should set out who can authorise an exception, how it would be recorded and what measures would keep the footway open.

Walking and cycling design

The drawings should show continuous routes through each construction stage, including temporary diversions. At present the permanent arrangement and the temporary traffic management proposals appear in different parts of the application. It is difficult to establish whether a route shown as available on one plan remains available when a compound entrance is operating on another. A single phase-by-phase plan, at a scale where crossing points and barriers are legible, would resolve much of this uncertainty.

The width of the shared path beside Merebank Road should be stated at its narrowest point, allowing for signs, drainage features and any safety barrier rather than measuring only between nominal corridor boundaries. Where the proposed route crosses an access used by construction vehicles, the design should explain priority, visibility and the circumstances in which a marshal would be required. These are design matters with consequences for the assessment of likely effects; they should not be described only as future contractor choices.

Landscape and visual effects

The landscape drawings show planting along the southern embankment of the Bracken Mere Freight Link, but the assessment relies on screening at a stage when some of that planting may not yet be established. The visualisations and assessment tables should distinguish the opening year from the point at which the proposed planting is reasonably expected to provide screening. Any reliance on early planting should be matched by a delivery commitment, including access for maintenance and replacement of failed stock.

The proposed lighting also needs to be shown with the landscape design. An unlit daytime viewpoint does not demonstrate the appearance of a junction or compound entrance during a winter evening. A plan showing lighting columns, directional fittings and the extent of illumination would allow the claimed reduction of spill to be tested. This need not require an entirely new landscape assessment if the applicant can demonstrate that the existing assessment already uses a suitably cautious lighting scenario.

Drainage and construction phasing

The drainage strategy refers to attenuation near Bracken Mere, while the construction sequence allows temporary hardstanding in parts of the same drainage catchment. The relationship between these two proposals should be made explicit. For each phase, the drainage drawings should identify the surface-water route, the available attenuation capacity, the proposed discharge control and the location of any temporary treatment measure. The final drainage arrangement should not be used as evidence that an earlier construction phase is adequately controlled unless it will already be in service.

Mere Vale Drainage Board should be able to identify the proposed discharge points and maintenance access from the submitted plans without relying on a later detailed design submission. If consent is sought on the basis that outfall positions may move, the permitted limits of that movement and any resulting change to the assessed effects should be stated. Similarly, where a swale is intended to serve both drainage and landscape functions, the drawings should show its working profile rather than treating it as an undefined area of green space.

Policy and securing mechanisms

The National Policy Statement for National Networks requires decisions to be based on the likely effects of the development and the proposed mitigation. A commitment to prepare a plan later is useful only where the application has established the parameters within which that plan must operate. The applicant should therefore provide a commitments register linking each mitigation measure to a drawing, an assessment assumption, a requirement or another proposed control. Entries should say when the measure must be in place and how compliance will be checked.

This would also make the examination more efficient. It would distinguish genuine matters of detailed implementation from design choices that could change the effects assessed. The requested information is not a call for every construction detail to be fixed now. It is a request for the traffic, route, landscape and drainage evidence to describe the same project, on the same phasing assumptions, with any remaining flexibility clearly bounded.

Further technical comments on the Bracken Mere Freight Link

The remaining issue is whether the transport, construction and environmental assessments can be read together without making different assumptions about the same phase of works. For example, the traffic assessment uses an operational junction layout, while the construction material refers to temporary access arrangements that may occupy part of that layout. The application should identify the period for which each arrangement is assumed to operate and show which traffic flows have been assigned to it. This is important for understanding the likely exposure of nearby communities to congestion, idling vehicles and construction activity. It does not require a new model for every minor change to the works programme.

**Traffic and access**

The junction assessment for the B472 Merebank Road and the A618 Fenway Spur appears to rely on average peak-hour flows. The figures should also be presented for the busiest construction month, with a clear account of how deliveries, spoil movements and ordinary freight traffic have been combined. The current description of construction vehicle routing is not sufficiently clear about whether traffic may approach from both directions on Merebank Road. If both approaches are permitted, each should be tested; if one is excluded, the exclusion should appear in an enforceable routing commitment rather than only in explanatory text.

Eastridge County Council's network data may provide a useful check on the base-year flows, but the assessment should state the survey dates, the adjustment factors and the forecast year used for each junction. A sensitivity test would help where the assumed distribution of freight movements materially affects queue lengths. The point is not that a particular threshold has necessarily been exceeded. It is that the examination needs to see whether the conclusions remain sound when a reasonable construction scenario is applied consistently.

The proposed crossing at Reedfold Lane should be shown on a drawing that includes the temporary fencing, visibility splays and any drainage features at the edge of the carriageway. The traffic management plan should state whether temporary signals, banksmen or timed delivery slots form part of the assessed scheme. These measures are sometimes described as options, but an optional measure cannot be treated as the reason an effect is acceptable unless the circumstances requiring its use are specified.

**Air quality and construction sequencing**

The air-quality chapter should be checked against the final vehicle assumptions. Where a junction model forecasts a queue extending past an access, the emissions assessment should explain whether that queue is represented in the traffic inputs or why it would not materially alter the result. Similarly, the earthworks programme should identify whether site preparation at Bracken Mere and road construction along the spur could take place concurrently. Concurrent activity may alter the location and duration of dust-generating works, even if the total volume of material moved is unchanged.

A construction environmental management plan can set out inspection and response procedures, but the assessed dust controls should be identifiable before consent is granted. The register proposed above could distinguish between measures assumed in the assessment, such as surfaced haul routes and covered loads, and additional measures to be selected following routine site inspections. It should also make clear which controls apply before a work area opens, rather than after an issue is recorded. This would allow the examination to judge the project as proposed, while leaving practical day-to-day management to the construction stage.

**Landscape and visual effects**

The landscape drawings show planting near the eastern embankment, but the visual assessment should clarify the height and maturity assumed at opening and at the later assessment year. Young planting should not be treated as an immediate screen. The drawings should also distinguish planting that is integral to the assessed mitigation from indicative planting that may move within the landscape corridor. If earthworks levels or the position of the acoustic barrier remain flexible, the permitted range should be shown on sections from the viewpoints used in the assessment.

There is a related question about lighting. The application should state which parts of the link would be lit during operation, which would have temporary construction lighting, and the hours or triggers assumed for each. An outline lighting strategy is useful only if its parameters correspond to the effects assessed. A commitment to minimise light spill is not a substitute for drawings or specifications showing the maximum extent of the installation. The same principle applies to vegetation removal: the assessment should identify the reasonable worst-case extent of clearance, even if the precise construction boundary is refined later.

**Drainage and ground conditions**

The drainage strategy should reconcile its catchment plan with the highway design drawings. The two documents appear to use different boundaries for runoff from the southern compound, making it difficult to tell which outfall has been assessed for the initial construction phase. Mere Vale Drainage Board should be able to verify the proposed discharge rates and maintenance access against one consistent plan. Where a temporary outfall is required, its capacity, period of use and method of removal should be stated rather than deferred entirely to a contractor's method statement.

The attenuation calculations should identify the design storm, climate-change allowance and assumed impermeable area for each phase. They should also explain how runoff would be managed before the permanent ponds become available. The assessment need not prescribe every pipe size, but it should demonstrate a workable sequence without relying on a permanent feature that has not yet been built. Any exceedance route should be shown at a scale that allows the relationship with the highway and construction areas to be understood.

**Requested clarification**

For the Bracken Mere Freight Link, the most useful response would be a short, coordinated schedule identifying the drawings and assessment inputs that control each phase. It should list construction traffic maxima, permitted routes, access arrangements, clearance limits, lighting parameters and temporary drainage measures, with cross-references to the proposed requirements. That schedule would address the uncertainty more effectively than separate statements that each topic can be settled later. It would also allow the Examining Authority to test whether the flexibility sought in the application remains within the effects actually assessed.

Further comments on the transport, drainage and landscape assessments

These comments concern the technical assumptions in the application for the Bracken Mere Freight Link. They do not ask the Examining Authority to select a particular engineering design, but they do ask that the design and its limits are clear enough to be examined and, later, enforced. A forecast benefit in the Transport Assessment is not itself a control on what happens during construction.

Traffic modelling

The Transport Assessment uses an average weekday to describe the existing network. That is a useful starting point, but the sensitivity tests need to show what happens when a lane restriction on Merebank Road coincides with the seasonal peak in freight movements. The junction tables in APP-078 show spare capacity at the Aster Junction in the central case, while the accompanying narrative acknowledges a longer queue in the higher-growth case. The queue results should be presented for each approach, not only as a junction-wide average. Otherwise a substantial delay on one arm can disappear into an acceptable overall figure.

Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd should also reconcile the construction programme with the traffic inputs. The earthworks schedule indicates overlapping activity in phases 2 and 3, whereas the vehicle forecast appears to treat the busiest import movements as occurring in separate periods. If that interpretation is wrong, a short note explaining the calculation would resolve it. If it is right, the combined peak should be tested. The same applies to empty return trips: the assessment should state whether these are counted in both the assignment diagrams and the daily vehicle totals.

Eastridge County Council has identified the B6724 as a sensitive diversion route. The proposed Construction Traffic Management Plan refers to preferred routes but does not say what evidence would trigger an alteration to delivery hours or temporary signal timings. It should include measurable thresholds, a procedure for recording complaints and observed queues, and a timescale for changing the arrangements. A monthly summary published after the event is useful for scrutiny, but it cannot substitute for a same-day response to a blocked junction. Temporary stopping near the works access should be treated as a separate scenario rather than assumed to be covered by the normal running model.

Noise and air quality

The assessment of construction noise is based on indicative plant and working areas. That is understandable at this stage, provided the worst credible combination of plant is tested and the eventual contractor cannot adopt a noisier arrangement without further checks. The outline management plan should specify where temporary barriers must be in place before particularly noisy operations begin, how their effectiveness will be checked, and what happens if monitoring shows that the predicted levels are exceeded. Describing barriers as available ‘where practicable’ leaves too much of the mitigation optional.

For air quality, the dust controls ought to distinguish material handling at the main compound from haul-road use and road sweeping at the public highway. Each has a different cause and a different effective response. The application relies on a commitment to visual inspections; it would be more helpful to state the inspection frequency during dry or windy weather and the record to be retained. General concern about pollution is not a substitute for a defined monitoring method, but nor should a modelled annual mean be treated as proof that short construction episodes need no management.

Drainage and flood risk

The Drainage Strategy proposes attenuation before discharge to East Canal Drain. The submitted drawings do not yet make it easy to compare the assumed impermeable area with the areas shown on the construction layout. Temporary surfacing, stockpiles and compound drainage all matter during the period before permanent features are complete. A construction-stage water management drawing should therefore be secured, with the points of collection, treatment and controlled discharge identified for each phase.

Mere Vale Drainage Board should be consulted on the final outfall details, including access for maintenance and the circumstances in which a penstock would be operated. The requirement needs to secure agreement on the relevant technical details, not simply require that the Board is notified. The exceedance route should also be shown on a plan that uses the same levels and boundaries as the approved engineering drawings. At present the flood-risk text and the drainage drawings appear to use different descriptions of the southern low point. That may be a labelling error, but it needs resolving before detailed design is signed off.

Landscape, ecology and reinstatement

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment illustrates screening at establishment and after 15 years. There should also be an intermediate view, because the first few growing seasons are likely to be when earthworks and newly planted bunds are most conspicuous. The planting specification needs clear minimum sizes, replacement obligations and a period of aftercare that starts when each area is planted rather than when the whole project opens. The location of lighting columns should be tested against the night-time views, not only the daytime photomontages.

The ecological material refers to badger activity in Bracken Mere Wood. That is a broad habitat description, not a reason to publish precise protected-species locations in the main report. The relevant point for this examination is whether the proposed working limits, lighting controls and pre-construction checks can be secured and audited. Likewise, the drainage design should be checked against the habitat creation drawings so that a maintenance access strip does not later remove planting counted as mitigation.

Requested outcome

These matters could be addressed through an updated set of consistent drawings, a sensitivity test covering overlapping construction peaks, and requirements with objective triggers for review. The National Policy Statement for National Networks is concerned with both the need for infrastructure and the quality of the evidence used to assess its effects. Approval should not depend on informal assurances that outstanding details will be settled later, when those details determine whether the stated mitigation will actually work.

Further technical points on the Bracken Mere Freight Link

The traffic assessment needs to be read alongside the air quality and noise chapters, rather than as a separate exercise. Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd has used a single set of forecast flows for much of the assessment, but the construction programme contains several periods with quite different demands. Earthworks, material deliveries and the eventual tie-in at the A4178 are not interchangeable. A monthly table showing heavy goods vehicle movements, workforce trips and any proposed road closures for each phase would make it possible to see whether the worst period has actually been tested. Daily averages alone could conceal a short but significant peak at the junctions closest to the works.

The stated construction hours also need clarification. The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan describes normal hours, while allowing exceptions for concrete pours, abnormal loads and traffic-management works. It does not give a reasonable estimate of how often those exceptions may be used. If out-of-hours movements are to be assessed as exceptional, there should be an enforceable limit and a procedure for recording them. Otherwise, the assessment should model a credible busier scenario, including vehicle queuing at the site gates and engines running during unloading. That would provide a sounder basis for the air quality and noise conclusions.

There is a similar issue with the operational traffic forecasts. The junction model reports acceptable average delay at Mere Gate Roundabout, yet the forecast tables show substantial variation between the morning peak, afternoon peak and weekend periods. The assessment should publish the turning movements and queue lengths for each tested period, not just a summary level of service. It should also explain what happens when a delivery vehicle cannot enter the freight site immediately. A queue that extends onto the public road could obstruct general traffic even if the modelled average delay appears small.

Eastridge County Council should be asked to confirm whether the model reflects its current committed highway schemes and the latest available traffic counts. The sensitivity test should include a lower-than-expected take-up of the proposed rail connection, since that would leave more freight on the roads. This is not an argument against rail freight; it is a request for the road network to be assessed against a plausible operating condition, with any necessary mitigation secured before opening rather than deferred to a later review.

The landscape drawings would also benefit from a more consistent set of assumptions. Some visualisations show planting at an established height, while the construction views necessarily show the site before that planting has matured. The Environmental Statement should identify the assumed planting height at opening, year 5 and year 15, and distinguish existing vegetation from proposed screening. Winter views are particularly important where the screening relies on deciduous trees. A wireline or clearly labelled photomontage from the public path on Mere Bank would help show the scale of the embankment, lighting columns and gantry without implying that new planting will screen them from day one.

Lighting is not only a landscape matter. The submitted layout identifies broad lighting zones but leaves the final luminaire specification to detailed design. The assessment should set maximum column heights, light spill limits at the site boundary and hours for non-essential lighting. A contour drawing showing predicted illuminance outside the Order limits would be more useful than a statement that the scheme will follow good practice. The controls should apply to temporary construction compounds as well as the permanent freight yard. They should also specify how complaints will be checked and what adjustments can be made if measured spill exceeds the approved limits.

On drainage, the proposed attenuation basins appear to have been sized using a design storm and an allowance for climate change, but the drawings do not make the exceedance routes easy to follow. The application should show where water goes if an inlet blocks or a storm exceeds the design capacity. In particular, the relationship between the basin outfall, the low section of Fen Lane and the existing ditch network needs to be legible on one plan with levels. Mere Vale Drainage Board should have an opportunity to confirm the assumed discharge rate and maintenance access before the detailed drainage scheme is approved.

The construction drainage proposals deserve the same attention. Stockpiles, temporary haul roads and stripped ground may create different runoff conditions from the completed scheme. The Code of Construction Practice should require inspection of silt controls before forecast heavy rain and after significant rainfall, with a recorded remedy where a measure fails. It should identify who can stop a discharge and how quickly replacement materials can be brought to site. These are practical details, but without them the commitment to prevent sediment entering watercourses is difficult to enforce.

The ecology material notes badgers in Bracken Wood and foraging bats along the wider Mere Vale corridor. Those are broad habitat descriptions, not reasons to publish precise locations in the public examination material. The useful planning question is whether construction lighting, vegetation clearance and the final drainage layout can be carried out within the assessed limits. If design changes are proposed later, the ecological checks should be updated before works start, and any revised mitigation should remain compatible with the drainage and lighting controls rather than being approved in isolation.

Finally, the requirements should make clear which documents have legal effect. There are references to an outline traffic plan, an outline drainage strategy and a framework landscape plan, but the wording does not always say which version governs if drawings are revised. A schedule of approved document numbers, together with a requirement for written approval of phase-specific plans, would reduce that uncertainty. Monitoring should have defined triggers and responses: for example, what happens if traffic queues exceed the assessed length, if a drainage inspection identifies sediment leaving the site, or if boundary light levels are above the approved limit. The Bracken Mere Freight Link can be assessed on its merits only if the tested assumptions are carried through into workable, enforceable controls.
