I would also like advance notice of any night work and a clear process for exceptional deliveries. The outline document says residents will be informed “where practicable”, which could mean almost anything. Notice should say what is happening, how long it is expected to last and whom to contact if conditions on the ground differ from the plan.

I do not expect the examination to eliminate every worry I have, or to treat my family's circumstances as a substitute for the evidence. My health is affected by poor air on some days, and I want the forecasts tested against the times and places where people will actually be exposed. If permission is granted, conditions and requirements should be specific enough to make mitigation happen before problems build up, rather than leaving residents to argue about the meaning of an outline plan afterwards.

Mara Fenwick

Supplementary health representation — Bracken Mere Freight Link

I am adding this note because, after reading the applicant’s latest air quality response, I do not think my earlier comments explained clearly enough why the timing of exposure matters to this household. I understand that the examination must assess the scheme against the applicable standards, not against one person’s experience. Even so, the averages in a table do not show what it is like to open the front door when a queue of HGVs is moving slowly past, or to walk home beside that queue.

I have been diagnosed with asthma and migraine. I use a prescribed salbutamol inhaler when needed and a beclometasone preventer inhaler each day. I mention these details so the Examining Authority understands why I have asked about short periods of dust and exhaust, not because I am asking it to make a medical finding. At an appointment with Dr Iona Vale of Wrenford Respiratory Practice, I was advised to keep track of occasions when breathing symptoms followed time outdoors. That record is for my own care; I have not enclosed it, and I do not suggest that it proves the freight link caused any existing symptoms.

My child, Ash Fenwick, aged 11, has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Changes to the usual walk and unexpected loud traffic can be difficult for my child. If a footway is closed with little notice, simply saying that another route is available does not deal with how that change works in practice. I would welcome a requirement for temporary routes to be marked before a closure begins, with information given in plain language and enough time for families to plan. That is a practical request about access, rather than a request for the examination to consider my child’s care arrangements.

The applicant, Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd, says the modelled annual concentrations remain below the relevant objectives. I have read that point. What I cannot work out from the response is whether the construction assessment tests a still morning, several vehicles waiting at the temporary junction and plant operating nearby at the same time. Those are the circumstances residents have described, but the answer seems to discuss each activity separately. Please could the applicant identify the assumptions about queuing, idling and the hours of the busiest deliveries in one place, instead of referring residents across several appendices.

I am particularly concerned about the proposed monitoring trigger. The document refers to reviewing controls if complaints are received, but a complaint made after an unpleasant morning cannot prevent that morning’s exposure. There should be a named person responsible for checking the agreed measures on site, a record of what was found and a clear route for changing the working method promptly. I am not asking for a promise that there will never be dust. I am asking what happens when the forecast and the conditions at the site boundary do not match.

At the community event, Cllr Elin Rowe asked whether the haul route signs would go up before the first substantial deliveries. I understood the answer to be yes, although the written plan still describes some signs as being provided “as necessary”. I would prefer the requirement to say which signs are needed from day one. My neighbour Rowan Peake, who is not submitting a representation, also raised the problem of drivers following a sat-nav through the residential streets. I have included that conversation only to explain why I looked again at the routing plan; it is not evidence of how many drivers will do so.

There is a similar gap in the discussion of walking routes. Eastridge County Council’s comments deal with the formal crossing points, but the crossing nearest the proposed works is not the only place people encounter the traffic. On school mornings people also wait where the pavement narrows beside the old boundary wall. A person standing there for a few minutes may be close to stationary engines even if the journey as a whole is short. Could the applicant show, on one readable plan, the pedestrian diversions, the likely HGV waiting areas and where any air quality checks would actually take place? I do not want a monitoring point chosen only because it is convenient to install equipment.

I have lived in this area for over 20 years and know that poor air and road noise did not begin with this application. Nor can I separate every headache or night of poor sleep from everything else going on in life. My wellbeing is affected by the uncertainty, especially when dates for disruptive work change. These are ordinary descriptions of how I feel, not substitutes for the technical assessment. They are why reliable notice and a contact who can act on a report matter to me.

Finally, I ask the Examining Authority to look at how the construction traffic plan, air quality controls and complaints procedure fit together. If each document says that the detail will be settled in another document later, residents cannot tell what protection is being examined now. A condition should identify the minimum measures, the point before work starts when they must be in place, and how a failure will be reported and corrected. If the evidence shows that a different measure is better, I am willing to read it. What I need is an answer specific enough to check against what happens on the ground.

Mara Fenwick

Supplementary health representation — Bracken Mere Freight Link

From: Mara Fenwick
Applicant: Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd

I am adding this note because the questions about dust and traffic emissions can sound rather abstract when read alongside the tables. I support the request in my earlier representation for controls that can be checked on the ground. This note explains why the timing of those controls matters in our household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat my experience as an air quality survey, and I do not suggest that every day when I feel unwell is caused by the proposed scheme.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma. My current treatment is a budesonide preventer inhaler twice daily and a salbutamol reliever inhaler when needed. Dr Iona Vale at Wrenford Respiratory Practice has advised me to pay attention to changes in symptoms during periods of poor air quality. I have not enclosed my medical records: they would not tell the Examining Authority what will come out of a particular lorry or where dust will settle. They do explain why an answer of “we will investigate if residents complain” is less reassuring than a clear measure put in place before work begins.

My child, Ash Fenwick, is 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Unexpected changes to the usual journey and loud activity close to home can be difficult for my child to manage. I know that a construction site cannot operate silently. What would help is a reliable programme of works, notice of changes and a route for getting a practical answer when the programme is not followed. A leaflet delivered after an activity has started is not advance notice. Nor is a web page helpful on its own if it is not kept up to date.

For context, we live at 14 Tern Rise, Wrenford, WZ7 4LP, near the route shown for construction vehicles on the applicant's plans. The address is given so that my comments can be understood geographically; I do not want it printed in the public version. The assessment appears to use averages for vehicle movements, but the experience outside a home is also affected by short periods when several vehicles arrive together. I would like the applicant to say whether its proposed controls cover those short periods, including idling while vehicles wait to enter the works. Please do not read this as a request to remove necessary deliveries. It is a request to explain where they will wait and who will intervene if the agreed arrangement is not working.

The dust management wording says that activities can be adjusted according to conditions. I would find it easier to understand if the applicant set out what observation triggers an adjustment, who records it, and how quickly action follows. Is there a named site role with authority to stop or change a dusty activity? Will the log distinguish a complaint received from a complaint resolved? It matters whether a resident can later see that an issue was checked, rather than being told only that the contractor received it. A simple record of dates, location, weather, action and outcome would be more useful than a general assurance that best practice will be used.

I have felt anxious about getting my child to school when the roads are busy, and my sleep has been poor while trying to understand the changing programme. Those are descriptions of how I feel, not additional diagnoses and not measurements of pollution. I mention them because the complaints process should be usable by somebody who has an immediate problem, not just somebody who has time to work through a long technical document. Please provide a telephone route as well as an online form, with information on when each is monitored. A generic mailbox such as complaints@brackenmere.example would be sensible if it is actually checked and the published procedure says when to expect a reply.

At the community event, Cllr Elin Rowe asked how residents would know about temporary changes to the haul route. I thought that was a useful question. A neighbour, Rowan Peake, mentioned having missed a previous notice about unrelated roadworks; I am not offering that conversation as evidence against this applicant, and my neighbour is not taking part in the examination. It simply reminded me that a notice system needs to reach people who do not routinely check a project website. Could notices be delivered to affected streets as well as posted online, and could the applicant say how far in advance that would normally happen?

I have lived in this area for over 20 years. There have been busy spells before, and I am not arguing that any increase in traffic automatically makes a development unacceptable. My concern is that the construction traffic, dust plan and health discussion must describe the same working arrangements. If one assessment assumes vehicles will not queue beside homes, the traffic plan needs to show where they will queue instead. If that place changes, the effects should be reconsidered before the change is made. Eastridge County Council may be able to check the highway arrangements, but residents also need a way to report what is happening at the gate on an ordinary working day.

I would be grateful if the Examining Authority could ask for a single, plain-language explanation of the measures that will apply from the first day of construction. It should say what is fixed by the consent, what can be altered later, who approves an alteration and how residents will be told. My hope is to be able to check the applicant's promises against a dated programme and a usable contact procedure. I am willing to consider evidence that the effects will be smaller than I fear, but I need the proposed safeguards to be specific enough to assess now.

Supplementary health representation – Bracken Mere Freight Link

From: Mara Fenwick

I am writing again because the explanation of what will happen at the construction gate still does not tell me what residents should expect on a normal weekday. My earlier comments were mainly about the hours and the route. I want to explain why the difference between a quiet day and a day with queuing lorries matters in my household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to assume that every construction vehicle will cause a health problem, but I do ask that the assessment deals with the people who are already affected by poor air.

I have diagnosed asthma and use a salbutamol inhaler when my breathing worsens. I also take a daily steroid preventer. These are not new concerns raised just because of this application. Dr Iona Vale at Wrenford Respiratory Practice has advised me to pay attention to days when dust and exhaust fumes are noticeable. I am not submitting my medical records, and I do not think residents should have to do that before the applicant explains how dust at the gate will actually be controlled.

My child, Ash Fenwick, is 11 and has a diagnosed sensory processing disorder. Unexpected noise and changes to the usual walk can be particularly difficult. I understand the traffic plan may be adjusted during construction, but a notice put up after a change is not much use when a family has already set out. Please could the applicant say how much warning will be given before a planned diversion, and whether the walking route will remain usable when vehicles are being held at the gate? I am concerned about the practical arrangements, not suggesting the scheme is responsible for my child's condition.

At the community event, Cllr Elin Rowe asked whether the proposed monitoring would include the first weeks of construction. I did not hear a clear answer. Rowan Peake, my neighbour, has also noticed vehicles waiting with engines on near the approach road, although that is an observation rather than a measurement of pollution. The air-quality figures supplied by Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd seem to deal with average conditions. What I cannot find is a simple explanation of what happens if several vehicles arrive together, the gate is shut, and dust from the road surface is blowing towards the houses. Saying that an issue can be reported is not the same as preventing it.

Poor sleep and worry about the works have affected my wellbeing, but those feelings are not a medical diagnosis. I would welcome a short, dated procedure setting out who checks dust and idling, what triggers action, and how quickly a complaint will be answered. It should also be clear whether Eastridge County Council checks the road arrangements or whether that is left entirely to the applicant. If there is evidence that the proposed controls work in the busiest periods, please put it where residents can read it, rather than leaving the detail to a later plan.

Mara Fenwick

Further technical points

The Bracken Mere Freight Link assessment should test the construction traffic forecast against the busiest hour, not just the daily average. The junction model for Merebank Road and the B4178 assumes vehicles arrive evenly, while the construction programme shows overlapping earthworks and bridge deliveries in phase 2. A sensitivity run with those movements combined would make the queue estimate more useful.

The dust assessment also relies on the haul route being kept damp. It does not say how that measure would work during a water-use restriction or when freezing conditions prevent spraying. Larkhaven Infrastructure Ltd should set out an alternative control and a measurable trigger for suspending movements.

Finally, the drainage drawings show a temporary compound beside the North Rill channel, but the phasing plan does not identify when its silt controls will be installed. Mere Vale Drainage Board’s comments on that sequence should be provided before the construction management plan is finalised. These are matters for the examination rather than details to defer entirely to the contractor.
